en: Catalogue of the *Xishi Heshang Zhengzong Zan* (Eulogies on the Orthodox Lineage of Master Xishi),

Master Bodhidharma and the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Dajian.
Chan Master Mazu of Jiangxi; Chan Master Shitou of Nanyue;

The Second Fascicle of the Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou,

Chan Master Shoushan Nian, Chan Master Fenyang Zhao,

Chan Master Huanglong Nan, Chan Master Baojue Xin,

Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin, Chan Master Nantang Zhiqing,

Chan Master Xuedou Mingjue, Chan Master Dongshan Cong,
Chan Master Yunju Shun, Chan Master Dajue Lian,
Chan Master Tianyi Hui, and Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben.
Chan Master Yuantong Xiu, Chan Master Datong Ben,
Chan Master Xuefeng Hui, and Chan Master Yuedang Chang of the Guiyang School.
Chan Master Shandao Danyuan of Mt. Gui; Chan Master Zhizhong of Yangshan;

Catalogue (End) Hymns in Praise of the Five Houses of the Orthodox Lineage Hymns in Praise of the Five Houses of the Orthodox Lineage with Preface

Those who wander at the gate of the Sage find it difficult to speak. These are merely the arguments of women and children within the inner chambers, whose soft red shoes and light silk slippers fear the pain of treading upon the ground;
how could they possibly suffice as a method for studying the Dharma? For the family of patch-robed monks, this is the crown of all sages.
A single pivot of the profound is turned, flipping over the iron mask so that even one’s own father does not recognize it. To manifest a single mechanism is like [the roar of] a great...
A mass of fire; a single word issued from it is like a raw iron stake—there is no place for you to draw near, no place for you to gnaw upon.
Probing the ancient and the modern with needle and scalpel, life itself is a fatal illness. What saint can be praised? What gate can one roam through?
What words can be avoided? Speaking all day long, one exhausts the Way; though one's words fill the world, there is no fault in the mouth. Whether praising or disparaging, [it is thus].
Whether suppressing or exalting, he exhaustively reveals the profound mysteries. His praise does not serve as an incentive for moderation; his censure does not stem from a desire to ruin the humble.

His suppression is not directed at the upright, and his exaltation is not merely the promotion of the virtuous. He repairs the disfigured and fills the amputated; he truncates the crane and extends the duck.

Employing unconventional methods and applying them in unexpected ways, every step provides a path for self-realization. Would anyone willingly accept shackles and cages, content to remain a petty man? Thus says this ignorant student.
Yelu: With a slender staff he carries the moon; with a tattered hat he encloses the clouds. He has wandered through rivers and lakes for nearly fifty years.

Although his eyes have penetrated the barriers, they are not yet fully clear; and while his words regarding ultimate truth are not yet perfectly precise, he has nonetheless caught a glimpse of the boundaries where the ancients fell short.
To attempt to embroider the great void with five-colored patterns would seem to be an overestimation of one's strength.

The preceding [remarks] involved praise and censure, as well as suppression and exaltation; they await the "Golden Scalpel" to scrape away the film so that those words which startle the crowd may be further elucidated.
Nevertheless, how could the eyebrows of Cuiyan avoid trailing on the ground?
In the year Jiayin of the Baoyou era, the Bhikṣu Shao Tan of Western Sichuan respectfully wrote this at the Fushan Chamber on Mount Lingjiu.
The First Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma, was the son of King Xiangzhi of South India; his clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. Because...
When the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, arrived in this kingdom while traveling to convert beings, the King offered him a priceless jewel.
At that time, the King had three sons. Desiring to test what they had attained, the Patriarch took the offered jewel and asked the three princes:
"This jewel is perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal it? The eldest son replied: "This is but a worldly treasure; it is not yet sufficient."
Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. This light of the world is not yet supreme; among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This clarity of the world is not yet supreme; among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme.
The radiance of this jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it. Once discerned, [it illuminates all].
This being done, one immediately recognizes it as a pearl. Once it is known to be a pearl, its preciousness becomes clear. If its preciousness were self-evident, the jewel would not be a jewel;
if its nature as a pearl were self-evident, the pearl would not be a pearl. That a pearl is not a pearl by itself means that it must rely upon the "wisdom-pearl" to distinguish the worldly pearl.
That a jewel is not a jewel by itself means that it must rely upon the "wisdom-jewel" to clarify the Dharma-jewel. Thus, the Master possesses—

When the Way is present, its treasure immediately manifests; when sentient beings possess the Way, their mind-treasure is likewise so. The Venerable One praised his eloquence and wisdom, changing his name to Bodhidharma.
After Xiangzhi grew weary of the world and passed away, he subsequently left the household life. The Master subdued the six schools: first, the School of Characteristics;
second, the School of Non-characteristics; third, the School of Samādhi and Prajñā; fourth, the School of Precepts and Conduct; fifth, the School of No-... [text ends]
He attained [the fruit]. The sixth was named Śānta. Later, he encountered King Heterodox-View (Vilomadarśana), who disparaged the Triple Gem.

A disciple of his, named Prajñāgupta, went secretly to the king’s presence and extensively expounded the essential points of the Dharma, engaging in a series of cross-examinations and inquiries. The Master [Śānta] knew from afar that Prajñāgupta had fallen into error regarding the meaning;
he immediately told Pāṭaliputra, "You must rescue him quickly. Pāṭaliputra replied, "I pray you lend me your supernatural power. As soon as he spoke, clouds arose.
"Your subordinate arrived before the King and stood there in silence. At that time, the King was in the midst of questioning Zongsheng;
suddenly seeing Louti arrive riding upon the clouds, he was so startled that he forgot his questions and answers. He asked: 'One who travels through the void—is this right or wrong? He replied:"
"I am neither heterodox nor orthodox; rather, I come to rectify both the orthodox and the heterodox. If Your Majesty’s mind is upright, I shall have neither heterodoxy nor orthodoxy.

Although the King was struck with wonder, his arrogance continued to burn fiercely, and he immediately banished Zongsheng. Latide said, "Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you banish this śramaṇa?
Though I lack understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me to the test. The King asked in anger, "Who is the Buddha? He replied:
He said, "To see one's nature is to be the Buddha. The King asked, "Do you, Master, see your nature? He replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside?
He replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning? I do not see it now.
He replied, "You are seeing its functioning right now; it is simply that you yourself do not see it. The King asked, "Does it exist within me? He replied, "If Your Majesty were to act—"
"It is used; there is nothing that is not used. If the King does not use it, its substance is likewise difficult to perceive.
The King said, "When it is being used, in how many places does it manifest? He replied, "When it manifests, there shall be eight [places].
The King said, "Tell me of these eight manifestations. Ratthapāla spoke in verse: "In the womb it is the body; dwelling in the world it is the person. In the eye it is called seeing."
In the ears it is called hearing; in the nose, the discernment of fragrance; in the mouth, discourse; in the hands, grasping; in the feet, running and wandering.

It manifests everywhere, encompassing all within the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*). Those who recognize it know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*saṃjñā*).
Upon hearing these verses, the King immediately attained awakening. He then repented of his former errors and inquired about the Dharma.

Essential Record. One day the Master said: "I observed that within the Great State of China there were those of great capacity. Thus, I crossed the seas and traversed the deserts to seek people for the sake of the Dharma.
Upon his initial arrival, he met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the holy truth? The Master replied, "Vast and empty—there is no sage.
The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not find resonance with this, and so...
Breaking off a reed, he crossed the river and arrived at Shaolin. There he sat facing a wall for nine years. He found the Second Patriarch amidst deep snow and said to him:
"Cease all external conditions; let the inner mind be free of agitation. When the mind is like a wall, one may enter the Way. Subsequently, he transmitted the robe.
The appended verse says: "I have come to this land To transmit the Dharma and save those lost in delusion. One flower opens into five petals; The fruiting occurs naturally.
Bodhiruci and Huiguang repeatedly administered medicinal poisons. By the sixth attempt, he could no longer be saved.
A prophecy said: "The raft on the Yangtze divides the jade waves; The torches open the golden locks. Five mouths travel together; In ninety years, there is neither 'other' nor 'self.'"
The Master, knowing his life-span had come to an end, wished to return to India. He commanded his disciples to each state their aspirations:
Daofu attained the skin, Zongchi attained the flesh, Daoyu attained the bone, and the Second Patriarch attained the marrow. After the Master entered *nirvāṇa*, he was buried at Mount Xiong’er.
Later, when the envoy Song Yun returned from the Western Regions, he encountered the Master on the Pamir Mountains; he saw the Master returning with a single shoe in hand. [Song Yun] returned.
He reported this to the Emperor. When the tomb was opened, there were indeed found only an empty coffin and a single shoe remaining.
The eulogy states:
"With a prominent nose and a dragon-like countenance, his azure eyes possessed the marks of a celestial being."
He renounced the golden wheel to leave the household life for the Noble Path;
he bestowed precious jewels upon his teachers to withstand their challenges;
from his feet arose clouds; and he drove away his disciples to eliminate the heterodox views of others.
The tongue turns back the surging waves; the ears harmonize with the land as the six patriarchs’ slander arises.
From the Red Land of the Divine Continent to the Middle Kingdom, the roots of the Mahāyāna are joined;
from the Eastern Realm to the Western Heaven, the model for the patch-robed monks is revealed.
Vast and empty, there is no sage; To go against the dragon’s scales is to cross the river with a single reed.
Silently contemplating the mind, one sits in a ghost cave for nine years;
One flower opens into five petals, Releasing courtyard snow that submerges the waist.
Turning poison into ghee, Laughing at the raft crossing the river as it divides the jade waves—
Whether like a wall or like a cliff, How often has this been the "separate transmission outside the teachings"?
To divide the marrow and the skin— Just right for a painful blow from my hand.
Feigning death, he hurriedly took his single sandal and returned. Alas, the people of the Great Tang Empire were all deceived by this barbarian while wide awake!
This was the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, Chan Master Dajian.
The Master’s name was Huineng. He was a native of Xinzhou and his secular surname was Lu. His family was poor, and he supported himself by gathering firewood.

One day, while carrying wood to the market, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he was struck with awe and asked the guest, "What dharma is this?
From whom did you receive it? The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*. It was received from..."
The Great Master Ren of Huangmei then informed his mother and traveled to Huangmei to pay his respects to the Fifth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan. The Patriarch asked, "What do you seek? He replied, "I seek only to become a Buddha.

The Patriarch said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha? He replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could the Buddha-nature be like that? The Patriarch marveled at this.
He then said, "Go and work in the fodder shed. The Master bowed and withdrew. He subsequently took up stones to pound rice. Later, hearing someone recite the verse of Beishou:
"The body is like a Bodhi tree; the mind is like a bright mirror stand. At all times diligently wipe it clean;
do not let it gather dust," the Master immediately requested someone to write his own verse beside it: "The Bodhi tree originally has no tree; the bright mirror likewise..."
It is not a stand. Originally there was not a single thing; where could dust and grime settle? Because the Patriarch bestowed the robe and bowl, he went secretly to Mount Dayu.
The Venerable Ming pursued him, and the Master placed the robe upon a rock, saying, "This robe represents the seal of faith;
can it be contested by force? Ming replied, "I have come to seek the Dharma, not for the sake of the robe. The Master said, "Do not think of good; do not think of evil..."
"Wrong! At such a time as this, what is the original face of Elder Ming before his parents were born? Ming attained great enlightenment.
On the eighth day of the first month of the first year of the Yifeng era (the Bingzi year), the Master arrived at Nanhai.
There he met Dharma Master Yinzong, who was preaching the sutras at Faxing Monastery. He heard two monks debating whether it was the wind or the banner that moved; one said, "The wind moves."
One person said, "The banner is moving. They argued back and forth without ceasing. The Master said, "May worldly people be permitted to interject in such high discourse?
It is simply that the wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind alone. When Yinzong heard this, he subsequently ordained him.
Wei Ju, the Prefectural Governor of Shaoyang, invited him to the Dafan Temple to turn the Wheel of Dharma and to receive the formless precepts of the Mind-Ground. His disciples...
Recorded as the *Platform Sutra*. Zen Master Nanyue Huairang was inspired by Zen Master Shuangfeng An of Mount Song;
he then went directly to visit the Master [Huineng]. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? Nanyue said, "From Mount Song.
The Master asked, "What is it that comes like this? Nanyue said, "To describe it as a thing is not to hit the mark. The Master asked, "Does it still require cultivation and realization?"
[The Master] said: "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, defilement is not permitted. The Master said:
"This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. When Master Qingyuan went to visit him, he asked:
"What must one attend to so as not to fall into stages? The Master said, "What have you been doing? Yuan said, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths.
The Master said, "Then into what stage would you fall? Yuan said, "Since I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what stages could there be?
The Master deeply approved of this. As the Master was about to pass away and intended to go to Xinzhou, the assembly said, "Master, if you depart from here..."
Before long, he returned. The Master said, "Leaves fall and return to their root; when you came, you had no mouth. He then spoke a verse:
"The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the nature of the flowers is suddenly realized, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously attained."
The eulogy says:
The Mind-Teaching of China— among the barbarian tribes of Lingnan,
where not a single character of writing was known— a woman who gathered firewood diligently served her mother.
At Huangmei’s mortar, the husks were pounded out; at Shizhu, he felt his waist grow light.
On the marketplace of Xinzhou, he fell flat on level ground; when his shoulder-pole broke, he knew the firewood was heavy.
The alligator’s eyes gleam and roll; why did Zen Master Chennming fight over robes and bowls?
The breath from the venomous serpent’s mouth is chillingly cold; He reviled Master Yinzong for claiming it was not the wind or the banner that moved.
Having swept away the family wealth of Mount Nanyue until not a single thing remained, He did not even acknowledge the Noble Truths;
He stirred up waves a thousand fathoms high at Qingyuan.
Opening the furnace of the master-craftsman, the village hunter gathers several pieces of refined gold;
he composes a volume of the *Platform Sūtra* within a stinking skin-bag, filling it with many antiquities.
When leaves fall they return to the root; when one comes, there is no mouth. A dead confession is difficult to overturn.
The earth contains all seeds; when rain falls everywhere, they all sprout.

Opening his eyes, he spoke of a dream—the mirror-like clarity of Caoxi for a thousand ages. This is not a mechanism of splitting arrows or cutting off the stream. For one who has been drowned by it, what use can there be?
The Chan Master Mazu of Jiangxi was named Daoyi.
He was a native of Shifang in Hanzhou and belonged to the Ma clan. His appearance was extraordinary; he had the gaze of a tiger and the gait of an ox.

Having received the Dharma from Nanyue, he later returned to his native region of Shu. The people clamored to welcome him. An old woman by the stream said, "I thought there was something extraordinary about you;
it turns out you are merely the little son of Ma Bobei. The Master then said, "I urge you not to return to your hometown;
if you return, the Way will not be accomplished. You old woman by the stream, you call me by my former name. He then returned once more to Jiangxi. [From] Xitian.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, prophesied: "A golden rooster shall release a single grain of millet to offer as sustenance to the arhats of the ten directions.
The Sixth Patriarch said to Nanyue, "After this, a colt shall emerge who will trample the people of the world to death.
When Shigong was a hunter, he passed before his teacher’s hermitage. Upon seeing him, the teacher asked, "Who are you?"
A hunter said, "I am a hunter. The Master asked, "Do you understand archery? He replied, "I understand archery. The Master asked, "With one arrow, how many do you shoot?
He replied, "With one arrow, I shoot one. The Master said, "You do not understand archery. The man asked, "Does the Master understand archery? The Master said, "I understand archery.
[The man] asked, "With one arrow, how many do you shoot? The Master said, "With one arrow, I shoot a whole flock. [The man] said, "Both of us are living beings."
Huiming asked, "Why do you shoot at that flock of birds? The Master said, "Since you know this to be so, why do you not shoot yourself?
Huiming replied, "If you were to command me to shoot myself, there would simply be no place to begin. The Master said, "This fellow's ignorance from kalpas past has been extinguished all at once.
Gong then cast away his bow and arrows and threw himself before the Master to leave the household life. Later, while the Master and Baizhang were walking along, they saw some water.
A wild duck. The Master asked, "Where has the wild duck gone? The Elder said, "It flew away. The Master then pinched the Elder's nose, and the Elder let out a cry of pain.
The Master said, "And yet you say it flew away. Thereupon, the Elder attained realization and went back to his quarters, weeping bitterly.
His colleagues asked, "What is the matter? The Elder said, "Go ask the Master. A colleague went to the Master’s room...
Dongzheng asked, "I do not know what has happened to Attendant Hai that he is weeping; let me go ask the Master. The Master said, "Go ask him yourself.
Dongzheng went with his attendant, and upon returning, he asked about it. Dongzheng laughed heartily. His attendant said, "He was just now weeping."
Now he laughed. Baizhang said, "Just now you were weeping; now you are laughing. When Layman Pang was visiting, he asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
The Master said, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single draught, and then I will tell you.
At these words, the Layman attained realization. Later, while the Master, Baizhang, Nanquan, and Zhizang were admiring the moon together...
The Master said, "At this very moment, how is it? Zang said, "It is precisely the time for cultivation. Zhaozhou said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings.
Nanquan shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "The Sutras return to the Tripitaka; Chan returns to the sea. Only Puyuan alone transcends the mundane world.
Later, he passed away at Letan.
The eulogy says:
With a tiger’s gaze and an ox’s gait, and whiskers like coiled dragons and a face of iron,
he extinguished the heart-essence of Bodhidharma’s Dharma-school.
In accordance with the cryptic prophecy of Prajñātāra:
"The golden rooster shall release a single grain from its beak;
calamity shall fester in secret, and a colt shall trample the people of the world to death—its evil reputation cannot be concealed."
The Deer-Shooting Seal at Stone Gong dispels ignorance;
the Wild Duck leads Baizhang as he twists his nose-tip and sucks in the river-mouth. [Zhu/tu] He kills Master Pang.
The mechanism for playing with the moon;
The pit buries eighty-four people, all wishing for the same—*alululu*. Forming a ball like a broken furnace, seven thousand *li* of flies scurry back and forth upon its ridge.
Called a "horse" by others, the winnowing basket has a family of its own.
With empty hands, he tapped the true pulse of Caoxi; throughout antiquity and the present, lineages have branched out like surging waves.
Linji attained the heart of the Way and his descendants have transmitted the lamp in succession.
I bow my head to the Great Dharma King of True Emptiness—vast and boundless, such that the people can find no words to praise him. I seek to trace his traces.
It was because of this. The Master Shitou of Nanyue was a successor to Qingyuan;
his name was Xiqian. He was a native of Duanzhou and surnamed Chen. While he was still a layman, he constantly felt weary of his local mountain villages.
The people were engaged in many licentious sacrifices. [Dongshan] would immediately seize their oxen and destroy the shrines before returning.

The elders of the district could not restrain them. Shishuang Qingyuan sent a letter to Nanyue, saying: "Once you have delivered this letter, return quickly. I have a small adze for you to go and dwell in the mountains.
When the Master arrived there, he did not present the letter; instead, he asked: "I do not admire the various sages, nor do I value myself..."
"How is it at that moment? Huairang said, "Your question is too high, my son. Why not ask about what is below?
The Master said, "I would rather sink forever in saṃsāra than seek the liberation of the sages. Huairang then ceased speaking. When the Master returned, he asked the original question again:

"Not long after you left, did you successfully deliver the letter? The Master replied, "The message was not conveyed, and the letter was not delivered. At the time of departure, I received your blessing."
"Even so, I still grant you this adze. Now, please. Yuan extended one foot. The Master prostrated himself.
On another day, he asked, "Does the Great Master of Caoxi recognize you, Master? Yuan said, "Do you recognize me? The Master said, "I recognize him; how could I not recognize him?
Yuan said, "Though there may be many horns, a single unicorn is enough. One day, the Master dreamed that he was riding with the Sixth Patriarch on a...
A tortoise was swimming in a deep pond. Jueyuan remarked, "The numinous tortoise represents wisdom; the pond represents the ocean of sagehood.

I and the Patriarch are riding together upon this numinous wisdom, swimming within the ocean of sagehood. During the Tiānbǎo era, to the east of Nán Temple on Mount Héng, there was a rock shaped like a platform.
[Deshan] built a hut upon it and was thus known as Shítóu Wúshàng (Stonehead Monk). Dèng Yìnfēng...
He took his leave of Mazu. Mazu asked, "Where are you going? Feng said, "I am going to Shitou. Mazu said, "The path at Shitou is slippery.
Feng replied, "Carrying my staff and wood with me, I perform my art wherever the stage appears.

He then went to the Master’s place, circumambulated the meditation seat once, struck the ground with his monk's staff, and asked, "What is the essential principle? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! Feng was speechless. He then returned.
He reported this to the Patriarch. The Patriarch said, "Go back and ask him again; wait for him to give an answer, and then you must let out two sighs.
Feng went back again and asked as before; the Master let out two sighs, and Feng was once more speechless. He returned and reported this to the Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "I told you that the path at Shitou is slippery. One day, Yaoshan was sitting on a rock. The Master saw him and asked, "Are you here?"
"What are you doing? Guishan replied, "I do nothing. The Master said, "If that is so, then you are sitting idly. Guishan said, "To sit idly is precisely what I am doing.
The Master said, "You say you do nothing; what is it that you do not do? Guishan said, "Even the thousand sages do not know it. The Master then praised him with a verse:
"From the beginning we have lived together, yet I did not know your name. Spontaneously we move along together."
Simply practicing thus—those of ancient sagehood could not yet recognize it; how could those of a casual or hasty disposition possibly understand it? A monk asked, "What is Chan?

He replied, "A common brick. "What is the Way? He replied, "A piece of wood. The Master composed the *Cantong qi* (Token of the Agreement with the Ultimate) and the *Ca'an ge* (Song of the Grass Hut), which were circulated throughout the world.
The eulogy says:
His karmic affinity was born in Duanduan; he received ordination at Caoxi.
The venom of the "tortoise-nose" snake sought to harm others; the heart of the "broken-mirror" bird was intent on devouring its mother.
Tired of the common people’s many licentious sacrifices, he demolished the shrines and seized the oxen to return them;
He corresponded with a monk of Mount Yue, and taking up his axe, he departed for the mountains.
Though the horns of the herd are many, a single unicorn is enough; Yet who among you can truly recognize Qingyuan?
In a deep pond, they share a single tortoise as they swim; In the end, who has ever dreamed of the Sixth Patriarch?
In a moment of crisis, many find slippery paths; Pushing Yinyong, he was left with his hands bound, falling over a precipice.
Living together, they did not know each other’s names; Facing Yaoshan, they slept soundly while indulging in delirious talk.
Death is close at hand—this is my plan; Sitting like a solid rock, clouds arise.
In response to Zen, he speaks as it comes; He hurls green bricks like rain.
Under the pine trees, he sings a leisurely song; The "Song of the Thatched Hermitage" does not fall within the bounds of the musical scales.
Amidst the chaotic mountains, he let out several wild cries. What words are these from the *Cantong qi*?

Alas, by the side of Caoxi, a separate branch has sprouted—one who, when emotions are forgotten and righteousness severed, gives birth to a grandson of the five rebellious acts and continues the lineage of an unfilial son.
The Chan Master Nanquan Yuan, whose name was Puyuan, was a native of Zhengzhou. His surname was Wang. After first meeting Mazu and attaining awakening, he resided at Nanquan.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Since my youth, Old Teacher Wang has raised a water buffalo. If I intend to pasture it on the east side of the stream, I cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass;
if I intend to pasture it on the west side of the stream, I likewise cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass.
It would be better to simply accept things as they are, yet even this remains entirely unperceived. There is a hermit at a hut at the foot of the mountain, whom people call..."
[The Master] said, "Recently, Master Nanquan has appeared in the world; why do you not go to pay him homage? He replied, "It is not only when Nanquan appears in the world that I would not go;

even if the thousand Buddhas were to arise, I still would not go. When the Master heard this, he ordered Zhaozhou to go and investigate him. Zhaozhou went there and immediately performed a prostration.
The host did not acknowledge him. Zhaozhou walked from west to east, and from east to west; yet the host still did not acknowledge him.

The Governor said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. He then drew down the curtain and returned home. When he related this to the Master, the Master said, "I have always suspected that fellow.
One day the Master went to a village estate; the master of the estate had prepared oil-cakes in anticipation to welcome him. The Master said:
"I, an old monk, usually go about without letting others know. How could you have discerned this so clearly?
The host replied, "Last night the local deity reported that the Master would come today. The Master said, "Wang Laoshi’s cultivation lacks power;
he has been seen by ghosts and spirits. At that time, a monk asked, "Since you are a great *kalyāṇamitra*, why were you nevertheless seen by ghosts and spirits?"
[The Master] looked out. The Master said, "Offer another portion of rice before the local deity. One day, the two head seats of the two halls were quarreling over a cat.
They came to inform the Master. The Master took up a knife, lifted the cat, and said, "If you can speak, I shall save the cat;
if you cannot speak, I shall kill it. Neither could respond. The Master then killed it. That evening, Zhaozhou returned from outside.
The Master brought up the previous story to show him. Zhaozhou took off his sandals, placed them on his head, and went out.
The Master said, "If you had been there, you could have saved the cat. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "Old Wang is selling himself; who will buy him?

At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and said, "I will buy him. The Master said, "Neither as something precious nor as something cheap—how will you buy him? The monk... [remained silent].
[The Master] was without response. A monk asked, "The Master resides in the hall; with what do you provide guidance? The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox;
when I rose at dawn, I had lost the fire. While the Master was performing manual labor in the mountains, a monk asked, "Where does the road to Nanquan lead?
The Master picked up his sickle and said, "This sickle of mine was bought for thirty coins. The monk said, [further questioning].
He did not ask about the *mao* grass sickle; rather, he asked, "Where does the road to Nanquan lead? The Master replied, "I am riding it most joyfully.
Once, while Grand Councilor Lu Xuan was playing double-sixes with someone, he saw the Master and pointed to the dice, saying, "Is it so? Or is it not so?"
Xincai asked, "How is it when departing? The Master picked up a pair of dice and said, "A stinking bone, eighteen.
Lu again asked, "In my home there is a stone slab; sometimes I sit upon it, sometimes I lie upon it. Now I intend to have it carved into a Buddha."
"Can it be obtained? The Master said, "It can. Lu said, "Is it not that it cannot be obtained? The Master said, "It cannot. When the Master was staying at the hermitage, a monk arrived.
The Master told him, "I am going up the mountain to do some work. Wait until mealtime; I will prepare the food, eat my share myself, and send one portion up for you.
After a short while, the monk ate his own portion first, then smashed all the household utensils and sat down upon the Master’s bed.

The Master lay down. The monk waited for him to come, but when he did not return, he went back and saw the Master lying on the monk’s bed. The Master also lay down beside him. The monk then got up and left.
Later, the Master said, "When I lived in the hermitage in the past, there was a clever practitioner;
I have not seen any news of him until now. One day, Lu Xun said to the Master, "Dharma Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; he understands that 'Heaven and Earth and I...'"

"Same root. All things and I are one body. The Master pointed to a flower in the courtyard and said, "Great Officer, when people of this age see this single stalk of a flower, it is as if they were dreaming.
Lu was at a loss for what to say. The Master asked the Dharma Master, "May you lecture on the sutras for me?
The Dharma Master replied, "It would only be appropriate if I were to lecture the sutras for you, and you were to explain Chan for me. The Master—
He said, "One cannot trade gold pellets for silver pellets.
He then ascended the hall and said, "You monks, at eighteen years of age, I, Old Man Wang, understood how to make a living. Is there anyone here now who understands how to make a living? Come forth!"
"I shall deliberate with you; it must be one who dwells among the mountains who can do so. After a long silence, he looked at the assembly, joined his palms, and said, "Take care.

If there is nothing else to attend to, each of you should practice your own cultivation. One day, the lay practitioner Gan-zhi came to serve congee and said, "I request the Master to recite the liturgy.
The Master said, "The lay practitioner Gan-zhi has served congee; I request the assembly to recite for the sake of the 'cat-spirit' and the 'white ox'."
He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, prostrated with his head to the ground, and then departed. When the Master arrived at the kitchen, he smashed the cauldron.
Zàn said:
"Alas! This Old Teacher Wang plants thorns everywhere;
Tending the oxen by the eastern and western streams, the rope is in his hand yet he knows not how to let it go or pull it in.
Slaying the cat before the hall, he secretly stretches the cord—how can right and wrong be distinguished?"
Casting the dice in disorder—those stinking bones, eighteen points, shouted as "wrong," leading one astray.
The thatched sickle, thirty coins bought;
it is neither expensive nor cheap. Who would be willing to bargain for this whole body?
Lost the fire, lost the ox; what is so extraordinary about dwelling in a single room?
Having been seen through by ghosts and spirits, you ate a piece of oil-cake on the farm and met Zhaozhou;
Zhenzhou produces large radishes.
A single flower is like a dream; who says heaven and earth share the same root?
At eighteen, his life’s work was complete—difficult to provide as a model for descendants.
Allowing Lu Xun to carve his name upon the stone while sitting, he followed evil and pursued the heterodox.
For the sake of Gan-zhi, he smashed the rice pot;
when the door opens, let the thief go—though a Buddha were to appear in the world, he would not depart. The Head of Nao-tou Hermitage could not avoid his lingering doubts;
after eating his fill, he indulges in sleep. The clever seeker does not know the news.
Exchanging golden pellets for silver pellets; there is not much to commend in this. One who wishes to act as a truly skillful spiritual friend must be like Baizhang Dazhi Chan Master.
The Master was a successor of Mazu; his name was Huaihai. He was a native of Fuzhou and surnamed Wang.

While attending Mazu for a second time, as he stood in attendance, Mazu looked at a whisk in the corner of his meditation seat. The Master said, "Is it used right here? Is it apart from being used right here?
Mazu asked, "When you open your two flaps of skin in the future, with what will you teach people? The Master picked up the whisk and held it upright. Mazu said, "Is it used right here?"
Setting aside this function, the Master hung the whisk back in its old place. The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout, and the Master immediately prostrated himself.

Later, lay devotees invited him to the borders of Xinwu in Hongzhou to reside at Mount Daxiong. Because the dwelling was situated amidst steep and rugged crags and peaks, it was called "Hundred Fathoms" (Bai Zhang).
After the Master had occupied it for less than a month, seekers of the profound mystery gathered from all directions, including those from Mount Gui and Huangbo.
At the beginning of one day, the Master said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is no small matter.
In the past, when I was struck by Mazu’s single shout, it left my ears deaf for three days. Hearing this, Huangbo involuntarily stuck out his tongue.
The Master asked, "Will you take up the lineage of Mazu in the future? Huangbo replied, "Not so. It is only because of what the Master has just mentioned that I have attained [this realization]."
[He] saw Mazu’s great capacity and great function, yet he did not recognize Mazu. [The Master said,] "If you succeed Mazu, your descendants will later lose their own selves.
The Master said, "One who sees as much as the teacher lacks half the teacher's virtue; only one whose insight surpasses the teacher is fit for transmission.
You possess an insight that far exceeds your teacher's. Huangbo then prostrated himself. Whenever the Master ascended the hall, there was an old man.
He followed the assembly to listen to the Dharma. One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, only the old man did not leave.
The Master asked, "Who are you? The old man replied, "I am no ordinary person. During the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain. Because a student questioned me—"

"Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall under the law of cause and effect, or not? Zhaozhou replied, "He does not fall under cause and effect. Consequently, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.
Now, I request you, Master, to provide a turning word on his behalf, so that he may be liberated from this wild fox body.

The Master said, "Ask the old fellow: 'Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall under the law of cause and effect, or not? The Master said, "He does not obscure cause and effect. The old man [immediately attained liberation].

Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. He prostrated and said, "I have already cast off my wild fox body. I dwell behind the mountain; I venture to request that you provide for me according to the rites for a deceased monk. The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly:

"After the meal, we shall escort a deceased monk. After the meal, the Master led the assembly to a cliff behind the mountain. With his staff, he pried out a dead fox and cremated it according to the Dharma. The record states: The Master asked, "What dharma did that old fellow preach? The fox replied, "I preached that 'the nature of mind is Buddha. The Master said, "That was not the correct principle; it was a slight error. Because of this, you have undergone five hundred lifetimes as a wild fox.

Now, do you still understand the meaning of 'the nature of mind is Buddha'? The fox said, "I understand. The Master said, "If so, recite it for me. The fox immediately spoke in verse: "The nature of mind is Buddha; Buddha is the nature of mind. Since the nature of mind is originally Buddha, Why seek Buddha elsewhere? Having spoken thus, the fox vanished. The Master said, "This is truly the case. If one does not attain realization within the words, one will surely fall into the path of beasts. You must all be careful! (Note: The term *jin-sòng* refers to the funeral rites and transport of a deceased monk.)
The ascetic Maitreya came from Hunan to see the Master and said, "Mount Guishan is extraordinary and sublime; one could gather a community of fifteen hundred there.
The Master said, "I, an old monk, wish to dwell there. Would that be possible? The ascetic replied, "That is not a place for the Master to reside. The Master asked, "Why?

The ascetic said, "The Master is a man of bone, while that mountain is a mountain of flesh. Even if you were to live there, your followers would never reach a thousand. The Master said, "As for me..."
"Is there anyone among the assembly who abides in *nirvāṇa*? Baotuo said, "Wait; let me observe them all. The Master ordered his attendant to summon the First Seat (the head monk).
The Master asked, "What is this man like? Baotuo made him cough and walk a few steps, then said, "This man is not suitable.
He then ordered the Kitchen Steward to be summoned. Baotuo said, "This one is truly the master of Mt. Mushi. That night, the Master summoned [Baotuo].
Daguang You entered the room and instructed him, saying, "My karmic conditions for transformation lie here; this is the sublime realm of Mount Guiyang.

You should reside there, succeed to my lineage, and extensively guide future students. At that time, Huilin heard of this and said, "I, this humble one, am honored to occupy the position of chief disciple;
why should Master You be the abbot? The Master replied, "If you can deliver a single phrase that transcends the ordinary before the assembly, I shall grant you the abbacy."
The Master held it up and pointed to the water pitcher, asking, "You must not call this a 'water pitcher.
What would you call it? Huahua replied, "I cannot call it a 'wooden bucket. The Master did not approve. He then asked Daoyou, who kicked the pitcher over. The Master laughed and said:
"The first seat has lost the mountain itself. Daoyou then went there. The Master established the *Chiqi* (Rules of Purity), praising them as follows:
"A mold of extraordinary caliber; a master craftsman of refined molding."
His gaunt bones stand out like jade carved; his azure eyes are bright as falling stars.
Having shed the wild fox skin, he is no longer ignorant of cause and effect.
Knowing how many times he has been praised and how many times reviled through the ages, he lets the waterfowl fall away for his own advantage. He runs back home to weep once and laugh once.
Jingzhou kicks over the water jar; Fangshan carries his mattock into the thousand peaks.
When Mazu picks up the whisk, The strange horse-bearer buries the green cliffs on level ground.
A lifetime of noseaches— This bone-chilling resentment is not easily dissolved.
For three days his ears were deaf; the poison that entered his heart was so sudden it could hardly be washed away.
Together they roamed the dragon’s lair of evil karma: the younger brother Huangbo was a friend to Pang, together they wrested the fierce tiger and rhinoceros from their womb;
the elder brother Nanquan had the younger brother Zhizang as his companion.
The monastic regulations are orderly and precise; they dig deep pits to trap men.
Their noble lineage continues in succession; they spread vast nets across the heavens.
They perform extraordinary feats of merit, no less than those of Shusun Tong or the "Old Hairy Barbarian. They build ten-thousand-year-old cities and fortresses—who can [resist them]?
In the vicinity [of Nanyuan].
Chan Master Zhaozhou Zhenji was a successor of Nanquan;
his name was Congshen, and he was a native of Caozhou, surnamed Hao. One day, he asked Nanquan: "If..."
"What is the Way? Quan said, "The ordinary mind is the Way. The Master asked, "Can one still direct oneself toward it? Quan said, "To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate from it.
The Master said, "If one does not intend it, how can one know it is the Way? Quan said, "The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing."
To know this is deluded cognition; not to know this is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one truly reaches the Way that is free from doubt, it is like the great void—vast, empty, and open.
How could one forcibly impose distinctions of right and wrong? Under these words, the Master awakened to the principle.
There was a monk traveling to Mount Wutai who asked an old woman, "In which direction does the path to Mount Wutai go? The woman said, "Go straight ahead. The monk then departed.
The old woman said, "What a fine monk! And yet he goes off like that. Later, a monk reported this to the Master. The Master said, "I shall go and put him to the test.
The next day, he went there and asked, "In which direction does the road to Mount Tai lead? The old woman said, "Go straight ahead.
The Master then departed. The old woman said, "What a fine monk! And yet he goes off like that. When the Master returned, he told the monk, "The old woman of Mount Tai—"
"I have thoroughly scrutinized you," he said. A monk asked, "I have long heard of Zhaozhou’s Stone Bridge; having arrived here, I see only a small footbridge.
The Master said, "You see only the footbridge; you do not see the Stone Bridge. The monk asked, "What is the Stone Bridge? The Master said:
He was one who could ride both donkeys and horses. One day, Wang Gong, the military governor of Zhending, brought his sons into the monastery.
As the Master sat there, he asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The King said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Since childhood I have observed the fasts until my body has grown old;
seeing others, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat. The King treated him with even greater reverence. A monk asked, "Does a dog possess Buddha-nature or not?"
The Master said, "No. The monk asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; why then does the dog have none?

The Master replied, "It is because it still possesses the consciousness of karmic afflictions (*karma-vijñāna*). When the Master arrived at Huangbo, Huangbo saw him coming and immediately shut the door to his quarters.
The Master then took a torch into the Dharma Hall and shouted, "Put out the fire! Put out the fire! Huangbo opened the door, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak!"
The Master said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled. Arriving at Zhuyou, he took up his staff and walked from east to west across the Dharma Hall.
Zhuyou asked, "What are you doing? The Master replied, "Probing the water. Zhuyou said, "There is not even a single drop here; what are you probing for?
The Master leaned the staff against the wall and walked away. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master—
It is said: "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Later, Fayan asked Jue Tiezui, "I have heard that Zhaozhou has a story about the cypress tree;
is this true? Jue replied, "The former master did not say such a thing. Do not slander the former master. A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine?
Feng said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom. The monk asked, "And what of those who drink from it? Feng said, "Not..."
[The monk] entered through the mouth. The Master heard this and said, "It cannot enter through the nostrils. The monk then asked, "What of the cold spring in the ancient ravine?
The Master said, "Bitter. [The monk] asked, "What of those who drink from it? He said, "Dead. The monk related this to Xuefeng.
Xuefeng looked toward him from afar, paid his respects, and said, "Zhaozhou is an ancient Buddha; from now on, he will no longer answer questions. Yan Yang asked, "If one brings nothing with them..."
"How is it when you come? The Master said, "Put it down. [Yan] asked, "Since you have brought nothing at all, what is there to put down?
The Master said, "If you cannot put it down, carry it away. Yan attained realization.
The eulogy says:
Zen lies at the edge of the lips; it exhausts the poison of Nanquan within the eyes of the patch-robed monks.
The great void is vast and empty—how could one forcibly impose right and wrong?
The heart of Snow Peak is dead; the cold spring of the ancient ravine is clearly distinguished.
Seeing the Great King, he does not descend from his bed to receive him. To manifest that our school honors the Dharma, there is one who examines the Hermitage Master;
he drags down the curtain and returns, knowing that this old king is suspicious of this fellow.
The *evodia* probes the water; leaning on the measuring line, he takes root.
The *berberis* saves from the fire; opening the gate, it strikes terror into the heart.
The dog has no Buddha-nature; a drawn blade, its cold flame contains frost.
At Mount Tai, he scrutinized the old woman; with one stroke of the blade, he severed the tangle of vines.
Jue Tiezui said that the former master did not have these words; it is a waste of breath to analyze them.
When Layman Yan asked, "Bring nothing forth," he bore the entire burden upon his shoulders.
He constructed a simple footbridge not only to ferry horses and donkeys across, but to extend through a hundred generations to rescue those who are submerged and lost,
enabling them to walk with level steps to the shore of Mahāyāna. — Master Huangbo Duanji.

The Master was a successor of Baizhang; his name was Xiyun. A native of Min, he first traveled to Tiantai, where he encountered a monk who spoke and laughed with him as if they were old acquaintances.

Upon looking closely at him, [the Master saw that] his gaze pierced others. They then walked together. When the waters of a mountain stream suddenly rose in flood, [the Master] planted his staff and stopped.
The monk led the Master across by hand; the Master said, "Brother, you go across yourself. Thereupon, the monk bared his clothes and stepped forward, treading upon the waves.
Like the earth, Baizhang looked back at the master and said, "Come across! Come across! The master scolded him, saying, "You self-realized fellow!
I should have known; I would have cut off your shins. The monk sighed and said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma;
I am not his equal. Having said this, he vanished. One day, Baizhang asked the master, "Where have you come from? The master replied, "I have come from gathering mushrooms beneath Mount Daxiong."
Baizhang said, “Did you see the tiger? The Master then let out a tiger’s roar. Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike;
the Master slapped him once. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned. Later, he ascended the hall and said, “There is a great tiger at the foot of Mount Daxiong.
All of you must watch out for it! Today, this old fellow Baizhang has been caught by its mouth. The Master [Huangbo] was there.

While serving as the head seat (shouzuo) at Nanquan, one day he took his bowl and sat in Nanquan’s own seat. When Nanquan entered the hall and saw him, he said to the Master, "Head Seat, since when have you been practicing the Way?
The Master replied, "Before the time of King Sound (Vipaśyin). Nanquan said, "You are still just a descendant of Old Teacher Wang.
The Master then moved to the second seat. When the Master was taking his leave, Nanquan saw him out the gate and, lifting up the Master's bamboo hat, said:
"The Elder’s physical stature is not large enough for his capacity; his hat is simply too small. The Master said, "Even so, the great trichiliocosm is entirely contained within it.
Baizhang Quan said, "Wang Laoshi, you have been caught! The Master donned his hat and departed. While the Master was at Yanguan, he was performing prostrations to the Buddha in the hall.
At that time, Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty was a śrāmaṇera and asked, "Not seeking in the Buddha, not seeking in the Dharma..."
Miaoyan asked, "I do not seek the Buddha; I do not seek the Dharma; I do not seek the Sangha. Elder, when you prostrate, what is it that you are doing?
The Master said, "I do not seek the Buddha; I do not seek the Dharma; I do not seek the Sangha. I always prostrate to such matters. Miaoyan said, "What is the use of prostrating?
The Master struck Miaoyan with his palm. Miaoyan said, "That was too coarse, sir. The Master said, "In a place like this, why speak of coarse or fine? It depends entirely on [the situation]."
Later, when Zong ascended the throne, he conferred upon him the title "Coarse-Acting Śramaṇa. Prime Minister Pei remonstrated with him, saying:
"Three times you have acted as 'Cutter' for Your Majesty, severing the three temporal limits; thus, it would be more appropriate to call you 'Cutter of Limits. Once, six new arrivals came to you.
Five of them performed prostrations, while one among them lifted up his sitting mat and drew a single circular diagram. You said: 'I have heard there is...'"
A pair of hunting dogs were extremely fierce. The monk said, "I have come following the sound of the antelope.

The Master said, "The antelope makes no sound; you have come seeking it. The monk said, "I have come following the tracks of the antelope. The Master said, "The antelope leaves no tracks; you have come seeking them. [The monk] said, "I have come following the footprints of the antelope.
[The Master] said, "The antelope leaves no footprints; you have come seeking them. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then it is a dead antelope."
The Master then ceased speaking. The next day he ascended the hall and said, "Yesterday I sought out the monk who was like a wild goat;
the monk came forth. The Master said, 'The case from yesterday remains unresolved; I have ceased my discourse. How do you understand it? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, 'I took you for a practitioner of true substance, but you are actually just a scholar-monk. He drove him out. Then he addressed the assembly, saying:
"All of you here are nothing but wine-dregs eaters. Traveling on pilgrimage like this, how could you have reached today?

Do you know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Zen masters? At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "If that is so, what about those in all quarters who lead disciples and manage assemblies?
The Master said, "I do not say there are no Zen masters; I simply say there are no teachers. The Master lived in poverty during his lay years.
The mother was old. Hearing that the Master resided at Huangbo, she came specifically to see him, but the Master paid her no heed.
Driven by hunger and cold, she went to the Da-yi ferry crossing, where she slipped and fell to her death; subsequently, she was reborn in heaven.

She appeared to the Master in a dream and said, "If I had accepted even a single grain of rice from you at that time, I would have fallen into hell; how could I have attained this day? Having bowed twice, she departed. One day, the Master clenched his fist.
He said: "The old monks of the world are all here. If I were to let slip even a single thread of opportunity, you would be able to run wild in every direction;
but if I do not let it pass, it will not take more than a single squeeze. A question was asked: "What is it like when it does not take more than a single squeeze? The Master said:
Pu. Prime Minister Pei held up a statue of the Buddha and knelt before him, saying, "I request you, Master, to bestow a name upon it. The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! Pei replied, "Yes.
The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you. Nanqian came to visit the Master. The Master asked, "How is it when no image of the three realms has yet appeared?
Nanqian said, "Is there such a thing as 'now'? The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment whether it exists or not..."
"What is it right now? Nan said, "Neither ancient nor modern. The Master said, "My Dharma-eye is already within you. The Master continued, "For the time being, attend to human affairs;
you ought not to be able to realize and embody [the truth]. You merely know how to learn words and tuck them into your bag, claiming everywhere, 'I understand Chan.
But can that take the place of birth and death? To treat elder masters with such contempt—you will sink into the earth."
The prison is like an arrow.
Commentary:
A coarse practitioner of the śramaṇa path, entirely lacking restraint and discipline.
He holds the Great Tang Emperor in his palm;
His face is as crimson as blood as he strikes the lad Linji.
Under Mount Daxiong, he emerges like a tiger— Yet it is before its claws and fangs have even formed.
At Dayudu Head, she threw herself off and killed her mother; Without distinguishing between enmity and gratitude, she existed before the time of Weiyin.
While traveling on the road, they vied for a seat; On level ground, they suffered a fall.
Hearing Baizhang’s words, his ears were deaf for three days; In shock, he spat out his tongue, turning it over root and all.
The pronghorn has left no trace; how could one know where the hunting hounds would find it?
The mountain stream swells with surging waves, yet he is deceived by the barbarian monk.
The small cap conceals the great trichiliocosm; where, then, can you place the Old Teacher?
A coarse fist grips all the monks under heaven; sometimes a single thread passes through, and it is said that the thousand-acre Southern Fayen is within you.
Just as a ghost was forced to divide its spoils with Minister Pei, an ancient Buddha was given a name—only to be needlessly defiled by him.
"You wine-dregs-eating fellow, do you still think there are no Zen masters in the Great Tang? You slighted this old monk;
you shall enter hell as swiftly as an arrow.
— Master Chen of Muzhou.

The Master’s name was Daozong; his secular surname was Chen. He was a descendant of King Li of Jiangnan. While traveling to visit the Buddha at Kaiyuan Temple, he encountered a monk as if they were old acquaintances.

Upon returning home, he informed his parents of his wish to leave the household life, and they granted him permission. Having received full ordination, he traveled to various regions and attained realization of the ultimate meaning under Huangbo.
Later, at the request of the fourfold assembly, he resided at Guanyin Temple, where his community regularly numbered over a hundred. Students came to him to seek instruction and inquiry.

He answered questions on the spot with such sharp and incisive words that no one could withstand his鋒 (fēng—literally "blade" or "edge"). Consequently, he was honored as a "Venerable Elder" (zūnsù) by practitioners from all quarters.
He once served as the head seat under Huangbo; at that time, Linji had just entered the assembly, and the Master recognized him as a vessel of great potential.

He directed him to see Huangbo to inquire about the fundamental meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and Huangbo struck him three times with his staff. When Yunmen first came to study with the Master, the Master bolted the door and pressed him inside.
Zhe Yunjiao then said, "The chariot-ruts of the Qin era. Yun was greatly enlightened. He subsequently pointed out Xuefeng to him. Later, the Master returned to Kaiyuan;
as his mother was elderly and had no other kin, he settled her in a quiet room, where she lived while he wove *púxié* sandals every day and sold the rice from their proceeds to support her.

Therefore, he was called "Chen the Straw Sandal Maker. When the rebels of Chao reached his borders, the Master placed a large shoe at the city gate. The rebels exerted all their strength but could not lift it;
sighing, they said, "There is a great sage in Muzhou," and they abandoned the city and departed, thus sparing the area from disturbance.

The Master asked a *zhuzhu* (lecturer), "What sutra are you preaching? He replied, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Master said, "May I ask about a passage of meaning? He replied, "Yes, you may. The Master then...
He kicked into the air, blew upon it once, and said, "What is the meaning of this? [The monk] replied, "This meaning does not exist in the sutras.
He said, "You empty-talking, deceitful fellow! You say there is no meaning in the story of the five hundred strongmen lifting the rock! At that time, a scholar visited the Master.
[The Master] said, "I claim to understand the calligraphic works of twenty-four masters. The Master pointed a single dot in the air with his staff and asked, "Do you understand? C'ai was at a loss.
[The Master] said, "And yet you say you understand the calligraphic works of twenty-four masters; you do not even recognize the 'eight strokes' of the character 'Yong' (永).

Later, while the monk was attending to him, the Master asked, "Are you a newly arrived guest? He replied, "Yes. [The Master] said, "For now, set aside this entanglement. Do you understand? He replied, "No."

The assembly gathered. [A monk] said, "I come bearing my shackles and presenting my petition; please lead me out yourself. The monk then departed. The Master called out, "Come! Come! I am truly asking you:
from where have you come? He replied, "Jiangxi. The Master said, "The Abbot of Letan is behind you; he fears you will speak recklessly. Do you see him? The monk was speechless.
The Master often remarked that those who respond to his teachings are like men carrying a single board; their gateways are steep and perilous, and few can pass through.
Permitted. Followed by one person, Minister Chen Cao.
The eulogy says:
This man of Han has carried his wooden board for a lifetime; he would never allow himself to be moved or changed by another.
Severing the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs— without relying on a lead blade to exchange the eyes of a monk,
it requires only a clod of earth to snap the fingers;
Linji’s study under Huangbo was like a live snake entering a bamboo tube.
He succeeded Yunmen as the heir to Xuefeng;
The meaning of a tortoise giving birth to a crane’s egg and five hundred men lifting a rock;
Kicking over the empty space with his toe, he overturned the "body-less" writings of the twenty-four houses; With his staff, he pointed toward the void to see.
He rebuked the newcomer, telling him to "put down the rotten entanglements of Jiangxi" which have no root;
he cast out the "chariot-rim of the Qin era," and dwelt in a quiet room to support his mother.
How much can a worn-out straw sandal be worth? Not even a few coins.
Hiding his body in an ancient temple, he treats his private possessions as if they were mere broken lacquer bowls;
He hangs large sandals at his gate, yet falsely assumes the title of "Holy One.
Sharing the seat [of authority], he attempts to revive the collapsing纲 (guiding principles), But he has blinded the eyes of both humans and devas.

His vital energy surged toward the Ox and Dipper constellations, reaching out to all quarters. Like a dying sparrow being pelted with stones from the ground, he exhausted every stratagem, yet in the end, he could only catch a common fellow.
This was Chan Master De Shan Jianxing.
The Master’s name was Xuánjiàn; he was a successor of Lóngtán and a native of Jiǎn State. His secular surname was Zhōu.

Initially, he lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his fame eclipsing that of all in Chengdū, and he was commonly known as Zhōu Jīngāng (Diamond Zhou). He once said to his fellow students: "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no loss;

a tiny speck is cast into a needle’s eye, yet its sharp point remains unmoved. Whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), only I know this. Upon hearing of the Chan [teachings] in the South...

The assembly was quite grand. The Master felt indignant and said, "A renunciant may study the subtle practices of the Buddha for a thousand kalpas and the majestic deportment of the Buddha for ten thousand kalpas, yet still not attain Buddhahood.
Yet this 'demon-child' from the South dares to speak of 'pointing directly at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
I shall destroy his lair and exterminate his kind to repay the Buddha’s grace. Thereupon, he took up the *Qinglong chao* (Blue Dragon Commentary).
He departed from Shu and was traveling on the road to Liyang when he saw an old woman selling cakes. Stopping to rest his shoulders, he bought some refreshments.
The woman pointed to his pack and asked, "What kind of texts are these? He replied, "The *Qinglong Shuchao* (Commentary on the Blue Dragon). She asked, "Which sutra do you lecture on?
He replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. She said, "I have a question for you; if you can answer it, I will give you these refreshments. If you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere."
He departed. In the sutra it says: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
I do not know which of these minds the Elder intends to point out. The Master remained silent. He went directly to Longtan and said, "I have long heard of Longtan;
yet now that I have arrived, the pond is not seen and the dragon does not appear. Longtan said, "You have personally arrived at the dragon's lair."
Dantan was silent and offered no reply, so he stayed there for the night. One evening, while standing in attendance, Dantan said, "It is deep in the night;
why do you not go out? Zhenzhong replied, "Goodbye," and then departed. He returned and said, "It is dark outside. Dantan lit a paper candle and handed it to him. Zhenzhong took it.
The pond was blown out by the wind and extinguished. The Master attained great enlightenment and immediately prostrated himself. Yunyan said, "What have you seen?
The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.

On the following day, Yunyan ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying, "In that group there is a fellow with teeth like a forest of swords and a mouth like a blood-basin; he cannot be turned back even by a single blow of the staff."
"Head! In the future, you shall stand atop a solitary peak and propagate my Way. The Master then piled the commentaries and sub-commentaries before the Dharma Hall, lit a fire, and said:
"To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void; to exhaust all worldly pivotal mechanisms [is likewise so]."
It was like a single drop cast into a vast abyss. He then burned it and took his leave, proceeding directly to Mount Mui. Carrying his double-layered mat, he ascended the Dharma Hall;
he went from east to west and from west to east, looking toward the abbot’s quarters and saying, "Is there anything?

Is there anything? The Master sat there without looking back. The Teacher said, "There is nothing. There is nothing," and then departed. Upon reaching the entrance of the gate, he said, "Even so, it is not."

He obtained some grass and, having prepared his formal robes and implements, entered again to meet him. As soon as he stepped across the threshold, he held up his sitting cloth (kaṣāya) and said, "Venerable Master!
Before the Master could reach for his whisk, the monk gave a shout and swept out of the hall with his sleeves. That evening, the Master asked the Head Seat, "Is the newcomer still here today?
The Head Seat replied, "At that time, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went out wearing straw sandals. The Master said, "..."
Later, this man went to the summit of a solitary peak and constructed a thatched hut; he was one who would scold the Buddhas and revile the Patriarchs.

One day, as the meal was late, the Master himself took up his bowl and passed through the hall. At that time, Xuefeng was serving as the steward (dianzuo) and said, "The bell has not yet sounded, and the drum has not yet rung;
where are you going with your bowl? The Master immediately returned to the abbot’s quarters. Xuefeng reported this to Yantou, who said, "Great!"
Xiaode Shan had not yet realized the "final word. When the Master heard of this, he ordered his attendant to invite Shan to him and said, "Why do you refuse to acknowledge me, old monk?
Shan secretly conveyed his intention. The next day, when the Master ascended the hall for the formal discourse, it was unlike anything he had done before.
Shan stood before the Sangha Hall and clapped his hands, saying, "I am glad that the old fellow at the head of the hall has finally understood the final word. Nevertheless..."
"He shall live for only three years. After three years, he indeed passed away. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"If you simply have no mind toward things and no things within the mind, it will naturally be empty yet spiritual, void yet wondrous. Were one to speak of its beginning and end in even the slightest degree, as small as the tip of a hair—"
All of this is self-deception. Why? A single thought tied to even a hair’s breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms;
a fleeting emotion arises and one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds; extraordinary features and inferior forms are all but illusory colors.
If you seek them, will you not be burdened? When you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction. In the end, there is no benefit whatsoever. —Xuefeng.
He asked the Master, "Regarding the matter of the ancestral vehicle from above, does this person [I] still have a share in it or not?
The Master said, "What are you saying? Feng attained realization. Attendant Kuok asked, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? The Master said, "What? What?

Kuok said, "When the Emperor issues a decree for the flying dragon horse, the lame tortoise sticks its head out. The Master ceased speaking. The next day, after the Master had finished his bath, Kuok—
Du Tang was with his teacher. The teacher patted him on the back and asked, "How was the case yesterday? Guo replied, "This old fellow has only just begun to see clearly today.
The teacher then let it rest. One day, the teacher went into the mountains with Waguan to chop wood.
The teacher gave a bowl of water to Guan; Guan took it and drank immediately. The teacher asked, "Do you understand? Guan said, "I do not understand. The teacher spoke again.
He gave a bowl of water to the coffin. The coffin took it and drank. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The coffin said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Why not strip off that which does not understand? The coffin said, "If I do not understand, what else would there be to strip off?
The Master said, "You are very much like an iron stake. From across the river, the Master saw Gao Ting and called out, "How do you do? He then shook his fan.

He summoned Gaoting, who attained sudden enlightenment and then strode away crosswise. Whenever the Master occupied a monastery, he would tear down the Buddha Hall, leaving only the Dharma Hall standing.
The eulogy says:
Carrying his tally-book, he ran south; Carrying the extinction of all demonic sons, He encountered a foul old woman who pointed out the three minds.
Seeing Xiaodang act with benevolence,
Longtan remained mute without a single word as he blew out the paper candle; Xuedou dispersed his family wealth,
while Deqiao built a thatched hut and reviled the Buddhas and patriarchs.
Reaching Mount Gui, he went forth with straw sandals on his back; He playfully manipulated the immediate pivot before his eyes.
When asked by Yantou, "Why do you not approve of this old monk? He understood the final phrase:
empty yet spiritual, void yet wondrous. Whenever he encountered someone, he would fling down a lump of rotten mud.
A hair swallows the ocean; mustard seeds are cast into a needle’s eye. Before the assembly, he snaps the Vajra scepter in two.
The venomous turtle-nosed snake arises from the vehicle of the *zongcheng* (the school of the lineage).
The dragon-horse gallops toward the "what" (*zemo*), racing through the midst of activity.
He hews wood, requires a tile coffin, and as soon as it is finished, he stops;

he fans himself with delight at the high pavilion and strides off crosswise—truly what is called "demolishing the Buddha hall" and "biting pigs and dogs," an old venerable one whose kindness does not conform to human sentiment. I imagine...
This flower-adorned ground is a place for those who cherish worldly splendor.

As for the Master of the Lower Seat, Chan Master Huo of Yantou—whose name was Quanhuo—he was a successor of Deshan and a native of Quanzhou, surnamed Ke. One day he went to visit Deshan; as he was just crossing the gate—

He then asked, "Is this an ordinary person or a sage? Sanshan shouted. The Master bowed. A monk later related this to Dongshan, who said, "Had it not been for Master Huo, it would have been very difficult to handle.
The Master said, "The old man Dongshan does not recognize good from bad; he has wrongly applied his words.
At that time, I was holding up with one hand while pressing down with the other. One day, he was gathered together with Xuefeng and Qingshan.

In the course of their conversation, they saw a bowl of water. Xingqing said, "When the water is clear, the moon appears. Feng said, "When the water is clear, the moon does not appear. The Master kicked it away and departed.
The Master and Xuefeng were leaving Deshan together when Deshan asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am leaving the Master for a while. Deshan asked, "What will you do after this?
The Master replied, "I shall not forget the Master. Deshan said, "On what do you rely? The Master replied, "I rely on... [The text ends here].

"How can such a statement exist? The Master said, "Have you not heard? When one's wisdom is equal to the teacher's, it is but half the teacher's virtue; only when one's wisdom surpasses the teacher's is one fit to receive the transmission.
[The student] said, "So it is, so it is. I shall protect and uphold it well myself. The Master was at Yantou in Ezhou.
During a period of monastic purges, he worked as a ferryman by a lake. He hung a board on each bank;
whenever someone wished to cross, they would strike the board once. The Master would then dance with his oars to welcome them.
One day, a woman came along carrying a child and said, "I do not ask about you dancing with your oars, but tell me, what about the woman?"
“Where did you get that child in your hand? The Master struck him. The old woman said, “I have given birth to seven sons;

six of them did not meet with a true知音 (zhīyīn—‘one who knows the sound’). This one alone is not even worth keeping,” and she threw him into the water. Later, the Master stayed at a hermitage on Mount Wòlóng (臥龍) in Dōngtíng (洞庭).
His disciples gathered there in great numbers. A monk asked, “Does one who has no teacher still have a way to manifest themselves?”
The Master said, "Before the sound, ancient rags have rotted away. He ascended the hall and said, "I once studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for seven or eight years.
Within it, there are one or two passages of meaning that seem like the talk of a patch-robed monk. He added, "Stop! Stop!

At that time, a monk came forward, bowed, and said, "We request the Master to speak for the sake of the assembly. The Master then said, "The intent of my teaching is like the three dots of the letter ∴."
First, place a dot toward the east; this opens the eyes of all Bodhisattvas. Second, place a dot toward the west; this awakens the life-faculty of all Bodhisattvas.
Third, place a dot toward the zenith; this opens the cranial aperture of all Bodhisattvas.
This is the primary meaning of the first section of the sutra. The intent of my teaching is like that of Maheśvara parting the [three] worlds.
On his face, he sticks out one eye. This is the meaning of the second section. My teaching’s intent is like a "poisoned drum":
when struck once, everyone who hears it, whether near or far, perishes. This is the meaning of the third section.
At that time, the Venerable Xiaoyan asked, “What is the poisoned drum? The Master pressed both hands upon his knees, leaned forward, and said, “Han Xin facing the throne.”
Diyan was without rival. Layi Shan went to visit Shishuang and asked, "What is it like when one cannot find peace whether going or staying?

Shishuang said, "You must simply exhaust [all attachments]. Layi Shan was not satisfied with this and went to consult Master [Linji]. He asked the same question as before. [Linji] said, "He goes and stays according to his own accord;
what business is it of yours to manage him? Layi Shan then took this to heart. One day he asked again, "Is it not true, Master, that thirty years ago..."
[The Master] said, "While at Dongshan, you did not approve of Dongshan. [Dongshan] replied, "That is true. [The Master] asked again, "Did you not succeed to Deshan and yet not approve of Deshan?
[Dongshan] replied, "That is true. [The Master] said, "I do not ask about your disapproval of Deshan; but as for Dongshan, what deficiency was there?
The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Dongshan loved the Buddha, but he simply lacked radiance. Dongshan bowed. The Master then questioned him.
The monk asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the Western Capital. The Master said, "After Huang Chao passed through, did you manage to recover the sword?
He replied, "I recovered it. The Master stepped forward, extended his neck, and said, "Hmph! The monk said, "Your head has fallen off, Master!
The Master laughed loudly. Later, the monk went to Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Yantou. Xuefeng asked, "What did Yantou say?"

Paddling the oars upon the shores of Lake Dongting, she leads the stinking old woman to cast away her child;

however, the karmic conditions did not harmonize. Later, he studied under Deshan, whereupon he attained enlightenment beneath the master’s words. The Master then took his leave of Dongshan.
Mountain asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "I am going back to the ridge. Mountain said, "By which path did you come out at that time?

The Master had no reply. The Master went with Yantou to Aoshan Inn in Lishu. They were detained there by snow.

[The monk] said, "In this life I have not found my footing; I have been traveling with that fellow Wensui, and everywhere I go, I am brought to ruin by him.

Xia said, "I am not yet settled here. Yankong said, "I thought that after this life you would go to the summit of a solitary peak to build a grass hut, there to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs;

“Ming, I will not leave you with this; I shall root it out for you. The Master said, “When I first arrived at Yanguan, I heard the teaching on the meaning of form and emptiness, and I attained a point of entry.
