The monk asked, "What about those who have neither said they are the Void nor become the Void? Xuansha said, "This is the one who can be the Unborn. The monk asked, "How can one be the Unborn? Xuansha said, "By saying, 'I am the Unborn. The monk asked, "What about those who have already said they are the Unborn? Xuansha said, "They are like a man who has already become the Unborn. The monk asked, "What about those who have neither said they are the Unborn nor become the Unborn? Xuansha said, "This is the one who can be the Non-abiding. The monk asked, "How can one be the Non-abiding? Xuansha said, "By saying, 'I am the Non-abiding. The monk asked, "What about those who have already said they are the Non-abiding? Xuansha said, "They are like a man who has already become the Non-abiding. The monk asked, "What about those who have neither said they are the Non-abiding nor become the Non-abiding? Xuansha said, "This is the one who can be the True Suchness. The monk asked, "How can one be True Suchness? Xuansha said, "By saying, 'I am True Suchness. The monk asked, "What about those who have already said they are True Suchness? Xuansha said, "They are like a man who has already become True Suchness. The monk asked, "What about those who have neither said they are True Suchness nor become True Suchness? Xuansha said, "This is the one who can be the Ultimate Reality. The monk asked, "How can one be Ultimate Reality? Xuansha said, "By saying, 'I am Ultimate Reality. The monk asked, "What about those who have already said they are Ultimate Reality? Xuansha said, "They are like a man who has already become Ultimate Reality. The monk asked, "What about those who have neither said they are Ultimate Reality nor become Ultimate Reality? Xuansha said, "This is the one who can be the Great Matter. The monk asked, "How can one be the Great Matter? Xuansha said, "By saying, 'I am the Great Matter. The monk asked, "What about those who have already said they are the Great Matter? Xuansha said, "They are like a man who has already become the Great Matter. The monk asked, "What about those who have neither said they are the Great Matter nor become the Great Matter? Xuansha said, "This is the one who can be the Unconditioned. The monk asked, "How can one be the Unconditioned? Xuansha said, "By saying, 'I am the Unconditioned. The monk asked, "What about those who have already said they are the Unconditioned? Xuansha
"It must be Brother Leng for it to be so. Nevertheless, I am not like that. The monk asked, "How about you, Master? The Master said, "What need is there for Nanshan?
He ascended the hall and said: "The entire great earth, when gathered up, is as small as a grain of millet."
He threw them before him. A lacquer bucket would not do. "Strike the drum for a general assembly to watch.
One day Xuansha said to the Master, "I am now going to employ the Great Function; how will you, Reverend, respond? The Master rolled out three wooden balls all at once.
Xuansha made a gesture as if cutting a stone stele. The Master said, "Only when you are personally present at Vulture Peak can you act like this. Xuansha said:
This, too, is one's own affair. The Military Commissioner of Min presented him with silver and a folding chair.
A monk asked, "Venerable Sir, having received such offerings from the Great King, how will you repay his kindness? The Master pressed the ground with his hand and said, "Strike me lightly.

Later, while Master Xiangguyuan was receiving people, he wished to go to Songshan to build a monastery and settle a community. He asked the Great Master (the nun) for the site of her hermitage, but she was unwilling. Because of this—
He engaged in seated meditation with [the nun] and made an agreement, saying: "Whoever emerges from meditative absorption before seven days have passed shall forfeit.

On the sixth day, the nun opened her eyes; the Master thereupon seized her foundation and established a temple. The Master personally inscribed a stele at the Grinding Court (Moyuan), which said: "Before the mountain, for all day long, there are no wolves or tigers;
beneath the grinding stones, throughout the year, there are no sparrows. To this day, tigers and sparrows are entirely absent.
The eulogy says:
Attaining this place was quite arduous; In its application, there is no clever artifice.
Entering Feiyuan Ridge, one does not recognize a single person.
Born in a land of lethal *gǔ* poison, how could one avoid even the slightest transgression?
A red-hot brick strikes and freezes through to the very bottom; meeting Deshan, he was ignited without the need for further talk.
Red-Eye bumps into a firebrand; traveling with Yantou, it takes but a single person.
At the gate of Mount Ao, he attained the Way;
In the dead of night, he went mad beneath Elephant Bone Rock.
He threw his whole body down and rolled out like a wooden ball; Xuansha hurriedly made a signboard.
A turtle-nosed snake lunges forth; Yunmen hurriedly beats the grass to open the door.
If you hesitate even slightly, you will be seized by the old monk Guan. It is no phoenix chick!
Listen as the drum is beaten for all to see: the entire great earth, gathered together, is not larger than a grain of millet.
Seventeen hundred spiritual friends were all scooped up from the tip of the ladle;
fifty or sixty *li* away at Xuefeng Mountain, they seized the small pagoda and the pebble from atop the meditation cushion at Pusan,
piling them up in several chaotic layers.
The ancient stream has cold springs swirling like the hoofprints of an ox; how deep can they be?
Before the mountain, throughout the entire day, there are no wolf cubs; listen as the old monk walks beneath the millstone.
Having been free of sparrows for all year, he need not worry about the consumption of his rice for the midday meal.
Having received the offerings of the Great King throughout his entire life, how might he repay this kindness? He pressed his hands against the earth and cried out urgently:
"Strike me! Strike me!
(From *Wujia Zhengzong Zan*, Scroll One)
Praise of the Five Patriarchs, Volume Two:
Linji Huizhao Chan Master of the Linji School.

The Master’s name was Yixuan. He was the son of the Xing family of Caozhou. Initially, while serving as a member of the assembly under Huangbo, the first seat in the hall urged him to engage in formal inquiry.
Consequently, he went up to the abbot’s quarters and asked, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Huangbo struck him. He asked this three times and was struck three times. He then took his leave of the seat, saying, “I have followed your exhortation to ask.”
[The monk] said, "I have only received the staff from Master Wuming; I shall now go to various quarters. Baso said, "You must first take leave of the Master before you may go.
Baso then went to the Head Seat (the Abbot) and informed him, "The monk who asked the question, though young, is truly in accordance with the Dharma.
If he comes to bid farewell, please receive him with skillful means. On the following day, the monk came to take his leave. Huangbo sent him to Gaoyang to visit Dayu. When the Master arrived there—

Yunmen was foolish. The Foolish One asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from Huangbo. Yunmen said, "What instructions did Huangbo give you? He replied, "Three times I asked him about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I was struck with his staff. I do not know what fault I committed. Yunmen said: "‘Huangbo has no other teaching; he only strikes people.

If you wish to understand the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, go back and ask him again. If he strikes you once more, come back and tell me how it feels. Later, when the monk returned and reported that Huangbo had struck him again, Yunmen said, 'I knew all along that Huangbo had no other teaching than this. "
Huangbo was so old-fashioned that he had already exhausted you; yet you come here again to ask whether there is a fault or not.
The Master said, "So it turns out Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma does not amount to much. Yuyu seized him by the collar and said, "You bed-wetting little ghost!"
Just now you asked whether there was a transgression or not, yet now you say, "Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much.
What principle have you seen that leads you to speak thus? The Master struck Yufu three times under the ribs. Yufu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo;
it is none of my business. The Master returned. When Huangbo saw him, he immediately asked, "Coming and going, coming and going..."
[The Master] said, "I have understood it thoroughly. The Master said, "It is only because my heart is as urgent as that of an old woman.
Huangbo said, "Daoyu is too talkative; when I see him, I will give him a severe beating. The Master said, "What do you mean by 'when I see him'? I shall beat you right now!
Huangbo said, "This madman has come here to pull at the tiger's whiskers. The Master then gave a shout. Huangbo told him to go to the meditation hall. At Mount Jing, there were five hundred monks.

Every day he practiced his daily rites while reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, yet not a single person came to seek instruction. Guishan wrote a letter to Linji Yixuan, detailing these matters. Yixuan instructed the Master to go;
upon arriving at Jingshan, the Master girded his waist and went straight up to the Dharma Hall. As soon as Guishan raised his head, the Master let out a shout.
Just as Guishan was about to open his mouth, the Master brushed his sleeves and departed. Shortly thereafter, a monk asked Guishan about the monk who had been there earlier.
When a certain monk uttered a profound statement, he gave a shout and said to the Master, "This monk has come from Huangbo. If you wish to know him, go ask him yourself.
At that time, more than half of the five hundred followers dispersed. Lopu served as his attendant; not finding resonance with the Master, he took his leave.
Later, the Master said, "Among them was a red-scaled carp, shaking its head and wagging its tail, heading toward the south. It did not stay.
"I know who will drown in whose family's pickle jar. When the Master was about to pass away, he said, "After my extinction, you must not extinguish my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Sansheng said, "How would we dare extinguish the Venerable Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye? The Master said:
Later, someone suddenly asked, "What did you say to him? Baizhang (Sheng) then shouted.
The Master said, "Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would perish at the hands of this blind donkey?"
The eulogy says:
A beam for the vast hall, a vessel for the pure temple;
its frost-scraping surface and cold flames press upon one.
The majestic spirit of the crouching beast; a stinking wind rolls across the earth as we behold Muzhou.
Having first learned to leap over hedges and vault walls, he took the palm from Huangbo and understood how to snatch the market for himself.
Requiting the grievance with sixty blows, he struck a fist into Dagu’s ribs;
with a shout, he dispersed five hundred monks, causing Jinshan to feel shortness of breath in his chest.
He unfurled the weapons and armor of the Three Mysteries, leaving a field of skulls cold across the earth.
Revealing the four types of discernment: On level ground, waves and billows arise;
in a blazing sky, snow and hail fly. To clarify the upward-pointing function alone is like a barefoot man galloping across the edge of ice—this is itself a singular standard of excellence.
To lament the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and extinguish it toward the blind donkey of the Three Sages—
to know the crimson-tailed carp and drown it in someone else’s pickle jar—
is to deserve the tongue-pulling hell for those who praise such things.
Those who disparage it shall be cast into boiling bronze and excrement, with the lingering heat of the winds of hell;
even after a hundred generations, the consequences will still persist. To seek the magic glue of the phoenix to mend the broken string is to distance oneself from the goal by a vast margin.
Chan Master Xinghua Jiang, whose name was Cunjiang, was a native of Weizhou. He first met Linji, who appointed him as his attendant.
When a newly arrived monk asked Linji, "Where have you come from? he replied, "From Luancheng. Linji said, "May I ask you something? He replied, "A novice does not understand."

[The Master] said, "To break up the Great Tang Dynasty and find someone who does not understand—such a person is hard to find. [Ji] went to the meditation hall. The Master asked, "Just now, when you arrived, were you trying to humble him or what?

Ji said, "Who am I to concern myself with whether he is humbled or not? The Master said: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 13, featuring Mazu Daoyi and Huangbo Xiyun.*
The Master (Heshang) immediately took a dead sparrow and snapped it on the ground, but he did not know how to cover it over with a turning phrase.
Jie asked, "How about you? The Master said, "Please let the Master act as the newcomer. Jie then said, "The new precept-holder does not understand.
The Master said, "Rather, this is my own fault. Jie said, "Your words conceal the sharp edge [of the truth]. As the Master hesitated, Jie then—
He struck him. When evening came, Linji said again, "Today when I questioned the newly arrived monk, I was 'striking a dying sparrow on the ground' or 'striking it in its nest.
But when you produced your words, I shouted and 'struck it toward the blue clouds. The Master said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. Linji then struck him.
Later, the Master went to Sansheng, where he requested to serve as the head seat (shouzuo). He often said, "I traveled southward."
Once, as he was traveling on foot, he encountered no one at all who could grasp the Buddha-dharma with the tip of his staff.
When Guishan Shengwen heard of this, he asked, "What kind of eye do you possess? The Master then gave a shout. Shengwen said, "It must be you who can achieve it.
When Dajue heard of this, he remarked, "How might the wind be made to blow into Dajue’s gate? Later, the Master arrived at Dajue and requested to serve as the head of the monastery.

One day, Master Jué called out to him, saying, "I have heard you say that during your travels throughout the south, you never once struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma with the tip of your staff.
What kind of eye do you possess? The Master then shouted. Jué raised his staff.
As the Master hesitated, Jué struck him. The Master shouted again, and Jué struck him once more. The following day, as the Master was passing by the Dharma Hall...
Juezhao summoned the head of the monastery, saying, "I have no doubt at all regarding your two shouts yesterday; try to explain them to me.
The Master replied, "I received a phrase concerning guest and host from my senior brother Sansheng, but I have been completely defeated by you, Senior Brother."
"I shall grant such-and-such a person a dharma-gate of peace and happiness. Jue said, "You blind fellow! You have come here to suffer defeat.
He stripped off his patched robe and gave him a severe beating. At these words, the Master realized the principle of how his late teacher Linji had received the staff from Huangbo.
Later, when he opened the hall for formal teaching, he offered incense and said: "This one stick of incense—if it were for Sansheng..."
"The Three Sages are too remote for me. To take the Great Awakened One [Buddha] as my teacher would be too distant for me.
It is better that I make offerings to my late teacher Linji. When Yunju was staying at Sanfeng, the Master asked him:

'If one temporarily borrows a question to serve as a "shadow-grass" (a preliminary probe), what then? Yunju had no reply. The Master said: 'I suspect you, Master, could not answer this question. It is better—'"
Having paid his respects, he withdrew. Twenty years later, Ju said, "If I were to reflect on that time now, I would not even say 'why bother?
Later, he sent a messenger to the Master’s place. The Master said, "When you, Preceptor, resided at Sanfeng, I asked you a question and you could not answer it.
Have you been able to answer it yet? The messenger recounted the previous conversation. The Master said, "Xinghua—then..."
"Not so. "How would it be better than saying 'it is unnecessary'? A monk asked the Master, "When they come from the four quarters and eight directions, what then?
The Master said, "Strike the one in the center. The monk bowed; the Master said, "Today Xinghua was attending a village feast.
On the way, he encountered a sudden storm of wind and rain, but managed to take shelter inside an old temple. He addressed the assembly, saying, "I..."
"I heard 'Aha! shouted from beneath the long corridor. Later, I heard 'Aha! shouted from the upper gallery. My sons, do not shout blindly or shout recklessly.

Even if you were to shout so powerfully that you could send Xinghua up to the thirty-third heaven and then crash back down until you were without a single breath of life, wait for Xinghua to recover and rise again, and he would still tell you gently and slowly that it is 'not yet. Why? Because I have never yet [reached] the Purple..."
"I am scattering real pearls from within the silk curtains for all of you; why do you shout 'Hu' in the midst of empty space?
The Master said to the rector Kebin, "Before long, you shall become a teacher who leads the assembly. Kebin replied, "I will not enter that community.
The Master asked, "Do you not enter because you have understood, or because you have not understood? Kebin said, "It is not like either of those. The Master then—
He struck him and addressed the assembly, saying: "The rector Kebin has been defeated in this Dharma-battle. He shall be fined five strings of cash and provided with one meal of rice and vegetables;
furthermore, he is not permitted to eat it. He shall be driven out of the monastery immediately. When the Master saw his fellow practitioners arrive, as soon as they entered the Dharma Hall...
The Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted. After walking two or three steps, the Master shouted again; the monk also shouted. The Master stepped forward and raised his staff.
The monk shouted once more. The Master said, "Look! This blind fellow still dares to act as the host.
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and drove him straight out of the Dharma Hall. At that time, a monk asked, "What offense did this monk commit against you, Master? The Master replied:
This fellow has just now arrived with his authority, his treasure, his illumination, and his function.
Yet, as soon as [the Master] held up his hand and made two horizontal gestures before him, he was unable to proceed. For a person such as this, when will it be that we do not strike him?
A monk asked, "The precious sword you have hidden for a long time, today on this stage I beg to borrow it for a moment. The Master said, "No."
[The Emperor] asked, "Why do you not lend it? The Master said, "Were it not for Zhang Hua’s eyes, one would merely be gazing at the light piercing the Dipper.
[The Emperor] asked, "What of one who uses it? The Master said, "Lying across the body to face the universe—who is there to raise their head?

Emperor Tongguang asked the Master, "I have conquered the Central Plains and obtained a treasure; no one has yet offered a price for it. The Master said, "Let me borrow Your Majesty’s treasure to look at it."
The Emperor pulled back the hem of his *fuhou* (headgear) with his hand to show it to him. The Master said, "This is the treasure of a sovereign; who would dare to offer a price for it?

The Emperor was greatly pleased and offered him robes and a title, but the Master would not accept them. He then presented him with a horse. As the Master mounted the horse, it suddenly startled, causing him to fall to the ground and injure his foot.

He had to walk with the aid of a crutch. He asked a monk, "Do you still recognize this old monk? The monk replied, "How could I fail to recognize the Master? The Master said: "Even though I have fallen from my high position, My head is still higher than before."
[The character is a variant of 踴]. Master Jiao said that it can be practiced but cannot be attained.
Zan said:
"A true son of Linji; the foremost seat-holder of Sansheng."
A shout as hot as a thunderclap,
a coarse spirit as vast as heaven;
beneath the skin there is no blood— having seen the Great Awakened One receive the painful staff, one realizes the former master.
The wooden teeth grow hair; reaching Yunju, I borrowed a question as a mere shadow-grass.
Encountering a violent wind and sudden rain while attending a village feast, who in an ancient temple could say they have turned their whole body toward the south?
Probing the tiger’s lair and the demon palace, not a single thing has ever been struck by the tip of my staff.
Raising his voice, he stops the shout: within the purple silk curtain, he scatters bright moon pearls.
Though they have eyes, they lack the sinews; at the feet of the *fuhou* cap, one discerns the sovereign.
Examining the treasure with a companion, he extends his hand across the gateway; both sides are exhausted of their dying arts.
Beating Kebin, he was discharged from the hospital; a meal of punishment rice for one hall. Deceiving others is not slight;
borrow a precious sword to behold it on the spot. Its light shoots up, piercing the Dipper;
meeting a blind man, he strikes a dying sparrow on the ground. His words conceal the point; his merit cannot compensate for his transgressions.
Facing the Dragon’s Countenance and riding the Imperial Steed, though one may attain the glory of a single victory, one's two feet are exhausted upon the ancestral path;
even with all one's strength, one cannot reach its end.
Chan Master Nanyuan Yong was a successor of Xinghua.
He was a native of Hebei; his Dharma name was Huiyong, and his secular name was Baoying.

The Master ascended the hall and said, "People everywhere possess only the eye for the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching, but they do not possess the function of the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching. A monk then asked, "How is it so?"
"This is the simultaneous application of the peck and the tap. The Master said, "The adept does not use the peck and the tap; at the moment of the peck and the tap, one misses it.

The monk said, "This is not yet where the student asks his question. The Master asked, "How do you ask your question? The monk said, "I miss it. The Master then struck him. The monk did not accept this.

Addressing the assembly, the Master said, "Upon the ball of red flesh, there stands a precipice ten thousand fathoms high. At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked about the "ball of red flesh."

[The monk] said, "It stands upright like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. "Is this not the Master’s own words? the monk asked. The Master replied, "Yes. The monk then overturned the meditation seat.
The Master said, "Look at this blind fellow making such a mess! As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and expelled him from the monastery. Another monk asked:
"How was it when the two kings met? he asked. The monk replied, "Blowing a *shichaba* flute at the crossroads.
He asked again, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? The monk replied, "If not ascending to heaven, then entering hell.

He asked, "And what about you, Master? The Master said, "Do you know where Baoying has landed? The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him with his whisk. The Master then questioned another monk: "Recently..."

[The Master] asked, "From where do you depart? [The monk] said, "Xiangzhou. [The Master] asked, "What kind of thing is it that comes like this? [The monk] said, "Venerable Sir, please try to say it yourself.

[The Master] said, "That which just now prostrated itself. [The monk] said, "Wrong. [The Master] asked, "In what way was that prostration wrong? [The monk] said, "A second offense will not be tolerated.
[The Master] said, "After thirty years of riding horses, you have now been thrown by a donkey. You blind fellow! Go to the hall for practice. A monk asked, "When a person..."

[The monk asked: "What is it like when meeting a blue-eyed one? [The Master] said: "A ghost contending with a lacquer bucket. A monk asked: "What is it like when an ancient hall is restored? [The Master] said:
"The eaves of the Hall of Light are tucked under the tiles. The monk said: "In that case, the adornments are fully complete.

[The Master] said: "Cutting the grass—the snake’s head falls off. A monk asked: "What is it like when joy and anger flash across the mind? [The Master] said: "The mountain torrents overflow and the peaks collapse. A monk asked: "It is like this..."
"What is a seamless stupa? He replied, "Seven flowers, eight rags. "How about the person within the stupa? He replied, "The head is not combed; the face is not washed.
A monk asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? He replied, "Minister Huang and Minister Li.
"What is their intent? He replied, "The ox-head points north; the horse-head points south. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from?"
The Master said, "At Longxing. The monk asked, "When you set out, were you not already leaving Ye County?
The monk then shouted. The Master said, "I am asking you earnestly; why do you act so aggressively again? The monk said, "Can it be called 'acting aggressively'?
The Master then shouted back, "Since you are acting aggressively, I too am acting aggressively. Come closer; I have no measure of transgression, and you have no measure of transgression either."
"Wrong! You blind fellow! Go to the hall!
The commentary says:
A single word settles the fundamental principle; a master does not wait for the "cracking" and "pecking."
The heir of Xinghua, with a heart as pure as ice and snow,
a direct descendant of Linji; possessing the horns and head of a qilin,
he stands ten thousand fathoms high upon a ball of raw flesh— flinging aside the meditation seat and striking the blind donkey with his staff.
Meeting the two kings at the crossroads, The sound of the rishatsu flute disrupts the refined music.
Where have all the sages gone? In vain you say they enter hell and do not ascend to heaven;
what thing comes in such a manner? Clearly playing the horse-ride, now one is struck down by a donkey.
A single faculty and a single object—shifting the constellations and displacing the stars;
a flash of joy, a flash of anger; overturning the mountain torrents and toppling the peaks;
hair uncombed and face unwashed. The person within the stupa has not yet been fully captured by the brush.
The horse heads north and the ox heads south; to measure the intent of the Patriarchal Teaching with the intellect is entirely wrong.
From the time of Chongyou Lao, they have acted as fellow practitioners, yet they have produced nothing but petty sectarianism.
Following the rise of Longxing Monastery, the monks have passed on their mutual animosity to one another.
Exhausting the eyes of a thousand sages, one seeks its traces and origins; yet under the bright sun and blue sky, there is only wind, rain, thunder, and hail.

Fengxue Zhao Chan Master—his name was Yanzhao—was a native of the Liu clan from Yuhang. Having initially frequented lecture halls to study *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he abandoned them and went to call upon Jing.
Qing asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "I have come directly from the East. Qing said, "Did you not cross the Small River?
He replied, "A great vessel sails alone through the void; there is no Small River to be crossed. Qing said, "The Mirror Water and Mount Qin—where even a crow cannot fly across.
Do not speak based on hearsay. He replied, "Even the vast blue ocean fears the power of the warships; my flying sails cross the Five Lakes across the Milky Way."
[The Master] held up the whisk upright and said, "What can be done about this? [The monk] asked, "What is this? [The Master] said, "As expected, you do not recognize it.

[The monk] said, "Appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding—it is used by you and me alike. [The Master] said, "Using a ladle to divine based on empty sounds; sleeping soundly while indulging in idle chatter.
[The monk] said, "A vast marsh hides mountains; a principle can subdue a leopard. [The Master] said, "Pardon your sins and release your transgressions; you must depart at once. [The monk] said, "..."
"You may go out and obtain it. He then departed and traveled north to Xiangmian, where he took up residence under Huayan.

Huayan asked him, "I have a 'Song of Herding Oxen'; I request that you, O Acharya, provide a response to it. The Master said: "The *kegu* drum beats like a whip, and the ox leaps like a leopard; In the distant village, the plum tree’s beak is full of worry. Later, he visited Nanyuan.
Nanyuan asked the Master, "Regarding the single blow of the staff in the South, how do you deliberate upon it? The Master replied, "It acts as..."

This was a most extraordinary deliberation. [Zhaozhou] then asked, "How do you deliberate upon this single blow here? Baizhang held his staff crosswise and said, "In the blow beneath the staff, there is the patience of non-arising;
when the occasion arises, the teacher is not seen. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and later went forth at Fengxue.
He succeeded Nan-yuan. A monk asked, "The ancient melody has no rhyme or meter; how can it be harmonized? He replied, "The wooden cock crows at midnight;
the straw dog barks at dawn. A monk asked, "What is the Master’s house style? He replied, "The crane may have its nine-fold heights, yet its wings find it hard to soar;
the horse may lack the thousand-li stride, yet it vainly pursues the wind. Addressing the assembly, he said, "If you are of the highest stream, each of you possesses your own realization."

"Those who have attained realization briefly reach the destination; those who have not yet attained realization are each heroes in their own right, born in this very place and extinguished in this very place.
Like the cracking of a tortoise shell—once it cracks, the pattern is formed; if it does not crack, it remains dull. When about to crack but does not, one must seize the moment directly.
The Governor of Yingzhou requested him to ascend the seat in the yamen, whereupon he said: "The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs resembles an iron ox."
The mechanism of this [awakening] is such that when one departs, one is sealed; when one abides, one is broken by the seal. As for neither departing nor abiding—is it the seal? Or is it not the seal?
At that time, the Elder Lupi came forth and asked, "I possess the mechanism of the iron ox; I request the Master not to apply the seal.
The Master said, "One accustomed to fishing for whales and leviathans in vast depths now laments the frog’s stride in the mud and sand. Lupi stood there in silence.
The Master shouted, "Elder, why do you not proceed with your words? Bi hesitated. The Master struck him with a fly-whisk and said, "Do you still remember the *huatou*?
Try to bring it up. As Bi was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again with the whisk. The Head Herdsman said, "The Buddha-dharma and the King’s law are one and the same.
The Master asked, "What have you seen? The Head Herdsman replied, "If one does not cut off what ought to be cut off, it will instead bring about its own retribution."
[The Master] descended from his seat. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "How is it that you are not the Buddha? The monk said, "I do not understand these profound words;
I pray the Master will point directly. He replied, "My home is east of the Sea Gate; the Fusang tree is the first to be illuminated by the sun.

A monk asked, "When both 'existence' and 'non-existence' are absent, what is it like when departing? He replied, "For three months, I am too weary to wander the paths beneath the flowers; my entire household sits in sorrow, doors closed against the rain."
At the Middle Gate, a monk asked, "When speech and silence involve both transcendence and subtlety, how can one pass through without transgression?
He replied, "I often recall that within the third month in Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant."
The Eulogy says:
"Mao-jin-dao" (a pun on the surname Mao and the character for 'knife').
Truly leaping over the hearth, he practiced the Tiantai *zhiguan* (calming and contemplation). In his youth, he swam in the puddles of the stream.
Thoroughly investigating the single transmission of Shaoshi, one proceeds directly to the innermost depths;
under the staff, the patience of non-arising is realized. The bitter poison of Zhongnan Temple enters the heart;
with the ladle, one listens to empty sounds. Holding up the mirror to clarify the principle, one is able to subdue the leopard.
A straw dog barks at the light; a wooden cock crows in the night. The melodies of ancient tunes are lost, their rhythms incomplete;
an old crane spreads its wings, a sick horse pursues the wind. Discussions of family tradition are in great disarray;
through a tube one peers at the place of birth and death— the crackling patterns on the tortoise shell reveal no clear signs.
Measuring the Patriarch’s mind with a ladle, The iron ox’s mechanism makes coming and going difficult to grasp. The seal is broken;
the rising sun first shines upon the near seas. The essential point of direct pointing is yet obscured.
At the tip of the plum tree in the distant village, Lu-dou— The song of the cowherd is difficult to harmonize and sing along with.
Existence and non-existence are both cut off at once; A whole household sits in sorrow with doors closed in the rain.
Speech and silence involve the subtle and the manifest; For three months, birds cry out chaotically beneath the flowers.
The mystery within mysteries, the wondrous within wonders— The潇洒 (xiāosǎ) monk of Zhejiang: there is no second person.
Chan Master Shoushan Nian was a successor of Fengxue;
his name was Shengnian. He was the son of the Di family from Lai Prefecture. Once, Master Nian and Zhen Yuantou went together to pay their respects to Fengxue.
Fengxue asked Zhen, "What is the Buddha’s 'speaking that which is not spoken'? Zhen replied, "A magpie on a tree."
Shang wept. Xue said, "Why do you perform so much 'foolish merit'? Why not investigate the words and phrases instead?
He asked the Master, who replied, "To manifest one's countenance is to reveal the ancient path; one does not fall into the mechanism of silent stillness.
Xue said to Zhen, "Why do you not look at the sub-commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*? One day, Baimiao Chu arrived at Ruzhou to spread the teachings, and Xue ordered the Master to go there.
He delivered a message. As soon as they met, [Fengxue] held up his sitting mat and asked, "If you unfold it, it is this;
if you do not unfold it, it is that. Zhao said, "Look for yourself. The Master then gave a shout. Zhao said, "I have personally met with teachers of old; I would never dare to act so recklessly.
[Fengxue] said, "The grass-thief has been utterly defeated. Zhao said, "If I see Master Fengxue tomorrow, I shall wait—"
He recounted each instance one by one, saying, "I have fulfilled my duty in every case; I must not forget. When the Master returned, he first related these matters to Xué.
Xué said, "Today you have once again captured a bandit for me. The Master replied, "A skilled hand does not flaunt its name.
The next day, as soon as they met, Xué brought up the previous conversation and said, "It is not only yesterday; today I have caught you with the stolen goods."

For this reason, it was given that name. The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha-dharma has been entrusted to kings, ministers, and powerful patrons, so that the lamp may be passed from one to another in an unbroken succession.
O Great Assembly, tell me: what is it that is being transmitted? After a long silence, he said: "It must be my elder brother Kāśyapa who can do it.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked: "How does this assembly on Vulture Peak differ from today's? The Master replied: "It is no different."
He fell into a pit and down a ditch. [The Master] said, "Why is it like this? He replied, "Blind.

[Someone] asked, "What is the house style of the Master? He replied, "A single word cuts off the mouths of a thousand rivers; only before a ten-thousand-fathom peak does one attain the profound mystery.

[Someone] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "At the side of King Chu’s city, the Ru River flows eastward. Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is truly..."

Without lingering on a single word or character, he then descended from his seat. A monk asked, "What is the mark of the Brahma-voice? He replied, "The braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs. The monk asked, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "The young bride riding the donkey, while her mother-in-law leads it. The monk asked, "In which phrase is this statement contained? He replied, "It cannot be contained within the Three Mysteries; how could the Four Phrases encompass it? The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? He replied, "It is like a man with a staff who has lost his way. The monk asked, "How can one find the way? He replied, "If you do not lose your way, you will naturally find it. The monk asked, "What is the ultimate principle? He replied, "A thousand sages have no place to set down their feet. The monk asked, "What is the Great Way? He replied, "The Great Way is broad and vast; it does not exclude the small. The monk asked, "What is the Small Way? He replied, "The Small Way is narrow and cramped; it does not admit the great. The monk asked, "What is the Middle Way? He replied, "The Middle Way is neither broad nor narrow; it is beyond all names and forms. The monk asked, "What is the Way of No-Way? He replied, "The Way of No-Way is where there is no 'way' to be found. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless is where even 'no-way' is absent. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Way is where both 'way' and 'no-way' are forgotten. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless is where even 'wayless' is extinguished. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless' is gone. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless is where even 'wayless wayless wayless' is utterly transcended. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless way' is completely absent. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless wayless way' is entirely non-existent. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless way' is completely void. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless way' is utterly beyond reach. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless way' is completely ungraspable. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless way' is entirely beyond the realm of speech. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He replied, "The Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way is where even 'wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless wayless way' is utterly transcended. The monk asked, "What is the Way of the Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Wayless Way? He said: "Heaven is long-lasting; earth is enduring; the sun and moon shine with equal brilliance. Entering the hall, he said:
"If you can realize it under the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher of Buddhas and patriarchs. If you realize it under the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher of gods and humans.
If you realize it under the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself. A monk asked: "What is the direct, shortcut path? He replied: "Sometimes in the mountains; sometimes..."
[The Master] was beneath a tree. [A monk] asked, "Where do the various sages of antiquity travel and practice? He replied, "They pull the plow and drag the harrow. [The monk] asked, "What is the Way?
He replied, "There is fire in the hearth, yet it is stirred without intent; everywhere one traverses freely and wanders at will. [The monk] asked, "What is one who is on the Way?
He replied, "Sitting and watching the beauty of the mist and clouds; not competing with the white clouds."
The eulogy says:
A blue dragon sporting in the ocean; a fine steed outstripping the herd;
having chewed the *kṣīravaktra* medicine, it has been exchanged bone for bone.
The gold used to stop the crying was cast away with all his heart;
He stirred his countenance upon the ancient road, yet was buried deep in a pit dug by Fengxue.
A master hand does not display its name; Bai Zhao was caught with the stolen goods.
The family style of this house is quite lax; at the mouths of a thousand rivers and before ten thousand peaks, the path is cut off, winding and turning many times.
Whether among the mountains or beneath the trees, the harmonious sounds are muffled and indistinct. They push the assembly on Vulture Peak into a ditch and down a pit.
Evil poison remains unextinguished in the heart; Driven by the supreme sages, one must pull the plow and drag the harrow amidst the braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs.
Who would dare wish to hear the Brahma-like tones of the true Buddha-body, eternal as earth and heaven?
To preserve that which has not yet been fully realized—this remains.
"Though one may use these three phrases to test the monks of the world, let me ask you: 'The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads it'—is this a worldly saying or not?
— Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao.
The Master’s name was Shanzhao. He was a native of Taiyuan, with the secular surname Yu. Initially, he went to visit Shoushan;

encountering him as the Master ascended the hall, the Master stepped forward and asked, “When Mazu ascended the hall and Baizhang rolled up his mat, what was the underlying meaning? Shoushan said, “The dragon’s sleeve is drawn back, and the entire body is revealed.
The Master asked, “What is your own understanding, Master? Shoushan said, “Where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.

Addressing the assembly: Every single phrase must possess the three gates of mystery (*san xuanmen*). Each gate of mystery must, in turn, possess the three essential paths (*san yaolu*). There is illumination (*zhao*) and there is timing (*shi*).

Sometimes illumination precedes function (*yong*); sometimes function precedes illumination; sometimes illumination and function occur simultaneously; and sometimes illumination and function do not occur at the same time.
Or, taking the case where illumination precedes function: this requires that we deliberate together. Or, taking the case where function precedes illumination...
"Shao! You must also be such a person before you can succeed. If illumination and function are simultaneous, how will you respond?
If illumination and function are not simultaneous, how will you manage them? He addressed the assembly, saying: "Fenyang has three secrets; it is difficult for monks to discern them.
If you further intend to ask 'How?'—the staff will be driven straight into your head! A monk asked: "How is it?"

This is a phrase for receiving beginners. [The Master] said: "You are a wandering monk (*pravrajita*). [The student] asked: "What is the phrase for discerning a monk? [The Master] said: "The sun rises in the west at dawn. [The student] asked:

"What is the phrase for the true command being put into effect? [The Master] said: "Bringing it from a thousand miles away to present one's old face. [The student] asked: "What is the phrase for settling heaven and earth? [The Master] said:
"In the continent of Uttarakuru, there grows long-grained rice; those who eat it have neither joy nor sorrow."
Zhen. A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest? He said, "Joining palms before the hermitage to question the World-Honored One.
"What is the host within the guest? He said, "Facing each other with no companion. "What is the guest within the host? He said, "Clouds spread across the sea;
drawing a sword to stir the Dragon Gate. "What is the host within the host? He said, "Three heads and six arms, upholding heaven and earth."
The wrathful Nātha struck the imperial bell. A monk asked, "What is the place where the student exerts effort? He replied, "Striking the Great Image at Jia Prefecture.
"What is the place where the student turns about? He replied, "Bathing the Iron Ox at Shan Prefecture.

"What is the place where the student finds intimacy? He replied, "Playing with the Lion in West River. Because it was bitterly cold in the north, the Master ended the night session. There was [a monk present].
A foreign bhikṣu arrived, shaking his mendicant's staff, and said to the Master, "There are six great beings in the assembly;

why do you not preach the Dharma? Having spoken, he ascended into the air and departed. The Master recorded this in a verse: "The foreign monk with the golden staff’s radiance Sought the Dharma and came to Fenyang.
These six men shall become great vessels; I urge you to proclaim it for them."
The eulogy says:
Lofty and solitary, transcending the world; serene and retiring, beyond compare—a rare treasure like the *zhī* fungus atop the ritual cauldron, an auspicious omen for the pure ancestral temple.
Jade groves and jeweled trees are treasures of the vast ocean;
the Great Elephant’s walking track leaves no trace of foxes.
Suddenly clarifying the meaning beyond words, the hair-puller draws forth and stirs the Dragon Gate— who recognizes the guest within the host?
The mechanism of the arrow-tip is released; the gates of the Three Mysteries are struck open.
With illumination and function established, there is the phrase that sets up heaven and earth. When eating long-grain rice, there is neither joy nor anger.
Xixia plays with lions, yet his claws and fangs are greatly lacking. Is the Way intimate or not?
In Shanfu, they spent all their strength trying to subdue the iron ox; yet it was difficult to turn it around.
This is the thief’s secret mechanism, which even the thousand sages did not know. To discern a monk, there are three keys;
the ghostly footprints were seen through by the barbarian monk. Only six people became great vessels.
Associating with those from Ye County, they were no different from those in the same pit;
chasing after Ciming with angry shouts, they offered rotten rice to idle deities as lightning rolled and winds swirled.
Having studied under seventy-two virtuous teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*), when they reached the point where mud and water are dragged along, it was most [difficult].
Suffering is identical with the ten wisdoms and the truth.
Chan Master Xingsheng of Yecheng was a successor of Shoushan;
his name was Guisong. He was the son of the Jia family of Jizhou. When the Master arrived at Shoushan, Shoushan raised his bamboo cane.
A monk asked, "If you call it a bamboo stick, it is 'contact'; if you do not call it a bamboo stick, it is 'avoidance. What shall I call it?
The Master seized the bamboo stick, snapped it in two, threw it on the ground, and said, "What is this? Shanshan said, "Blind! The Master then bowed.

Another monk asked, "I have received the Master’s instruction regarding a single drop of the Dharma-ocean; as for the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, what is it like? The Master replied, "The Hall of the High Ancestor."
Formerly, Fan Kui was angry. One must know that ten thousand *li* away, smoke and dust are cut off. A monk asked, "The chamber of Vimalakīrti does not take the sun and moon for its illumination.

[The Master] said, "His eyebrows are parted in eight characters. The monk asked, "I do not understand the meaning of this. [The Master] said, "His two ears hang down to his shoulders. A monk asked, "What is the pure Dharma-body?
[The Master] said, "A bamboo tally used as a toilet cleaner. He asked, "What is Vairocana? [The Master] said, "..."
The Master said, "In the Sangha, years of ordination determine rank; among the laity, seniority by age determines order. A questioner asked, "What is the place of profound depth?
He replied, "The cat has the merit of drinking blood; the tiger has the virtue of raising the dead. The questioner asked, "Is it not this very thing?

He replied, "Pounding in the southeast, grinding and pushing in the northwest. Addressing the assembly, he said, "Regarding the life-blood of the ancestral masters—whether ordinary or holy—there were Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa."

Heaven and hell, boiling cauldrons and glowing coals, the ox-headed jailers, the myriad phenomena of the universe, the sun, moon, and stars, the worlds of other directions and this realm—whether sentient or insentient beings—he draws a single line with his hand and says: "All enter this school.
Within this school, one can both kill people and bring them to life. To kill, one must have the sword that kills; to bring to life, one must...

"This is a phrase that brings people back to life. What is the 'sword that kills' and the 'phrase that brings people back to life'? Anyone who can speak it, come forward and say it before the assembly.
If you cannot speak it, you will have brought your entire life to naught. The Master’s countenance was stern and cold, and he was revered by all.
When the two monks Tiānyī Huái and Fúshān Yuǎn arrived, wishing to seek residence there, they encountered the snow and the bitter cold. The Master took some water...

As the water was being poured over him, the others all departed in anger; only the two men adjusted their robes and remained seated. When evening came, the Master arrived and scolded them, saying, "If you do not leave, I shall beat you.
Yuanren stepped forward and said, "I have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master.
How could I leave because of a single ladle of water? Even if you were to beat me to death, I would still not go. The Master laughed and said, "You..."

The two [monks] wished to practice Chan meditation, so they went to register as resident monks. Subsequently, Yuan was invited to serve as the head cook (dianzuo). This account is found in the *Wuku* (Armory);
it is not recorded here in detail.
The eulogy says:
The collar-iron weighs a thousand catties; stubborn and unruly, there is no one to rival him.
He divides his livelihood from Mount Fen and supports himself;
he has utterly ruined the private inheritance of the Linji house.
The pure body—using a toilet brush upside down or holding it crosswise, touching the back of the mechanism;
throwing bamboo rakes about with reckless abandon like wild tosses—before the Hall of the High Ancestor, Fan Kuai’s wrath was provoked; the ancestral wind has been insulted too much.
In Vimalakīrti’s chamber, the sun and moon shine bright; those who grasp at the literal meaning cannot fathom its intent.
The Master Vairocana, the Lord of the Dharmakāya, needlessly divides and analyzes; monks rank by their years of ordination, and laypeople by their age.
They perform the rites of raising the dead and swearing oaths of blood, their commentaries jumbled and confused—like a pestle pounding in the southeast while a millstone grinds in the northwest.
Huangbo’s intestines are as cold as frost on his face; His vast robes are frozen into ice.
He smelts copper for his liver and gallbladder, forging iron for his heart;

He drives Fushan away until he climbs the wall—no handle to grasp, yet he brings forth a malevolent disposition. A phrase that revives the living, a blade that kills; It thunders through the clear sky.

Pilili. Chan Master Fushan Yuanjian, whose name was Fayuan and whose style name was Yuanjian, was a successor of Yexian. He was a native of Zhengzhou and a son of the Wang family. Entering the hall, he said: "All..."
When the Buddha appears in the world, he establishes the gates of transformation without departing from the wisdom-eye of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

This is like the three eyes of Maheśvara and the three dots of the syllable *I*. Why is this? One eye is so tightly sealed that water cannot leak through; it is difficult for the ordained and the laity to distinguish one another.
One eye encompasses the entire great earth; the ten directions are unobstructed and pervasive. One eye surveys both high and low in a single glance, such that all myriad species behold it together.
Although it is so, if one is a monk of true substance, only when meeting him on the road with a distinct eye of right discernment will it be possible.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know what exists; the cat and the white ox, however, do know what exists.
Now tell me, what is it that they know exists? After a long silence: "In the deep autumn, rain falls across a thousand screens; at sunset, a single flute plays in the wind atop the towers."
When Wuzu Yan the Venerable was traveling to visit various masters, the Master said to him, "You have come late; I am old. You should rely on Baiyun.

Although I do not know him personally, I have seen his verse on the story of Linji’s three blows of the staff, and it is most profound and accurate. Yan then went to see Baiyun and attained the essential meaning.
The Master [Wuzu] then received Qing Huayan and entrusted to him the robe and sandals he had been granted by Dayang, ordering him to continue the lineage.
The Dongshan School’s verse says: Mount Sumeru stands in the vast void; the sun and moon cling to it as they revolve. The myriad peaks gradually lean upon one another;
only then do the white clouds begin to change. The wind of Shaolin rises from the thickets; the bamboo curtain at Caoxi is rolled up. The golden phoenix roosts in the dragon’s nest.

How could the imperial moss be crushed by carriage wheels? At first, when the Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang heard of the Master’s extraordinary brilliance, he saw him but had no way to distinguish his excellence.
Consequently, while playing chess with a guest, the Master sat beside them. The Duke called off the game and requested that the Master expound the Dharma based on the chessboard.

The Master immediately ordered the drum to be beaten for the formal assembly, and ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like two parties playing a game of chess. What does this mean?"

The opponent knows one's intent; when the opportunity arises, there must be no yielding. If you merely string together five stones and surround three, you must also penetrate a single path before you succeed.
There is a certain class of people who only know how to secure their own position by closing the gates, but do not understand how to seize the corners and break through the passes.

When their hard formations and tiger-mouths are displayed side by side, once the board is broken, their laborious maneuvers are in vain. Therefore it is said: "Fat borders are easy to obtain; a lean belly is difficult to maintain."

Seeking, contemplating, and acting—this leads to frequent loss of contact. When the mind is coarse, one repeatedly strikes one's head. Cease boasting of being a master of the game; do not vainly speak of immortals.
Whether you win the board or exceed the counting sticks is of no concern; tell me, before black and white have even been distinguished, where does that first move fall? After a long silence, he said:
"Of the nineteen paths from the beginning, how many people have wandered in delusion and attained awakening? The Master sighed deeply for a long time.
The Master retired to Huishengyan (Cave of the Sage’s Assembly) to expound the profound meanings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and composed the Nine Bends (*jiu dai*). He said:
"If one relies upon the Dharma-gate of Perfect Ultimate Reality, there are originally ten numerical categories. Now, these nine bends have already been explained for you all.
Is there yet another bend that you can see? If you can see it clearly, then please come forward and speak of it. If you can explain it clearly..."
"I allow you to pass through the preceding nine stages with the perfectly luminous eye of the Way. If your vision is not intimate and direct, your explanations will be inconsistent.
To rely solely on my words and take them as your own understanding is called slandering the Dharma. When you reach this point, what do you all say? The assembly was silent.
The Master rebuked him and sent him away. When the Master was young, he entered Sichuan with Da-guan Ying, Xue Da-tou, and seven or eight others to visit the Venerable Xiang-lin Yuan.

There, at Shuijing Gong (Crystal Palace), they investigated the essential principles of the Yunmen school; on several occasions they encountered hostile treatment, but the Master escaped through his wisdom.

Because the assembly recognized that the Master was proficient in administrative affairs, they called him Yuan Lu Gong (Master Yuan the Registrar). In his later years, the Master obtained the attendant Zishi.
He was greatly pleased. Whenever he received someone, he would invariably provide them with resources.
Zhan said:
"A living monk is simply one."
When the mouth is hungry, it swallows Buddhas and Patriarchs; wherever the feet reach, they stir up the monastic groves.
A hibernating dragon within its case, a "blown-hair" sword—its majesty prevails throughout the myriad kingdoms.
A bright moon pearl emerging from the womb of an old oyster—its radiance penetrates beyond the eight directions.
Pointing to the old Dongshan, he seized the seal of the direct transmission of the White Clouds;
unwilling to bestow it upon others himself, he compelled Qing Huayan to receive the robe of the secret entrustment from Ming'an. Disaster has befallen you, but the fault lies with me;
the immortal’s single game of chess was secretly arranged within the board. On the path of the spiritual mechanism, one must break through the barriers.
Mahesvara’s three eyes stand upright at the crown of his head; before the skull-cup, he loses his illumination as he probes the essential principles of Yunmen.
He tramples through the clouds of Mount Shu in his tattered straw sandals, embodying the ancestral style of the Xu family;
he steals the key and arrogantly opens the lock of the Fragrant Accumulation Hall.
In the deep autumn, rain falls across the curtains of a thousand homes; the Buddhas of the three periods have not permitted such mockery.
At sunset, the wind carries a single flute through the towers and pavilions; what clarity can be found in a white ox or a stray cat?
Dragging along the ninefold teachings, they emerge from within the thicket of entangling vines.
Having retired from the myriad affairs of state, he reclined with his pillow high within the Seongnyan Cave for a short while;
thus he won the reputation of being a "lazy fellow. In his old age, he became a "demon," leading Attendant Jasi to enter the weeds with his whole body.
Chan Master Ciming Yuan’s dharma name was Chuyuan.
He was a successor of Fenyang and a native of the Li clan of Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar; his mother was virtuous and urged him to leave the household life.
Together with Guquan, Yanyou, and others, he went to see Fenyang. After awakening to the essential meaning, he and several companions, including Dayu, took their leave of Fenyang.
They took turns declining to serve as the head of the assembly. Yang [Yunfeng] presented a verse, saying: "The heavens have no head; by the walls of Jizhou City, spears and halberds are displayed.
A general on a single horse passes beneath the forest; within the walls of Yuanzhou City, there is a clamor and din.
The Master said, "What kind of person am I that I would dare accept such a prediction? Thereupon he became the head. After taking his leave, he resided at Fuyan. When Huanglong saw him, he...
He was conceited in his own estimation. The Master rebuked him sternly and presented the story of Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman to Long.

Long had no reply. It was several days later before he attained realization, whereupon he offered this verse: “Prominent in the forest of monks is Zhaozhou; The old woman was exposed, leaving no trace. Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror;
Travelers need not regard the road as an enemy. He further inscribed the character “you” (有) on the palm of his hand.
The Master saw him and said, "It is well indeed, yet there is one character that is not so. Long then opened his palm to show it to him, and the Master gave his seal of approval.
Later, when Yangqi was attending upon him, he asked, "When the dark birds warble their songs and leave the clouds to enter the tangled peaks, what then?
The Master said, "I walk amidst the wild weeds; you, moreover, have entered a deep village. Yangqi said, "An official does not permit even a needle."
He asked another question. The Master then gave a shout. Qí said, "A fine shout! The Master shouted again. Qí also shouted. The Master shouted twice in succession.
Seeing that Quàn Dàdào was approaching, the Master asked, "A single cloud spans the valley mouth; from where does the traveler come?
Quàn looked around and said, "Where did the fire come from last night? It has burned out the graves of the ancients. The Master said, "Not yet. Speak further."
Quán made the sound of a tiger. The Master struck his meditation mat once. Quán then pushed the Master down onto the seat. The Master made the sound of a tiger again.
Quán said, "I have encountered more than seventy virtuous teachers, but only today have I met a true master. At that time, Zhendi was serving as the attendant for Shanzhi;
he had returned from Jinluan and was raising objections. The Master rebuked him, saying, "It has not even been a month since the summer retreat ended, yet you are already [challenging me]."
"Having reached this point, you have destroyed the forest; what urgent matter is there? Zhuan said, "It is simply that I have not yet penetrated through the Great Matter.
The Master asked, "What do you take to be the essential core of the Buddha-dharma? Zhuan said, "Cloudless, clouds arise upon the ridge; moonlit, the moon falls into the heart of the waves.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "With wrinkled face and missing teeth, you still harbor such a view! Zhuan said, "I pray that you will resolve this for me. The Master said:

"You asked me about the previous conversation regarding Ultimate Truth. The Master said, "Cloudless, a peak rises above; moon present, it falls into the heart of the waves. Zhen subsequently attained realization.

Later, when the Master was visited by two men, he ascended the hall and said: "In this brisk and cool landscape, companions visit a place of stillness. Tea is brewed with water from the mountain peaks;
incense is burned with firewood from within the caves. Be careful and heedful. The two gentlemen, Yang and Li, [then] served the Master.
Dharma Friend. The dialogue is seen in the Master’s own biography.
The eulogy says:
Even before emerging from the mother’s womb, He already possessed a resolve that transcends the mundane world.
Wearied by the scholar’s cap, he cast aside the books of Eastern Lu; entering the Patriarch’s chamber, he struck at the meaning of the Westward Coming.
Following conditions with carefree expansiveness, he plays upon waves a thousand fathoms deep, where even a fish that swallows a boat finds room;
his great wisdom is profoundly clear, for the nine-bent pearl was threaded only by the aid of the silkworm.
He concealed himself within the military ranks and met Fenyang amidst the wild grasses of the frontier;
he verified the "old woman" and boiled the "Yellow Dragon" in the southern golden furnace.
Bearing this heavy trust of the sacred culture, a single thread held up a thousand pounds.
The General spreads his halberds and spears by the city walls; alone, he faces ten thousand cavalry in the deep village’s withered grass.
Sharing the same track as Yangqi yet following a different path, amidst wild fires and ancient tombs, he listens to the valley spring falling down and rising up again of its own accord.
A hawk strikes at the mountain peak, its murderous breath steaming the clouds;
A tiger crouches amidst the frost, its stench swirling across the earth.
It sweeps away the deluded child’s frantic views and understandings: In the heart of the waves there is a moon; atop the ridge there is no cloud.
Thanking my fellow scholars for visiting my desolate retreat: I burn firewood from the caves and cook water from the mountains.
In the late autumn at the ancestral temple, I reflect that to protect the city, one must first capture the Imperial Academician Yang and the Commandery Marshal Li.
Chan Master Yangqi Hui’s name was Fanghui.
His secular surname was Liang, and he was a native of Yichun in Yuanzhou. When Ciming was residing at Nanxuan, the Master went there to attend upon him.
Later, when [Ciming] moved to Shishuang, the Master requested and was appointed as the Superintendent (Jansi). Whenever Ciming finished his meal, he would invariably go for walks in the mountains.

The Master observed that [Zhao]ming had not gone far before he struck the drum to assemble the community. Zhaoming hurried back and asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "The evening session. Zhaoming then addressed the assembly;
from this, the monastic community came to call it the "evening session" (*wanshan*). Later, when the Master appeared in the world and had just ascended the seat, a monk stepped forward.
The Master said, "Before the old fisherman has cast his line, a leaping scale has come surging through the waves. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "I do not believe you."
"Way. The monk clapped his hands and returned to the assembly. The Master said, "How much wind from the Dragon King can he endure?
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves. The monk said, "Is it not just this very thing? The Master said, "Elder of Hunan.
After finishing his address to the assembly, the Master descended from his seat. Jiufeng Qin held him back, saying, "I am glad to have found a fellow practitioner."
The Master asked, "As for the matter of being fellow practitioners, how is it? [Qin] said, "Yangqi pulls the plow; Jiufeng drags the harrow.
The Master said, "At such a time as this, is Yangqi in front, or is Jiufeng in front? As Qin hesitated, the Master pushed him away and said, "I thought you were a fellow practitioner;
it turns out you are not. From that time on, his reputation spread throughout all quarters. One day, he ascended the hall and said, "When Yangqi first settled in this house..."
The walls were sparse; the entire bed was covered with snow and true pearls. He shrank his neck and sighed in dark lamentation. After a long while, he said:
"I am suddenly reminded of the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees. Master Zanshi of Qingzhou Peak said: "One must understand that it is like a jade carver refining a *fanyu* gem;
the *wufu* stones are cast aside. Thus, those whose radiance is magnificent and grand, who are able to carry on their family legacy, are like the *Biluo* Stele, for which no counterfeit exists."
The eulogy says:
His divine faculties are keen and awakened; his transcendent spirit is lofty and expansive.
He asks the way while leading the murmuring birds through the chaotic peaks.
Lowering the hook to catch leaping fish as they dart through the waves,
he pressed upon Ciming for the evening sermon; drawing up his robes to beat the drum,
he joined with Jiufeng as companions, pulling the plow and supporting the ox.
Striding across a three-legged donkey, he gallops with swift steps and treads upon the heads of elephants and dragons;
dwelling in a solitary hermitage, he scatters pearls and chestnuts like ice and snow across his bed.
To grasp this, one must have the capacity to swallow and spit it out like Baiyun Yuan.
The broken-legged cauldron is entrusted to Baoning Yong to wield and refine;
its chisel and axe ring out with a sharp resonance. Like the artisan Shi removing plaster and whitewash, his tongs and hammer are subtle and precise;
like the jade-worker refining the *fanyu* gem, he polishes it to perfection.
Thus, the single transmission of Shaoshi was entirely brought under his command. When he observed later generations who, lacking integrity, stole his robes and sought fame,
did he not feel ashamed before his teacher?—
Master Nanyuan of Huanglong.
The Master’s name was Huinán. He was a successor of Címíng and the son of the Zhāng family of Xìnzhōu. He received full ordination at Huáiyù Mountain. Initially, he received certification from Lètán;
thereafter, leading his disciples, he traveled to various regions, maintaining a sense of self-importance. By chance, he met Yúnyfēng Yuè while traveling together through the Western Mountains.

During their conversation at night, [Fengxue] asked about the essential meaning transmitted by Letan. The Master (Zhaozhou) spoke of its core. Yuanze said, "What Letan transmits is like quicksilver and silver;
it may be admired as a mere plaything, but it flows away as soon as it enters the furnace. If you wish to resolve this matter clearly, you must see Ciming.

The Master threw his pillow at him in anger. Yuanze did not speak to him again. The Master pondered this in silence and said: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends with "The Master pondered this in silence and said," indicating the narrative continues beyond the provided excerpt.*
Yue delighted in Cuiyan, who caused me to see clearly. Even if I had attained something, what would it have to do with Yue?

At dawn he set out, but upon reaching the halfway point, he heard that Ciming was not engaged in formal practice; thus, he did not go there. He stayed at Fuyan, where Xian appointed him as the Secretary.
Shortly thereafter, Xian passed away, and the Prefectural Governor appointed Ming to succeed him. The Master said, "Yue told me to see him; now he sits here."

He waited for Ming to arrive. Upon seeing him from afar, both his mind and countenance became solemn. During the evening *can* (assembly), the Master severely rebuked the heterodox interpretations of various quarters.
He then said, "A great man undertaking this matter seeks definitive discernment; how can you harbor doubt within your breast? You have come seeking instruction with incense in hand.
Ming replied, "I am a secretary traveling with disciples; if there is business, we may sit and deliberate upon it. The Master then ordered the attendant—
Yuanming advanced his seat. The Master firmly declined. Yuanming said, "The Secretary has studied Yunmen Chan; he must be well-versed in its essential meaning.
Regarding the saying, 'Letting off three blows of the staff at Dongshan'—should one receive them or not? The Master replied, "One should receive them. Yuanming spoke with a grave expression.

Upon hearing the sound of a staff, he would say, "He deserves a blow. From dawn until dusk, whenever he heard the cries of crows and magpies, or the sounds of bells, fish-shaped gongs, drums, and wooden clappers, he would likewise say, "He should receive a blow.
When would the receiving of blows ever come to an end? The Master’s face flushed with heat and sweat poured down; only later did he realize the underlying meaning.
The Master resided at Huanglong and used "The Buddha’s Hand," "The Donkey’s Foot," and "Birth Conditions" to test his students. He was known as Huanglong.
The Three Gates: Juehu (Tiger at the Corner) was Ciming. People praised him, saying: "Juehu of Shishuang—his gaze radiates a majesty that reaches a hundred paces.
A book says: "If one throws the bright moon pearl or the night-shining jade into the darkness, everyone will instinctively draw their swords and stare at it."
The encomium says:
Receiving the scriptures on Huaiyu Mountain, he drills into the piles of worn-out paper;
his spirit pierces through heaven and earth, his bold resolve surging with vigor.
His reputation was widespread throughout the rivers and lakes;
he struck Yunfeng with a pillow. When the strange mercury and silver enter the furnace, they flow; he struck his own chest.

Upon hearing the sound of the staff, he realized he deserved to receive it—how shameful and painful! Ciming’s perfection is attained by knocking upon the breast. How could one not accept the blow when hearing its sound?
The Abbot of the Assembly: the thorny *liji* fruit; Ten years of shared practice:
the "Dharma-seal of the Melon" for those who have transcended the holy and the profane. Half a lifetime of enduring indignity:
sitting by the thoroughfare to sell one's wares. When a fallen hairpin or dropped earring is found, the desire for it has already vanished.
Establishing three barriers to test men: the Buddha’s hand and the donkey’s hoof—approach them and the soul is snatched away;
the tiger’s eye, its radiance shaking for a hundred paces, the yellow dragon’s nostrils flare as it rouses the slumbering beasts of the nine abysses.
This is what is called Linji’s mastery in perpetuating his lineage. Illuminating past and present, it is like the bright moon, the luminous pearl, and the night-shining jade.
Master Baojue Xin.
The Master’s name was Zuxin. He was a successor of Huanglong and a native of Nanxiong. His secular surname was Wu. In his youth, he studied Confucian classics;

at the age of nineteen, he lost his sight, but after his mother prayed for him, his vision was restored. He left the household life after offering a poem and received ordination. Initially, he visited Xuefeng and remained there for three years.

Subsequently, in the fourth year of the Huanglong era, there was no point of entry for him. One day, while pouring out hot water to wash his hands, he had an awakening, yet his spiritual capacity had not yet been unleashed.

Later, while staying at Shishuang, he read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). Upon reaching the passage where a monk asked Duofu, "What is the single cluster of bamboo of Duofu?
Duofu replied, "One stalk, two stalks, leaning. The monk said, "I do not understand. Duofu said, "Three stalks, four stalks, bent. At this, [he attained sudden realization].
He saw that when his two masters slept, their hands were in the same position. Later, after the previous Dragon (Huanglong) entered extinction, this master succeeded him as the abbot.
In his room, he frequently raised his fist and said, "To call it a 'fist' is to hit [the mark]; not to call it a 'fist' is to miss [the mark]. Few among the assembly attained realization.
When Zhang Wujin visited the master, he offered this verse: "I have long heard of the dragon within the Yellow Dragon Mountains; Upon arriving, I see only an old mountain-dweller."

There was no place for him to enter. At that time, there was a cat nearby. The Master pointed at it and said, "Do you see that one who wishes to catch a mouse?
Its two eyes stare fixedly without blinking; its four paws crouch upon the ground without moving; all its faculties are directed forward; its head and tail are in a straight line;

and there is nothing it raises that does not hit the mark. If you can be like this—your mind free from distracting conditions and your six sense-faculties naturally stilled—you may remain in silent contemplation."
He investigated until he never missed a single point. Under the Master’s words, he attained great enlightenment. When Lingyuan visited the Master, he was reflecting on Xuefeng’s words;
becoming weary, he began walking meditation (caṅkrama). As he stepped, he left his sandals behind; as he bent down to retrieve them, he attained great enlightenment.
