The eulogy says:
This master of the mountain in his true colors—With a single punch, he distinguishes between back and touch.
The eyes that penetrate all directions, once blind, are again restored to sight;
the books that fill the rafters are cast aside with no further succession.
To sever one's arm and settle the mind is the essence of the secret transmission—empty-handed, one plunges into boiling water.
Penetrating the perilous barrier of Buddha’s hands and donkey’s feet, The steep mechanism bites the arrowhead, alive yet buried in the mountain valley.
The cassia fragrance disperses before the crags near and far;
seeing this directly, much blessing arrives. At the edge of the courtyard, the bamboo stalks divide into slants and curves.
Dust flies and the heavens are obscured, difficult to sweep away;
Idle antiques must be avoided lest they become a cat’s chest-bump that hinders its catching mice—when cleverness is exhausted, clumsiness arises. Who can employ their wits to the end?
Only by following conditions as they come can one enter without error; To slay the spiritual source, blunt iron is superior to a razor-sharp blade.
Selected among the Buddhas, he attained the highest rank; The "poisonous arsenic" that killed Daxin was not yet the true venom.
He possesses the cool radiance of the moon over a midnight emerald pool;
With a jade axe, he skillfully repairs it, and with a pure lute, he plucks the strings of the "Yangchun" and "Baixue" melodies. He personally joins them together with the "luan-jiao" glue.
The descendants of Huanglong are as numerous as the sun and moon; they are difficult to count. Though there may be many horns, having but one of these unicorns is quite sufficient.
— Chan Master Baiyun Endian.
The Master’s name was Shouduan. He was the son of the Ge family of Hengzhou. He received the tonsure under the Chan Master Yushan of Chaling.
Initially, he went to see Yangqi, who asked him, "I have heard that when your preceptor fell over the bridge, he attained realization and composed a verse that is quite extraordinary.
Can you recite it? The Master immediately recited: "I possess a divine pearl, Long locked away by the dust of worldly toil. This morning..."
When the dust is cleared, the light arises, illuminating the myriad peaks of the mountains and rivers. Qizhao laughed loudly and departed.
The Master was startled and could not sleep all night. At dawn, he questioned him again. Qizhao said, "Did you see yesterday’s 'night-fox' being beaten?

When the attendant Qing-su was about to pass away, he visited Guizong, and during their night conversation, they reached this matter.

"This is it. Fan said, "The Excellency knows only the final phrase of purity and simplicity, yet when the true reality and the true medicine manifest before you, you fail to awaken to them.
They were all astonished and asked, "Is this truly so? He replied, "If you have doubts, then seek elsewhere.

At these words, they all suddenly realized the Master’s point of application. They then lit incense and looked toward Guizong to repent for their former conduct at Dongshan. One day, they received the Master’s guidance.
He chanted it and read it with great joy, saying to Yuanwu, "How shameful! In this age of the Dharma’s decline, there is such a true spiritual friend.
When the Master was traveling, he was accompanied by two monks. Upon arriving at the place of Xue Datou at Guyin, he asked, "When three people travel together, there must be one who possesses wisdom.
What is this 'one wisdom'? The two monks were speechless. The Master stepped down from his shoulder and responded immediately.

The eulogy says:
His life’s conditions lay beyond the conventional;
He broke free from the scholar’s cap and roamed through all quarters, his spirit ever self-reliant. Though he exhausted the direct pointing to the mind, he could not yet find peace.
Swallowing the Nine-and-Eight Cloud-Dreams within the breast—there is never so much as a mustard seed of obstruction;
Flooding the Eight-Thousand-Verse River of Shu upon the tongue—there is always ample wave and surge.
I ask, where did you obtain these two shoes? Amidst the accumulated greenery, the Southern Current surges upward; the path of the mechanism is alive.
Dragging a cloth skirt, he emits the stench of excrement; In Tuṣita Heaven, he delights in sniffing dry skulls.
All his life he brandishes a great banner, Achieving great merit upon the dragon-and-snake battlefield.
He tramples the donkey’s hooves at the Three Passes, And gallops through ten shadows amidst a herd of steeds.
The teaching of the final phrase is inexhaustible; if you have doubts, seek another teacher elsewhere.

the Old Dongshan praises from behind. Whenever meeting people, he repeatedly joins his palms in greeting.
Before Xue Datou, he was struck with a shout; Having no place to set his face in shame, the peacock’s feathers are inherently poisonous.
The tiger’s body is originally striped;
the wondrous point one wishes to speak of is beyond words. The moon shifts its light onto the flower shadows upon the balustrade.
The Fifth Patriarch, Chan Master Fayan:
His name was Fayen; he succeeded Baiyun. He was the son of the Deng family from Mianzhou.

Initially, while listening to lectures in Chengdu, he cited the case of a non-Buddhist heretic from Xitian who established a doctrinal proposition and questioned a disciple of the Buddha, saying: "When a Bodhisattva attains the Way, his spirit and wisdom merge in darkness."

When principle and object meet, there is no distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized. Ultimately, by what means is realization achieved? The disciple’s argument fell into error;

consequently, the bells and drums were not struck. He entered and exited through the rear gate and returned wearing his *kāṣāya* robe. When the Tripitaka Master arrived, he gathered the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) once more and explained:
"It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves. Thus, the Way was subdued. He then questioned the various Dharma masters, saying: "Cold..."
That it was "warm" (the stage of *ūṣmagata*) could be known; however, I do not yet understand the principle of "self-knowing. Everyone remained silent.

One among them said, "If you wish to clarify this, you must go south to see one who has realized the essence of the Buddha-mind school. The Master then traveled south. Upon reaching Xingyuan, he stayed there for some time.
When his former teacher heard of this, he sent a letter saying: "You have emerged from the jar of fermented soy sauce, only to enter the jar of pickled vegetables again."
The Master then set out on his journey. Upon arriving at Fushan, he raised this question regarding the meaning of the teaching. Fushan said, "The Tathāgata has secret words;
Kāśyapa did not conceal them. The Master’s doubts were thereby resolved. Fushan then directed him to visit Baiyun.

When the Master arrived there, he asked about the story of the *maṇi* jewel and attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse of realization, saying: "A plot of vacant land before the mountain— With palms joined, I earnestly asked."

The Patriarch said: "How many times have I sold it only to buy it back again? It is for my love of the pines and bamboos that draw in the pure wind. Yunyin approved this and addressed the assembly, saying:
"In general, when studying under a teacher, one must be like a swift hawk striking a sparrow; as soon as it hits the ground, it flies away.
If it remains crouching or sitting there, it is of no use. In a small lecture, he said: "For more than ten years, I have traveled the seas in search of the Way, and I have seen..."

Later, they came before Baoyun, where they bit into a single iron *gān* (a savory stew) and found it possessed every flavor.
But tell me, how would you express the single phrase of this *gān*? He then said: "The cockscomb flower blooms, beautifying the early autumn."

Prajñā is the sharp blade; wisdom is the torch.

he went to Chengdu’s Daci Temple to hear lectures and inquire into the principle of self-knowledge.

Seeing the perfect mirror, one realizes that the Tathāgata has secret words;
he loves the fields before the mountain. Pines and bamboos draw in the pure wind, striking a dialect beyond the ordinary; Yangping scatters white rain.
The sound of the *kūṭaja* bird’s call spreads like a plum blossom; In the dark, it gnaws at the grieving heart.
Purple cockscomb flowers dye the tips of the silk threads; Mistakenly taken for a *kañcika* garment, the beggar gains his seat.
He patrols the quarters, boasting that the attendant understands Zen.
Lustrous jade is without flaw; the grinding courtyard is shared with women singing and dancing.
The hundred flavors of the "Iron Sour and Bitter" are complete, left entirely to the living patch-robed monk to swallow or spit out.
To the very end, who can understand its sweetness or bitterness?
Chan Master Yuanwu Qin, whose name was Keqin, was a successor of Dongshan. He was the son of the Luo family from Pengzhou. Initially, he attended lectures in Chengdu;
Lord Fan of Shu composed a poem to encourage him to travel on pilgrimage, which said: "Chengdu is indeed a land of great prosperity, yet one must stop there only because of its flowers."

Deluded by wine, he subsequently left Sichuan and went to rely on [Master] Shan at Mount Dongshan. Finding no point of entry, he took his leave of Fojian. Shan said, "When you reach the region of Zhejiang, you will be struck by a fever;

only then will you remember me. When the Master arrived at Jinshan, he fell gravely ill. Fojian was also ill at Dinghui Temple, so he wrote a letter to arrange a meeting. Once their illnesses had subsided, they returned to Mount Dongshan.

"The one who will extinguish my lineage is Keqin. Later, after the Master returned to reside at Zhaojue, he heard that Nantang had returned to lay life. The Master remembered him;
hearing from others that he was selling incense in the city, the Master sent a novice boy there to buy some.

While waiting for him to hand over the incense, the Master asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He observed what words and phrases the man would offer, and immediately took note of them.
He returned. Following the instructions, the boy went there and asked. The Abbot held up some incense and said, "This packet of incense sells for only five coins.

The boy returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "This fellow is still here! He then personally encouraged him to become a monk once again. The Master established himself at Daisui and subsequently resided at Zhaojue.
Later, while Daci was in attendance, the Master one day ascended the hall and cited Yunmen’s teaching on the Buddhas.
Regarding the "Place of Origin" (the story of "Walking on Water at East Mountain"): [Zhaozhou] held up his staff and said, "I am not like that.

Suppose someone were to ask me, 'What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? I would simply say to him: 'A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. Hui attained realization.
Later, when he served as the Head Seat and presided over the *bǐngfú* (the whisk), a village monk approached him the following day and asked, "Last night, the Head Seat..."
The Master called for the Head Seat (Shouzuo) to give a formal discourse. The Master pinched his nose with his finger once, and as he descended from the dais, the assembly burst into laughter.
Huì immediately went up to the Abbot’s quarters to take his leave. The Master said, "Head Seat, last night the Buddhas of the three periods were reviled by you;
the Patriarchs of the six generations were reviled by you. I merely pinched my nose lightly, yet you could not even depart. Huì was unaware that he was breaking into a cold sweat. The Master—
Jiashan took up Xuedou’s words and titled his work the *Biyán jí* (Blue Cliff Records). The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* states: "A son should be like Sun Zhongmou;
the sons of Jingsheng are nothing but piglets and dogs. As for the golden duck, the Master revealed the verse through the sound of Xiaoyu.
As for the stone cicada, it refers to the Master’s burial at the Jin River upon his passing into nirvana.
The encomium says:
With the majestic bearing of one who has eaten oxen and the spirited spirit of a crane poised on tiptoe,
Master Fan of Shu counsels departure from the flourishing and opulent land of Zhusjin.
The old man of Dongshan curses for the sake of ripening the grain in Jiangnan;
within the voice of the sick child Xiaoyu, he recognizes the bridge of a donkey’s saddle as his father’s jaw.
Within the lines of the "Warm Breeze" verse, he seizes the rat-trap glue and treats it as his own family kin.
He instructed the youth to purchase incense; he pulled the pearl from the Southern Hall back to the Pu-hu River.
He moved the earth of Qinglin; he let the Buddha-eye leap forth at Longjin.
He upheld the teachings of Biyan, yet he dragged through the mud and carried the water.
Reviving the legacy of Zhaojue— listen to the clashing jade and ringing metal beneath your feet;
having already received the seal of the extinction of the lineage upon your nose,
how could you lack the heart of a cow licking its calf?
The golden duck’s incense has faded; one returns home drunk from amidst the lutes and songs.
Stone cicadas bloom among the flowers; laughing, he walks through the brocade-lined riverbanks. Heaven protects this culture.
Among the eleven generations since Linji, there was born a "Zhongmou" (a grandson); even though his son Jingsheng was a mere commoner.
Like a dragon galloping or a tiger bounding, it is difficult to follow in their fragrant dust.

Chan Master Nantang Jing, whose name was Yuanjing, was a successor of the Fifth Patriarch. He was a native of Langzhou and surnamed Zhao. While the Master was at the Patriarch’s stupa, the Patriarch raised [the case] and said:
"The mind is itself Buddha. Mazu carrying a wooden board, Nanquan killing the cat, and Zhaozhou’s "dog has no Buddha-nature" story—these are all instances of his skillful maneuvering.
In responding to them, he was entirely without obstruction. Later, when the story of the "wild dog" was raised, his answer was slightly delayed.

Yunmen suddenly turned his face and said, "It is not so. The Master asked, "If it is not so, then how? Yunmen said, "This is not so; together with what came before, it is not so at all. The Master [said], "..."
The monk said, "I pray that the Master will compassionately grant me instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Look at how Zihu’s dog takes people's heads above and takes people's feet below.
Those who enter the gate must look well. As soon as he saw a monk enter, he would say, "Look at the dog!
[He added,] "If you can offer a turning phrase at the point where Zihu says 'look at the dog,' you will leave Zihu speechless and allow this old monk to clamp his jaws shut."

"Kou! This was the point of final resolution. The Master was fond of eating chicken, and the assembly detested this. Mountan [Zhaozhou] knew of it. One day, when entering the room for instruction, the Master hid a chicken in his sleeve.
When Mountan raised a koan to interrogate him, the Master drew the chicken out from his sleeve and made it crow.

Mountan then laughed. The Master resided at Daisui. Previously, there had been a dragon dwelling in the abbot’s quarters and sleeping chamber; for generations, no one had dared to approach them. When the Master arrived, he intended to...

The master was lying down. The head monk informed him, but the master did not look back and continued to lie there. He saw a dragon lying on his bed; the master pushed it away with his hand, saying, "Old beast!
Leave half the couch for this old monk," and then lay down. When he woke up, the dragon was gone, and from that time on, it did not return.
There was a Dharma heir in Ye County who lived at Fangshui in Hanzhou. He presented a verse to the assembly, which said: "In the pool of Fangshui..."
The "Turtle-Nosed Snake": As soon as one directs the mind toward it, it wriggles away. Who can pull the snake’s head out? For two hundred years, no one has offered a word on this.
After the Master had finished citing the three phrases, he added a comment, saying: "A turtle-nosed snake in a square pool of water. A monk asked:
"What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'? He replied: "Vivaciously seize the Demon King by the nostrils and pierce him through. [The monk asked: "What is..."
"Neither person nor environment can take it away. He said, "Riding a white ox through the marketplace in broad daylight.

While Yung-ch’iu Ching was in deep meditation, the Master brought up the story of Hsiang-yen regarding the dragon’s roar in the withered tree. After the Master had questioned him back and forth, Ching attained realization. The Master said, "Do not remain in the cold ravine where strange grasses grow green;
sitting amidst the white clouds, your lineage will not flourish. Ching said, "I must brandish the sword; if I do not brandish the sword, I am but a fisherman."
His father was nesting in a tree. The Master, startled, said, "You little fellow! Take care! and departed. He returned to Shitou, who was a stone mason by profession and could not read.

Longing for the life of a monk, he sought someone to orally transmit the *Lotus Sūtra* to him; he then memorized it through silent recitation. He entered the service of his master, performing tasks such as sweeping.
One day, the master ordered him to fetch some stones. As he turned back with them, holding a hammer and striking at the stone, he continued to recite the sūtra without ceasing. The master remarked:
He said, "Today it is hollow and jagged; tomorrow it will be hollow and jagged. When birth and death arrive, how shall one resolve this?

He was struck with sudden realization, set aside his vessel, and prostrated himself, seeking the ultimate Dharma. Consequently, he followed [the Master] to the abbot’s quarters, where he was instructed to cease reciting the sutras and instead contemplate the koan of Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman.
After a long time, he was chipping at a stone. The stone was hard; he struck it with all his might, and suddenly, he caught sight of a flash of fire. Thereupon—
He attained enlightenment. He presented a verse, saying: "Having exhausted all effort, there is nothing at all to grasp. The sparks fly apart; the original [nature] was always right here.
The Master said, "You have penetrated it thoroughly. He again presented a verse, saying: "The three armies do not move, yet the banners flash. The old woman is truly the foot of the Demon King.
Zhaozhou’s handleless iron broom sweeps away all dust and smoke; the wind whistles coolly. The Master nodded in approval.
He subsequently became a monk and later entered the world to succeed his master. In the preface to the *Recorded Sayings of Stonehead* composed by Mr. Jin-yun, it is said:

"In his later years, the Fifth Patriarch obtained Nantang, who was coarse, violent, and fierce; he overstepped the bounds of Xuanze and Yuanhui. When heaven was exhausted and earth was narrow, he threw himself upon the great Sui.
Turning back the hands that wield the hammer against stone at Stonehead, he struck upward at the firm and lofty heights. Since his exertion of strength was so crude..."
With a single blow, he penetrated through. Later, he sat in meditation amidst the mountains of Diaoyu; his character was as rugged and steep as the cliffs, ten times more so than his master’s.

His fierce nature was like lethal arsenic, leaving no room for a morsel to pass down. Because the Master’s transcendent liberation set him apart from the crowd, Dongshan established the Nantang Hall specifically for him to dwell in.
Thus he received his name.
The eulogy says:
A monk from beyond the ordinary; born with no worldly intellect.
Vivaciously seizing the Demon King by the nostrils to pierce them, He deliberately causes the Baizhang monasteries to fall into ruin.
With eyes turned back to glare at his mother, A sinister wind like a fierce tiger emerges from the forest;
The village atmosphere oppresses one, As he rides a yellow ox through the marketplace in broad daylight.
Just as a water-snake has pulled its head out but cannot get it back in—exhausting all one’s strength with no way to resolve it—your "fox-dog" speech comes too late.
Together with what preceded it, it is entirely not sandalwood mixed with cow dung; this bundle of fragrance sells for only five cash.
Steep cliffs and Guaiya; watch as the little fellow displays his slight skill—boiling a chicken to eat.
His mouth is full of rank stench, accompanying Longmian;
his entire body is covered in mud and water.
A single hook hangs coldly upon the pine treetops as the moon; how many such expansive sentiments are there in the peaks of Huailin?
As the fragrant breeze carries the heralds of spring flowers, one feasts before the peony screens with great elegance.
Brandishing a precious sword with ease, the lightning flashes across the sky at Jingyuchou.
Casting down the iron hammer, the golden sound of the stone returns as it is thrown to the ground;
both holy and profane sentiments are exhausted, and even the Buddha-eye finds no trace. It is no wonder that the venerable masters Pu, Xu, and Deng established a separate hall to accommodate him.
The Buddha-inspected Master Qin, whose dharma name was Huìqín, was a successor of the Fifth Patriarch. He was the son of the Wáng family of Shūzhōu.

When he first visited the Fifth Patriarch, he repeatedly contemplated the phrase, “This one reality alone is true; all else is not real,” until he attained a realization. However, because the Patriarch did not grant him formal certification, he took his leave. Later...
He returned once more. It happened that the Patriarch was presiding over the assembly when a monk stepped forward and asked: "A monk once asked Zhaozhou, 'What is the house style of the Master?
Zhaozhou replied, 'This old monk is deaf; why do you not ask in a loud voice? When the monk asked again, Zhaozhou said, 'You asked about my house style, and I have already recognized yours.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and immediately went to the abbot’s quarters to seek certification.

The principle was thus established, and the Master was unable to answer. The following day, he suddenly attained realization and said to Wuxue, "Dongsi asked for only one grain, yet Yangshan poured out an entire wicker basket.
Wuxue deeply approved of this. Initially he resided at Taiping; next, he resided at Zhongshan. Entering the hall for a discourse, he said:
"The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Peach blossoms are red, plum blossoms are white—who says that their harmonious blending is not the Way?"
A single color. The swallow speaks; the oriole sings. Who says that "guan-guan" is but a single sound?

Failing to penetrate the pivot of the Patriarch’s gate, one mistakenly takes mountains and rivers for one's own eyes. A monk asked, "I have heard that you, Master, personally saw the Fifth Patriarch—is this true?
The Master said, "The iron ox chews through the golden grass. On the anniversary of the Patriarch’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "At this time last year, the red furnace..."
A flake of snow flies. Today is the same time as last year. Cao E reads the night inscription. This final phrase—no Buddha-eye can peer into it.
Upon the peak of White Lotus Mountain, the red sun circles Mount Sumeru. The bird pecks at the coral tree; the whale swallows the *lìshuǐ* rhinoceros.
The foundation of the Great Peace remains; for ten thousand ages, it is inherited by Yangqi. This verse concerns the occasion when Bodhidharma met the King of Liang.
The Verse of Circumstance says: The first bell tolls at the Agate Pavilion; at midday, the Azure Dragon sleeps most soundly. Again, the drum is struck atop the Phoenix Terrace;
at midnight, the auspicious phoenix has not yet begun its dance. The imperial foundation is as firm as a massive rock;
the foreign monk has spent his life’s strength in vain. Turning back toward Shaolin, he departs; fallen flowers fill the ground, spring in disarray. The Verse of Confirmation:
Regarding the occasion of the Elder’s visit to Linji, it is said: "The mechanism of a crashing thunderbolt met with Zhaozhou;
to benefit others, one must reach the point of final consummation. Holding aloft within his palm the Xiangshanzi, he ascends straight up to the high-twelfth story."
The eulogy says:
The clouds deepen over the Huai fields; Mount Longmian is small.
The young of the dragon and the phoenix have shed their shells and emerged; the splendor of the mountains and rivers has been utterly captivated.
In his breast, spears and armor stand in dense array like ten thousand cavalry; his spirit is as stern as the autumn wind.
From beneath his tongue, flutes and pipes harmonize the five notes; his speech is like the song of spring birds.
Having boiled medicinal herbs for ninety days at Mount Susai, he harbors a deep resentment toward the Eastern Mountain.
A single bell tolls at the Agate Pavilion;
lost in the shadows of the myriad phenomena, one encounters Bodhidharma. How often has one recognized this family style amidst the heap of sounds and forms?
When has one ever penetrated the barrier of the Patriarch?
Clearly elucidating the final word: the sea whale swallows the rhinoceros horn from the Li River;
having personally seen the former master arrive, the iron ox chews the golden grass.
For the sake of others, one must be urgent: the son of Xiangshan watches Zhaozhou lift it up onto several stories of a tower.
Seeing righteousness, he acts with courage; the pearl of the Zhenhai clan is revered through generations. Yangshan emptied out a *kao-lao* basket from his room;
his room-mechanism was so steep that others could hardly approach it. When Yuntai was nearly exhausted, he was captured alive;
beneath his brush, he plows deep, and I myself am enriched. Those in the Han Garden specialize in crafting elegant prose.

Seated beneath the azure oil-bannered standard, he established the foundation for a period of Great Peace. Upon arriving at Mount Zhong, the Venerable Bao of the Liang dynasty grasped his hand and laughed heartily,
"Hehe!"— thus spoke Chan Master Foyuan.
The Master’s name was Qingyuan. He was the successor of the Fifth Patriarch and a son of the Li family from Qiongzhou.

In his youth, he was a scholar who often relied on his own intellectual pride while under the guidance of the Patriarch. Whenever he questioned the Patriarch, the latter would invariably say, "I do not understand;
I am not as good as you," or further, "It is better that you understand it yourself. For a long time, he made no progress and finally asked, "The Master’s gate is high and steep; I, this humble one—"
"I cannot sit in the lower seat. Who may I approach for instruction? I beg you to point the way. The Patriarch said, "The Head Seat Yuanli’s realization is identical to my own.
The Master immediately went to visit him. It was cold, and Yuanli was just then warming himself by a fire.
The Master stated his request, whereupon Yuanli led him by the ear and walked away, saying, "I do not understand. I am not as good as you. You must understand it well yourself. The Master—
The monk said, "I wished for you to grant me an opening, yet you merely played with me. How can this be considered the Dharma for people?

Linji said, "If you were to awaken, you would finally understand the twists and turns of today. The monk felt ashamed and hurried back to the guest prefect’s quarters. While sitting in contemplation during the night, he felt cold;
as he stirred the embers, he attained great enlightenment and suddenly saw the point of application of the two elders. He then said, "Deeply stirring the ashes, there is something arising."

All was peaceful. It was simply like this. He then lit a lamp and read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). Upon reaching the account of "Breaking the Hearth and Falling," it perfectly accorded with what he had realized himself.
He recited the verse: "The sorrowful birds cry out; I don my robes and sit through the night. Stirring the embers, I awaken to my whole life;

Exhausting the spirit, I return to breaking the hearth and falling. The matter is clear, yet people remain deluded; Who can harmonize with these subtle words? Thinking of this, I shall never forget; The gate stands open."
Few people passed by. When Yuanwu heard that the Master had realized the essential meaning [of the Dharma], he knocked on the door at the fifth watch.

The Master then presented what he had attained. Yuanwu said, "As for the story of Qinglin moving earth, it says: 'The Iron-Wheel-Turning Emperor issues his decree throughout the realm. How do you understand this?
The Master replied, "In the palace of Śakra, a general amnesty is proclaimed. Yuanwu said, "I am glad, brother, that you possess a phrase that brings life to others. Later...
Xuedou said: "I do not understand; it is not as good as yours. It is laughable that a thousand flowers bloom from the tip of a pestle.

Sudhana wandered in vain through a hundred cities; when has he ever trodden upon his own ground? Fojian composed a verse on the occasion of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra giving rise to views of Buddha and Dharma:
"Within the shadows of multicolored clouds, an immortal appears, Holding a red silk fan to shield [the sun]."
[The Master] said, "Face! You must urgently look at the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal's hand. When the Master heard this, he was greatly pleased.
Wuzu said, "This verse can be applied everywhere. While he was staying at Longmen, a monk was bitten by a snake.
[Wuzu] raised the case in the hall, saying, "Since you are a monk of Longmen, why were you bitten by a snake? None of the assembly’s responses were in accord. Gao'an Wuzhuo...
[The Master] said, "Truly, he has manifested the marks of a great man. The Teacher nodded in agreement.

When Yuanwu heard this while at Zhaojue, he sighed and remarked, "With such a son at Longmen, the Way of Dongshan shall not remain desolate. The Master has three records of his own reflections that have been transmitted to the world.
The Eulogy says:
Silent yet divine; speaking, he is always appropriate.
Heaven bestowed a spirit upon his bones; The Sage nurtured him in the womb without harm.
My karmic journey led me to the East of Lu, where I shamelessly attended upon Confucius to receive the essential meanings of the Classics;
yet I sought the Westward Transmission, only to suffer the indignity of being rebuked by Old Dongshan for my lack of decorum.
Whether you understand it or not, hurry back to sit in meditation; stir the ashes to seek the floating bubbles.
Whether they have arrived or not, all are invited to tea; Clear bowls turn over waves of snow.
In the hands of the Immortal is a crimson silk fan; To see it, one must look with the eyes of Xianren.

It is fitting to personally enter the Palace of Śakra to proclaim a decree of amnesty; The imperial edict reaches the green forests, and all who were destined for death are released with full compassion.
The Dragon Gate rises ten thousand fathoms high, where thunder roars in the clear sky as the dragon’s tail flares;
the Qiong River plunges a thousand fathoms deep, where the current is cut to produce the fragrant elephant.
The pestle blossoms with flowers—Master Xu Xuetang leads Śāriputra on a pilgrimage.
Regarding the monk bitten by a snake: Listen to Gao’an’s manifestation of the marks of a great man as he speaks of mind and nature;
do not concern yourself with him. I have written this "Threefold Self-Reflection" as a model for those who practice Chan in the monasteries of all ages.
Chan Master Daguigao’s dharma name was Zonggao.
He was a successor of Yuanwu and a native of the Xi family of Xuancheng. Initially, he studied under Zhantang as his attendant.
When Zhantang’s illness became critical, the Master asked, "If the Master does not recover from this illness, whom shall I rely upon after you are gone? Zhantang replied, "Qin..."

"Bazi is truly excellent. Although I do not know him personally, if you were to meet him, he would surely be able to accomplish the great matter. Later, [Wuzhun] went to see Wuguo and attained his essential instruction.
The Master (Wuzhun) acted as an intermediary for Tangjian when he sought a stele inscription from Wu Jin. Long’an Zhao wrote a letter of introduction for him to see Jin.
Jin remarked, "The diamond eye resides upon the tip of the official’s brush. Jin continued, "If that is so, then I..."
He pointed out the light for others, causing it to illuminate both heaven and earth. The Master stepped forward, bowed, and said, "The late Master was most fortunate;
thank you, Excellency, for the inscription for his stupa. [The official] laughed heartily. While the Master was at Mount Jing, he composed this verse:

"A single shot from the divine-arm bow Pierces through a thousand layers of armor. When viewed from the gate of the patched-robed monks, What is it but a pair of stinking leather shoes? At that time, the imperial court...

Just as he was about to fashion the Shenbi bow, the Chancellor of Qin reported that the Master had been privately discussing matters with Zhang Jiucheng and was simultaneously satirizing the imperial court.
Consequently, he was exiled to Hengzhou, then to Meizhou, for a total of seventeen years. Upon his release and return, he resided again at Jingshan.
When he returned from Meizhou to Fuzhou, Chancellor Zhang invited him to Yangyu, where he spent an entire summer in intensive practice.
There were thirteen people, with Guishan Guang at their head and Zhao Juji as the second participant.
[Guishan] said to them, "After this old monk has departed, if anyone else teaches you Chan, saying, 'How do you investigate this koan? or 'How do you understand that causal connection?
then immediately scoop up hot excrement and splash it over them. Remember this! When the Master heard Yang'an Jinlun’s proclamations, he was greatly delighted.
He then said, "The true lineage of Yangqi rests with this old man. He subsequently sent him the robe of orthodox transmission along with a verse, saying:
"Severing the path atop the First Peak of the Golden Wheel, A thousand demons and a hundred monsters all hide their traces. In recent years I have received a true message:
It reports that the true lineage of Yangqi is now unobstructed."
The eulogy says:
The flowered papaya tree; the Bao family tiger and foxes have vanished their tracks; wind arises from the dark trees.
The snow and frost are overcome by the warmth of spring’s grace;
the adamantine eye is pointed out by the tip of the brush.
Because Longan leaned back against it, he was buried alive beneath the words of "Fragrant Breeze in the Hall. One cannot help but resent Zhan Tang for pointing it out to Qin Ba.
Overturning Wushiling Hill, he brandishes his black bamboo staff wildly,
scattering the clouds over the Five Peaks; breaking his staff,
he props it east and west as Yunmen reveals the truth, yet deceives the common folk.
The Old Man returns again with joy;
Deceiving Buddhas and Patriarchs like a fierce general meeting his foe— Seizing the thief’s horse and riding off, someone else teaches you Chan:
Scoop up hot excrement and splash it upon him!
Exiled to Hengzhou and Meizhou for seventeen years, The stench of his leather boots permeated the Brahma Heaven.
Thirteen men sought justice at Yangyu, While the sound of the "poisoned drum" resounded throughout the world.
He did not treat the Buddha-dharma as mere human sentiment; He entrusted the authentic transmission of Yangqi’s lineage to his nephew, Jinlunhua.
This is the way it should be according to the Dharma-king’s decree.
Chan Master Hongluo Long (Shao-long) was a native of Hezhou who succeeded Yuanwu. Initially, he met Changlu Xin and attained a general understanding of the teachings.
When someone brought a transmission of Yuanwu’s words to him, the Master read it and sighed, saying, "I imagine the essence produced from fermented vinegar;

though it has not yet been poured into my intestines or drenched my stomach, it nonetheless makes one feel a sense of exhilaration. My only regret is that I have not yet heard his voice. He then went to see Yuanwu. One day...
He entered the room. Huineng asked, "When seeing the very act of seeing, that seeing is not [true] seeing; seeing is already apart from seeing, so seeing cannot reach it.

He raised his fist and asked, "Do you see this? Huineng replied, "I see. Huineng said, "This is like placing a head atop a head. At these words, the Master attained sudden and profound enlightenment. Huineng rebuked him, saying, "What have you seen?
Huineng replied, "The dense bamboo does not hinder the flowing water from passing through. Huineng approved of him. Later, he became the Abbot (Zang).
The Master said, "People say that Abbot Long is so mild and easygoing; how could he possibly achieve anything? Wuzu said, "He is a sleeping tiger. Ascending the hall, he said:
"If there is any display or entrustment, it all falls into the present age. If there is neither display nor entrustment, one falls into pits and ditches.
Even if you are such that the wind cannot blow in and the rain cannot strike you, when scrutinized, you will not even be able to save yourself. Have you not seen it said: 'Directly...'"
It is like the moon’s reflection in a cold pond, or the sound of a bell in a silent night; it is never diminished by being struck, nor does it disperse when it encounters waves.
Yet this is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. (The Master) picks up his staff, draws a line, and says:
“With this stroke, I have severed the master of Dharma’s many years of entanglements. The Nodding Stone, without realizing it, claps its hands and laughs loudly. But tell me, what is he laughing at?
If you see his cheek behind his head, do not associate with him. He ascended the hall and said: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the myriad phenomena are dense and manifold.
The intent lies right before the eyes, yet it is difficult to discern as it suddenly emerges. It is not a dharma of the present moment, yet one encounters it at every touch.

It is not something reached by the ears or the eyes, yet it is not separate from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Although this is so, you must still step upon the pivotal bolt of the higher realm."

The Son has finally attained it. Thus it is said: "It refuses to stay within the cage; though called, it does not turn its head. Buddhas and Patriarchs made no arrangements for it, and to this day it has no fixed location.
If it is thus, there is no need to laboriously collect the mind. The gates of the multi-storied pavilion open; without moving a single step, one reaches all hundred cities.
[He suddenly seizes his staff and draws a line, saying: "When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it down—[it is bottomless]."

He carried it home in a basket. A monk asked, "What is the true source of the Great Way? He replied, "Muddling with the mud and mixing with the water. The monk asked, "What is it like when one proceeds in this very manner?
He replied, "Cutting off the heel of the straw sandals. Some have said: "To long for the Way is like a thirsty horse galloping toward a spring;
responding to stimuli is like a wrathful lion tearing through rock. Others have said: "The vinegar-fly within its jar finds its own joy."
Whenever Fei Changfang saw a certain master hanging a calabash over his stall, he would pay him a visit;
they would then enter the calabash together, which was truly a realm of divine transcendents.
The eulogy says:
His breast and mind are as cool as autumn; his smiles and speech are as warm as spring.
Like a precious *chuiji* jade kept within its casket, he remains hidden, awaiting the right price.
The shadow of the pearl rolling on the platter falls without a trace;
I admire the secret transmission of the mind at Shaoshi. A thirsty horse gallops swiftly toward the water beneath the crags;
the flavor of the green cliffs is free of unmeaning words. The vinegar-fly rejoices in its own world within the jar.
The road is long; tread upon the heel of the straw sandals.
Seeking the source on the Great Way, though the bamboos are dense, the flowing water passes through unimpeded.
Seeing one raise a coarse fist, he picks up a coarse radish. The Nodding Head Rock laughs: the thicket of complications is severed.
Performing the Great Treasury of the Canon, The slumbering tiger is entangled by the binding cords;
In the deep pool, the sword’s qi is cold, harboring frost.
Chopping away ignorance and stubbornness upon the ancient whetstone, Peach blossoms cluster like brocade within the deep cavern; Before the wind, he speaks his parting words to his beloved child.
Encountering a dead snake on the road, one carries it home in a bottomless basket—of what use is it?
Amidst the spring warmth and a hundred birds, one leans idly against the curved balustrade, speechless.
The dragon and phoenix of Mount Dongshan—the true descendants of Linji.
The jade pitcher is unstained by dust; it is a separate world of its own.

Chan Master Ying’an Huā, whose Dharma name was Tánhuā, was a successor of Hǔqiū and the son of the Jiāng family of Qí Prefecture. When he first traveled to study under various masters, he encountered the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) entering the room for instruction.
The Master approached him. The Abbot said, "What have you come for? The Master replied, "To take the head of the Head Seat.
The Abbot said, "You are a young man to speak such words; you will vomit blood! The Master said, "I shall not vomit blood;
it is the Head Seat who will vomit blood! Later, it indeed happened exactly as the Master had said. The Master served as an attendant at Suichu in Shuinan and entered the room [for formal training].

Next, Nan caught hold of him and said, "Attendant, wait while I deliberate upon a public case (gong'an) with you. The Master said, "The entire great earth is this public case; what is there to deliberate upon?
Nan was of dull faculties, so the Master shook his sleeves and departed. Later, he saw Huqiu, who appointed him as the *karmadāna* (Vina).
When Huqiu intended to appoint him as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*), many under his guidance had already attained realization. At that time, a senior elder in the assembly spoke:

The Master was born later [than his teacher]. When the teacher heard of this, he composed a verse, saying: "The green mountains by the river are not yet old; The spring colors atop the house are made to linger.
People say the peach blossoms in the cave are tender; Yet perhaps there is no such branch in the human world. He then departed. Later, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Seventy monks from thirty-three provinces—donkey jaws and horse necks, detested by all. If those in other quarters were truly..."
With hands clasped in prayer, today there is no cause for reaching Pure Radiance. Entering the hall, he said: "The meaning of the five hundred laborers lifting the rock:
walking with hands cast off before a ten-thousand-fathom cliff. The world of the ten directions is a single mass of iron; white hair grows upon the back of empty space."
Even if you were to cast off your greasy cap and strip away your stinking cloth robe, you would still deserve a beating at the gate of Baoen. Why?
Because rising in the middle of the night and sitting with knees bent, the Morning Star appears before the monk. [He] ascended the hall and said:
"If you deliberate upon this as a single phrase, who does not know how to eat porridge and eat rice? If you do not deliberate upon it as a single phrase..."
"Measuring! The worms in a pit of excrement would laugh the Master to death. [He suddenly brandishes his staff and says: "The offense of this staff fills the heavens;
it is banished to the Two Iron Encircling Mountains. Now tell me, does Jianfu have any fault or not? [He strikes once.]

Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. A monk asked, "In the past, a monk asked Yunmen, 'What is the pure dharmakāya? Yunmen replied, 'A flower garden railing. What is the meaning of this? Yunmen said, "Deep-sand [the sandman] squints his eyes. The monk asked, "If it is this very thing, one buries oneself; if it is not this very thing, one辜负 (gu fù) the former sages. Beyond these two paths, what is the place where mud and water are blended? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither self nor other? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither right nor wrong? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither gain nor loss? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither birth nor death? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither going nor coming? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the Way nor non-Way? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the Dharma nor the non-Dharma? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the Patriarchal Hall nor the Buddha Hall? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the mountain gate nor the main hall? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the staff nor the whisk? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the robe nor the bowl? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the incense burner nor the candle stand? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the altar nor the shrine? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the mountain peak nor the valley floor? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the sky nor the earth? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the sun nor the moon? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the stars nor the constellations? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the wind nor the rain? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the teacher's fist nor the student's fist? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the master's eye nor the disciple's eye? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about when there is neither the raising of the whisk nor the striking of the staff? Yunmen said, "Wait one more hour. The monk asked, "What about
"Please, Master, tell me the Way. He said, "The jade chopsticks prop up the tiger's mouth. A monk asked, "I do not ask about raising the oar and dancing with the paddle;
but tell me, from where did the child in the old woman’s hand come? Yantou tapped the side of the boat three times. "I do not understand the meaning of this," [the monk] said.
[Yantou] replied, "A fired brick strikes and freezes through to the bottom. [The monk] asked, "If you had been asked this at that time, Master, what would you have said?"
[The Master] said to him: "I would strike him dead with a single blow of the staff. [The monk] said: "This old monk is much like one who buys a hat and tries to fit it to the head [of another].
[The Master] said: "Where did you see Yantou? [The monk] said: "Zha! [The Master] said: "A contrived Chan practitioner. [The Master] said: "An old woman gave birth to seven sons."
"Six people did not meet with a true知音 (zhīyīn—'one who knows the sound'). This one person alone was also not enough; he simply threw him into the water. [The monk asked: "And how about that?
[Dongshan] said: "Do not show off so much. [The monk asked: "Yantou involuntarily stuck out his tongue. What was his meaning? [Dongshan] said: "In joy, we share the same delight.

Rāhu enters the life-sign, yet it does not strike and kill a person—it is certain to be struck and killed by others. Shishuang approved of this. At the memorial service for Huiqiu, he offered incense and said:
"Throughout my life I have had little luck; I ran into that witless old monk. I exhausted every skill and artifice, yet I could never find a way to settle with him."
From this point on, lay down your weapons and arms; wear clothes and eat food according to your lot.
For twenty years you have sat upon a curved wooden chair, hanging up a goat’s head while selling dog meat—what credentials do you think you have?
Nevertheless, on the day incense is burned once a year, it causes people’s resentment to deepen for all eternity.
The eulogy says:
A man of Qiyang; ghosts fear seeing him, for white hairs grow from his back, and he hides dark arrows deep within ancient tombs.
He severed the head and departed; hot blood sprayed and splashed against the Head Seat as he shook his sleeves and left.
Laughing at the slow-witted mind of Shuinan, he cast away the child at the Han-yang Ferry—where joy is shared in common.
Demoted to the Iron Ring Mountains with a staff in hand—how could one avoid being struck down?
Picking up and breaking the jade chopsticks, he forcibly props them against the tiger’s maw at the cliff’s edge.
He composes a poem on an off-rhyme; in vain does he claim the peach blossoms in the cave are fresh.
The Yakṣa-heart and Bodhisattva-face; Speaking the Southern Record, walking on the edge of a sword, the True Dharma-eye that shatters the sand-pot;
Leading the attendant Jie to roll in a patch of weeds;
Seventy monks with donkey-jaws and horse-chins; Thinning out the various quarters, not possessing hands, yet netting them all within.
For twenty years, dog meat and sheep heads; remembering my late teacher, I clenched my teeth in resentment.
I have transmitted the orthodox lineage of Yangqi and caused the shadow of Mount Jinlun to fall upon a thousand rivers.
I have succeeded to the fragrant dust of Hongzhi, and the light from the Seagull-Intimacy Pond shines in all eight directions.

Transcending the school and differing from the common perspective, he truly did not fail the Sun Buddha’s appraisal. He ensured that the source for future generations would be profound and the stream far-reaching.
Chan Master Wan’an Yan, whose dharma name was Daoyan, was a successor of Dahui. Born into the Bao family of Dongchuan, he had long studied under Yuanwu while at Jinshan. Because...
Once, while a whirlwind was raging, it caused the monks to commit suicide; because she did not die through her wisdom, she was taken captive by barbarians, from whom she later managed to escape.
She realized the truth of returning to stillness and again relied upon Dahuì. When Wuzhuo had not yet become a monk, Dahuì housed her in the abbot’s quarters;
the Master (Zhaozhou) frequently rebuked her. Dahuì said, "Although she is a woman, she possesses great strengths. The Master would not consent. Dahuì constrained him to meet with her.
The Master, having no choice, sent word to announce his arrival. Zhe said, "Head Seat, shall we meet in the manner of the Buddha-dharma, or shall we meet in the manner of worldly dharma?
The Head Seat replied, "In the manner of the Buddha-dharma. Zhe said, "Then go and invite the Master to enter from the side.
When the Master arrived before the curtain, he saw that Zhe was lying on his back upon the bed, naked without a single thread of cloth. The Master pointed and asked, "What place is this? Zhe replied:
"The Buddhas of the three periods, the six generations of patriarchs, and the elder monks of the world—all emerge from within this.
The Master said, "Does it permit this old monk to enter as well? Xuedou said, "In this place, we do not ferry over donkeys; we ferry over horses. The Master was speechless. Xuedou said:
Having finished his formal greeting with the Head Seat, he turned around to look inside. The Master left in embarrassment. Huì said, "It was not that this old beast lacks discernment.
The Master felt ashamed. Huì entered the room and raised the case of Nanquan’s dwelling in a hermitage.
While the Master was working on the mountain, a monk arrived. [The Master] gave him the cause-and-condition story of ordering him to cook rice for a meal.
The Master said: "On the coral pillow, two rows of tears; half are thinking of you, half are resenting you. Huìlín had the attendant take down the name plaque, saying:
"This single turning word alone is sufficient to repay the Buddha's kindness. Initially he resided at Dōrin; later he returned to his hometown and stayed at Ungtō. A monk asked: "How is it?"
The Buddha said, "How is the Dharma? Zhigong replied, "A young lady of yellow silk; a grandson’s mortar for pickles. "How is the Sangha?
He replied, "Xie Sanlang on the fishing boat. In an address to the assembly, he said:
"The chopsticks do not jostle the spoon; the rat does not gnaw the steamer lid. When Han Zicang and the Master were fleeing from bandits, he wrote a poem which says: "Formerly with the two..."
My son dwelt in the clarity of his mind; fleeing the rebels, he fled by night into the southern mountains. The weather was cold as he further trod upon the marshy paths;

under the black moon, he mistakenly arrived at Yangmei Ridge. Crossing perilous terrain and climbing steep heights for four or five *li*, he traveled a short distance further until he crossed a mountain stream.
At dawn, he begged fire from a rustic householder and hid deep within a rocky cave for ten days. The people of Min all sighed, lamenting that my provisions were exhausted.
A monk from Shu has fallen further into the midst of demonic vapors; people say his life was as narrow as escaping through the eye of a needle. My sincere grief and your physical ailment are shared;

by the spring wind’s intoxicating breath, we sit together at a temple by the willows, discussing dream-matters within a dream. Do not disdain this meager meal of rice and a stalk of pickled vegetables;
in these commanderies and kingdoms, the war-drums are now silent.
The eulogy says:
A qilin with the head and horns of a dragon; the lineage of the Gong and Ye families in wielding the bow and handling the leatherwork;
a neck-iron of three hundred jin—extraordinary among his peers and stubbornly defiant.
Several dots of ink tattooed upon his brow—this unconventional elegance was already complete within Yuanwu’s chamber;
the colorful painting was finished, lacking only a single stroke to open the eyes.
Seeing the opportunity at Mount Fuyuan, he acted; there was no need for three more turns of the head.
Before the brocade curtains, one soul was severed; In return, she met the deadly hand of a woman.
Upon the coral pillow, two rows of tears; It was difficult to escape the schemes of the hermitage master.
His words were groundless; He boasted that mice do not bite the steamer lids.
Seizing the moment, he galloped forth; riding a fine steed, he charged straight at the smoke-filled pavilion.
He trampled the bridge over Tiger Creek and cast Master Fashi far away, leaving him to be buried alive in the Lotus Society.
Having traveled to the end of the roads through barbarian miasmas, he followed Master Gaofeng into exile, fleeing far away to Meizhou.
Sweeping away the ominous miasma, the altars of state were secured with a single stroke of the robe;
His meritorious deeds at Lingyan—wielding his halberd against the dust and wind of the Buddha-sun, he relied on a three-foot sword.
With the strategic ingenuity of "borrowing chopsticks," he cleared the marshy paths through the Yangmei forest; He had long since recalled the South Mountain for evading the rebel hordes.
Cloud Peak Temple on Oxhead Mountain— In the evening, thoughts turn toward returning to West Shu to rest.
If you ask this old man again about the true essence of being a monk, Xie Sanlang will likely not be found in his fishing boat.
Chan Master Lǎn’ān Xū, whose dharma name was Dìngxū, was a successor of Dahui. He was the son of the Lin family of Fuzhou. Originally, he practiced the Confucian curriculum;

however, upon entering a temple and seeing the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* (Yíjiào jīng), he attained realization after reading several fascicles. Desiring to leave the household life, his mother tried to dissuade him by citing the difficulty of her recent marriage arrangements. The Master said:
The peach blossoms and apricot flowers are all entrusted at once to the spring breeze; the green bamboos and yellow chrysanthemums shall henceforth be his companions forever.

Having bid farewell to his kin and shaved his head, he traveled with a single staff through Lake Xiang, visiting renowned masters everywhere. His mind had no object of attachment, and his body had no place of reliance.

He built a hermitage on the summit of Qiang Peak. Later, he met Dahui. One day, Dahui asked him, "When you do not let anything out from within, nor let anything enter from without—how is it at such a time?
As the Master was about to open his mouth, Dahui took up his bamboo staff and struck him three times across the spine.
The Master attained great enlightenment. Dahui sealed this with a verse, saying: "The eye of Mahesvara stands upright in the crown of your head; behind your elbow..."
A life-taking talisman slants and hangs; it blinds the eyes. Cast off the talisman! Zhaozhou hangs a gourd on the eastern wall. Entering the hall, he said:
"The Lazy Old Man is the laziest among the lazy; he is too lazy to preach Chan. He values neither himself nor the sages of old."
Furthermore, who governs your earth? Who governs your heavens? Wandering at ease beyond the mundane world, there is nothing to do;
though the sun has risen three *zhang* high, you still sleep. Ascending the hall, he said: "The meaning within the phrase; the phrase within the meaning—Mount Sumeru towers over the vast river.
The phrase cuts through the meaning; the meaning cuts through the phrase—a hero looses a wild arrow. Even if your fangs are like sword-trees and your mouth is like a blood-basin, [it matters not]."
They merely display their verbal acumen and falsely inflate their spirit. Thus, when Vimalakīrti remained silent, he had already fallen into prolixity;
when Mahākāśyapa closed his door, he had already exposed the family’s disgrace.

As for the rest—the old fellow from Waguan, the Great Master Yantou, and others who, atop the peaks of Qiang, grasped at the wind and stirred up the waves, playing with divine transformations—they deserve thirty blows beneath their heels. But tell me, where does their fault lie?
"Where is it? After a long silence, he said: "The mechanism was not made by Han Guang; do not treat your own inner capacity as something trivial.
On the twenty-fifth day, he ascended the hall and said: "Before the twenty-fifth day, the masses of yin have subsided and the clay dragon closes its door.
After the twenty-fifth day, the first yang returns and the iron tree blooms in flower. Precisely on the twenty-fifth day, the dust..."

Intoxicated guests—some riding donkeys, some riding horses—move from street to street, congratulating one another. A leisurely man beyond the mundane world, his head shrouded in a patched robe, sits in meditation by the hearth.
The wind whistles, the rain patters, all is cold and still. Who cares for you, Master Zhang, Daoist Ji, or Layman Hu?
As Mudan was in the midst of his inquiry, the Master raised the story of the outsider who asked the Buddha, "I do not ask..."

The Hermit bowed and said, "Were it not for the matters of today, how could I help but respond to the immediate opportunity before me? The Master approved this and presented a verse to the Hermit of Fen, saying:
"The wind is fierce at the riverhead and the flower-foam flies; North and south they meet, yet no brow is unknitted. Only the Chan master Fen..."
The Handsome One’s Hand: He casually won the silken prize and returned home.
