If you can follow this teaching, You will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood

He transmitted it, saying: "The grass before Mount Yangguang relies on you to await its price; where the extraordinary sprouts flourish, the spiritual root is deep, secret, and firm. Its conclusion states:
"One who has attained the Dharma must remain hidden among the masses for ten years before they may propagate it; one should receive it by bowing from afar.
The Master once explained Caoshan’s three kinds of speech, stating that one must clearly understand the shifting positions (*zhuowei*) before one can grasp them. The first is called *zuo* (acting).
The "water buffalo" is falling into conformity with its kind; it is the turning of the body and speech of a śramaṇa, an occurrence within the realm of heterogeneity.
If one does not understand this meaning, there will be obstruction. It simply requires that one’s single thought-moment be free from self-interest;
then there is a path for emerging from the body. Second, "not accepting food" is falling into nobility; one must first realize the state beyond and then act within the state of coming.
Lǚ: "If one does not leave this position empty, one will sit within the noble and honored. Third, 'not severing sound and form' means falling everywhere;
because one does not understand sound and form, one falls everywhere. One must find a way to emerge from within sound and form.
What is the phrase outside of sound and form? He said: "Sound is not sound by itself; form is not form by itself. Therefore it is said:
"One does not point to one's own palm. To which palm, then, should one point? Fushan Zanshi’s eulogy for his teacher’s portrait says: "A black dog with hooves of refined silver;
a white elephant ridden upon Mount Kunlun. Being unimpeded in these two, a wooden horse neighs amidst the flames."
The eulogy says:
A child of evil and poison;
such a little fellow was born by way of transference at the ferryhead of Hanyang.
Within Zhitong Temple, he stands out with unbridled brilliance,
overturning the field of Perfect Enlightenment; Leaping into the realm where words and explanations fail,
he shatters the mirror of the Qin dynasty, Revealing the state before one's parents were even born.
The path of speech is difficult to express with faith; The words of the ancestral vehicle are like ashes and soil mixed together—filling the jar, it cannot be poured out.
All people on this great earth endure hunger and swallow their own rations;
Beyond the thousand sages, they let go of their hands and walk on; Entering the reeds, they laugh as they ride away on a white horse.
No one stands in attendance within the jeweled hall; though you plant the *wutong* trees, how can you avoid the phoenix’s perching?
Since the message has been communicated, it is regrettable that the lion’s claws and fangs are not yet complete;
because the karmic conditions do not harmonize, the father and son of the green mountains remain at odds.
Water flows horizontally atop the summit of Mount Sumeru; the mass of doubt regarding the Dharma-body has not yet been pierced.
On the peaks of Yangguang Mountain, the sprouts flourish luxuriantly; as he offers his final confession, old tears fall in profusion.
Old Liangshan is too oppressive and constraining; a black rooster lays a swan’s egg.
Master Yuanlu’s records are so muddled as to be beyond measure;
amidst this heap of black dogs, rotten silver hooves, sounds, and sights, you insist there is a path for one’s own emergence.
If it were not for the Dean of the Academy, who would accept these cracked leather shoes and drenched Zen robes?
Chan Master Touzi Qing’s dharma name was Yiqing.

He was a successor of Dayang and a native of the Li clan from Qingshe. Initially, he studied the *Śataśāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas), whereupon he sighed, saying, "The path of three great kalpas is long;

what benefit is there in exhausting myself? He went to Luoyang to listen to lectures on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, at which his understanding was like pearls strung together. When the lecture reached the section on the various groves...
The Bodhisattva’s verse was the very nature of his own mind. He had a sudden realization and said, "The Dharma is beyond words;
how could it be expounded? He departed. He went to visit Fushan at Huishengyan. Fushan had dreamed that he obtained a fine hawk and raised it; upon waking, the Master arrived.
Fushan took this to be an auspicious omen and kept him for three years. Fushan asked, "When the non-Buddhists questioned the Buddha, they did not ask about the presence of words, nor did they ask..."

[The Master] was speechless. The World-Honored One remained silent. [The Master] wondered, "How is this? As he was about to speak further, the Mountain covered his mouth. Thereupon, the Master attained enlightenment.
Rising from his prostrations, the Mountain asked, "Have you attained a wondrous realization of the profound mechanism? He replied, "Even if there were a wondrous realization, it must be spat out.
At that time, Zishi was standing nearby and said, "Today Qing Huayan has finally broken out in a sweat after being ill. The Master looked back at him and said, "It is fitting."

"Seize the dog's mouth! You chatter on and on; I shall immediately vomit. [Zhaozhou] gave the mountain monk a pair of leather sandals and a cloth robe, charging him to continue the Dongshan school for him.
He ascended the hall and said: "When the vehicle of the ultimate teaching is raised, both ordinary and sage leave no trace.

The gate of the multi-storied pavilion opens, and we meet face-to-face beyond conventional forms. Even if one attains awakening by rolling up the curtain, how can one avoid being a bystander? Meeting peach blossoms in spring..."
It increases the ailment of the eye. Thus an ancient said: "The path that goes upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages.
O worthy ones, since it is not transmitted, why did the Iron Ox gallop over to the kingdom of Silla? He shouted: "The one who reaches it must know the shock in the darkness.
A monk asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind do you succeed? He replied: "Before the Nameless One, a single arrow was shot."

Passing beyond two layers of mountains, he ascended the hall and said: "Silence sinks one into the realm of darkness; speech causes one to fall into a deep pit. To attempt to grasp it is like the vast distance between heaven and earth;
to cast it aside is to wander through a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas. The great waves are vast and boundless, white surf surging to the heavens—the bright pearl that anchors the sea."
"Who will take charge of this? After a long silence, he struck the meditation staff and said, "All shattered to pieces! He addressed the assembly, saying:
"If one discusses this matter, it is like a phoenix soaring to the heavens, leaving no trace; or a wild goat hanging from a branch, where can its tracks be found?
A golden dragon does not dwell in a cold pool; how could a hare nest within the shadow of the moon? Should host and guest be established, they must be in the realm of Vipaśyin."
The Master shook his head. Their questions and answers were already fully expressed; this was merely a song sung by the side of the path of the profound and mysterious.
If one can do so, one is still only halfway there. Look further with focused eyes, and there will be no need for a formal meeting. The Master then explained the Five Ranks of Sovereign and Subject:

"Now, when the vast sky is of a single color, how can stars and moon be distinguished? When the great earth is without partiality, flourishing and withering differ of their own accord. Therefore, the Dharma is not a different dharma."
How could delusion and awakening ever be reached? The mind is not of itself the mind; it is through the provisional use of words and images that it is proclaimed.
These words are both partial and perfect, direct and ultimate, inclusive and harmonious. This Dharma does not fall into the trap of right and wrong, nor is it concerned with the myriad phenomena.
When the profound intent merges with the moon reflected in water, the source of the school blends with the golden river. Not falling into empty stillness, the path returns to its wondrous mystery.

The Master cited the saying of Dayang, "Pointing out the Qin-dynasty mirror," and offered this verse: "Correctness within partiality: at midnight, the sky is bright, yet one feels ashamed of one's own reflection.
Amidst the hazy colors of the mist, the boundaries of the rivers are discerned; all is merged in a state that does not fall back into the Qin-dynasty mirror."
The encomium says:
Heaven sent down a brilliant spirit; Nature gave birth to a pillar of wisdom.
Though he studied Abhidharma, he did not yet penetrate the net; In his pursuit of the profound Flower Garland, he only increased his shackles.
Entering Fushan was an inauspicious dream; what use is a falcon with broken wings?
Having already fallen into the wind beneath the cave, a dog that stumbles at its own hooves is ultimately difficult to cure.
A golden phoenix borrows a dragon’s nest to roost—how could it have known it would fall into the heavy siege of the Sage?
A fine horse moves at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow; At first, it does not wait for the World-Honored One.
For a long time, the mind's own nature is thus; The Buddha also forcibly names this "wondrous awakening" and "mysterious mechanism," But I immediately vomit it up.
The Iron Ox gallops through the kingdom of Silla; On the upward path, a thousand sages have not transmitted it.
The Stone Woman lightly bends the moon-child bow; With a single arrow, she pierces through two layers of mountains.
The Pearl of the Dragon King is smashed to pieces; In the place where speech and silence do not reach, one has not yet learned how to turn the body.
Adding a layer of brilliance to the Qin-dynasty mirror—before light and darkness were yet distinguished, how could there be room for a hand to emerge?
Where did that rabbit find its resting place in the shadow of the moon? From where did this news arrive?
The golden dragon does not remain in the cold pool; this fellow seeks another path to run.

Although chapters are divided into the partial and the complete, one does not fall into emptiness or stagnation. Upon reaching the ultimate state where the turning position returns its merit, how could one ever know that it exists?
— Master Fuyong Kai.
The Master succeeded Touzi; his name was Daokai. He was the son of the Cui family from Yizhou.
When he first visited Touzi, he asked, "The words and phrases of the Buddhas and patriarchs are like the daily tea and rice of a household. Apart from these, do you have any other words for people?
Touzi replied, "Tell me, when the Son of Heaven issues an edict within the realm, does he still need the aid of Yu, Tang, Yao, or Shun? As the Master was about to respond, Touzi [interrupted].
Wiping his whisk, the Master struck the student’s mouth and said, “From the moment you first conceived the thought [to come here], you have already received twenty blows.
The student was immediately enlightened; he bowed twice and departed. The Master called out, “Wait a moment, Ācārya! The student did not look back and said, “Have you reached the ground of non-doubt?
The student then covered his ears. One day, while attending the Master as they strolled through the garden, the Master handed him his staff and said, “This is what you ought to possess.”
[The Master] said, "It is so. [Yunmen] said, "Carrying the Master's shoes and holding his staff for him is not considered an extra burden.

[The Master] said, "There is another companion here. [Yunmen] said, "That one person does not accept the teaching; you may leave now. When evening came, [Yunmen] said to him, "The conversation we had this morning was not yet finished.

[The Master] said, "Please bring it up again. [Yunmen] said, "Born in the hour of the Rabbit (Mao), born in the month of the Dog (Wu). The Master immediately lit a lamp and approached, saying, "Bring it here. [Yunmen] said, "What has come up?"
[The Master] went down. [The attendant] said, "It is not at all in vain. [The Master] said, "You are by my side; it is only right that you should act thus.

[The attendant] said, "Every household has its servants and maids. [The Master] said, "But for one of my advanced years, I cannot do without you. [The attendant] said, "With such earnestness as this, there is surely a way to repay your kindness.
Ascending the hall, he said: "By day, one enters the Garden of Jeta, where the bright moon hangs in the sky; by night, one ascends Vulture Peak..."
Mountains; the sun blinding the eyes; crows like snow; solitary wild geese in flocks; iron dogs barking as they scale the heavens;
clay oxen fighting as they enter the sea. At such a moment as this, the ten directions gather together—how can "self" and "other" be distinguished?
Within the ancient Buddha-fields and under the gate of the Patriarchs, let us all extend a single hand to receive the visiting masters who come and go, O worthy ones!
"Let us say, what kind of matter has been accomplished? After a long silence, he said: 'I plant an extra tree without shadow, to leave for later generations to behold.
A monk asked: 'The song of the Hu family does not fall into the five musical notes; its melody rises above the azure heavens. I pray you, Master, to sing it for us.
He replied: 'The wooden cock crows at midnight; the iron phoenix calls when the day breaks. [The monk asked: 'If that is so, then a single line of the song contains [the whole meaning]...'"
"A melody for a thousand ages. The assembly of monks and laypeople are all connoisseurs. He said, "The tongueless youth can continue the verse.
[The Emperor] said, "A master of the school, the eye of humanity and heaven. [He added,] "Take away those two pieces of skin!

In the first year of the Daguan era, Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of the Capital, memorialized that the Master’s spiritual conduct was preeminent within the monastic community and should be honored with official recognition. The Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes and the title of "Ding" (Calm).
When Chan Master Zhao received the imperial decree brought by an inner attendant, he expressed his gratitude and then set forth his own resolve:

"At the time I left the household life, I made a solemn vow not to pursue fame or profit, but to study the Way with single-minded devotion to provide spiritual support for my nine generations of kin. If I were to violate this vow..."

"One must be prepared to sacrifice one's body and life. Because his parents had granted him permission to leave the household life on these grounds, he thought, "If I do not now maintain my original resolve and instead surreptitiously usurp this imperial favor, the Buddha-Dharma will decline.
Thereupon, he composed a formal petition to decline the offer. An imperial decree was issued to the Capital Governor, strictly ordering him to accept the appointment.

The Master remained firm in his refusal and would not turn back; for defying the command, he was sentenced to punishment. By imperial order, he was taken into custody and handed over to the authorities. The authorities...
Recognizing the Master’s loyalty and sincerity, [the official] asked, "Are you ill? The Master replied, "I have been ill in ordinary times; now, in truth, I am not.

The official said, "If you say you are ill, you may be exempt from punishment according to the law. The Master said, "I fully appreciate your kind intention, but falsehood is not what I find at peace with.

I shall accept the execution with tranquility and proceed. Those who followed him were like people returning to a bustling market. Upon reaching Zizhou, he rented a house to live in, and his students drew closer than ever. It was clear.

In the winter of that year, by imperial decree, he was permitted to reside at his own convenience. He established a hermitage at Fuyong, where the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds. He extensively propagated the Caodong school. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"This mountain monk has no achievements worthy of note, yet I have the misfortune of presiding over this mountain gate. How could I sit idly while consuming the communal property and utterly forget the entrustment of the former sages?
Now, following the example of the ancients, I shall establish the protocols for a *zhuchi* (abbot) and settle them with you all; henceforth, [I shall not act otherwise]."

Descend the mountain. Do not attend the meal offering; do not dispatch a fundraising emissary. Instead, take the annual yield from the monastery’s estates and divide it into three hundred and sixty equal portions.
Take one portion each day, neither increasing nor decreasing the amount according to circumstances. If sufficient for a full meal, prepare a meal;
if insufficient, prepare porridge; if still insufficient, prepare rice broth. For newly arrived guests, serve tea upon their arrival.

It was simply boiled water; he no longer brewed or prepared tea. He established only a single tea hall, from which he would go himself to fetch and use it, striving to minimize external conditions so as to focus exclusively on realizing the Way.
After the Master was released and returned home, the authorities wished to remove his facial branding. The Master said, "This is the imperial decree of the late Emperor."
"How could he possibly leave? The Emperor remarked that this old man had been stubborn and headstrong throughout his life. Regarding Master Lingyuan’s eulogy, it says:

"Only when the heavens are covered in heavy snow do one see the pine and bamboo; even the lovely grasses and delicate flowers are part of the Great Transformation. To have secretly coveted worldly glory would truly be to辜负 (betray) such grace.
The eulogy concludes: "He said: [followed by the verse].
The stubborn old venerable one is forged from cast iron;
his commands throughout the world do not rely on Yao, Shun, Yu, or Tang.
Within the lineage beneath the cave, how could there be any distinction between the biased and the correct, or between the direct and the indirect?
Truly reaching the stage where there is no doubt, Quickly cover those two ears and cease!
Only then can one be called a master of the ancestral school; One must be able to restrain those two pieces of skin from going out.
The tunes of the Hu family lack melody; Do not, for heaven’s sake, speak of the wooden cock crowing at midnight.
In the school of the Patriarchs, there is no room for merit or achievement; In vain they stretch forth their hands to plant a tree that casts no shadow.
Those who travel together do not accept the teaching;
To have them come and go carrying staffs and slippers is entirely in vain. Who among all households has no servants or slaves?
The barren woman casts her shuttle; the wooden man unfolds his brocade. He who wields the basket and the loom inherits the family tradition;
the mud ox enters the sea, and the iron dog soars to the clouds. This tangled vine is uniquely able to spread along the path;
its graceful form and shadow depart for Zichuan. With the integrity of pine and bamboo, how could it ever disdain the snow and frost?
Majestic and dignified, the Han envoy returns; The lotus flower receives the dew and rain directly.
Sufficient gruel, sufficient rice—through the three hundred and sixty days, one discusses family matters over the hearthfire.
Monk or layman? For thirty-six thousand nights, we discuss dreams while lying side by side on the same bed.
With my white hair hanging low, I still cherish the late Emperor’s calligraphy as if it were fresh;
yet seeing myself among the seductive weeds and ephemeral flowers, having arrogantly usurped worldly glory through the workings of fate, I am so ashamed that my sweat falls like rain.
Chan Master Danxia Chun was a successor of Fuyong;
his secular name was Zichun, and he was the son of the Jia family from Jianzhou. The Master ascended the hall and cited:
"Deshan said, 'In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to anyone. Deshan speaking in this way only knew how to enter the grass."
He was seeking someone, yet he did not realize his entire body was covered in mud and water. Looking closely, he saw that [the person] possessed only one eye. Danxia, however, was not like this.
"In our school, there are words and phrases that cannot be cut open even with a golden blade.

The profound and mysterious ultimate meaning: the stone woman conceives a child at night. He addressed the assembly, citing Master Zhao: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is one..."
"The Jewel is hidden within the mountain of form. Master Zao spoke thus, yet he only knew how to point toward tracks and discuss traces;
he was unable to provide direct instruction to others. Today, Danxia splits open the universe and shatters the mountain of form to bring it forth for all of you.
Those with eyes, discern it! *Claps once.* Do you see? "The egret standing in the snow is not the same color as it"—this is clarity.
The moon, the reeds, and the flowers are not like him. [He] ascends the hall: "The precious moon flows with radiance;
the clear pool has its reflection. The water has no intention to soak the moon; the moon has no mind to divide its light. When water and moon are both forgotten, only then can one be called 'severed.
Therefore it is said: 'The matter of ascending to heaven must be cast away; the matter of reaching completion must be discarded. The sound of gold hitting the ground—'"

"You must look back. If you can do so, only then will you understand how to walk among those of different species. [The Master] asked, "When people arrive here, do they still fully comprehend one another?
After a long silence, he said: "When walking, one does not lift the steps of the mundane world; Clad in fur and bearing horns, one mingles with the mud and dust.
Ascending the hall, it stands tall at midday yet still lacks half its height; In the silent dead of night, it remains incomplete. The six gates have never been closed."

Zhiyao was always present before the bright moon as he came and went. A monk asked, "What was it like before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch? He replied, "The golden chrysanthemums have just begun to bloom;
bees compete to gather them. The monk asked, "What was it like after he saw him? He replied, "The stalks wither and the flowers fall; there is nothing left to rely upon.
While Zhenxie was engaged in his studies, the Master asked him, "What is one's own self prior to the empty kalpa? As Zhenxie was about to respond, the Master struck him.

The Master said, "You are being too noisy; go for now. One day, while ascending Mount Bōmú (Bowl Basin Peak), he suddenly attained enlightenment. Upon returning to stand in attendance, the Master struck him with his palm and said, "I thought you knew it.
He ceased his joy and bowed. The following day, the Master ascended the hall and said: "The sun shines upon the solitary peak, its colors emerald."
"The moon descends upon the mountain stream; it is cold. "The Patriarch’s mysterious and wondrous instruction: do not settle it within an inch of the mind. He then descended from his seat.
Xie stepped forward directly and said, "Today you have ascended the seat; you shall no longer be able to deceive me.
The Master said, "Try to cite for me what I said when I ascended the seat today. After a long silence, the Master said, "I thought you had suddenly awakened. Xie then departed. Hongzhi.
After the formal session, the Master asked, "What is the self prior to the empty kalpa? Zhi said, "A shrimp at the bottom of the well swallows the moon;
at the third watch, one does not borrow the night-bright curtain. The Master said, "Not yet. Speak further.
As Zhi was about to deliberate, the Master struck him with his whisk and said, "And you say it is not borrowed! At these words, Zhi attained great enlightenment.
The eulogy says:
A bright pearl born from within an oyster’s belly; A wild crane amidst a flock of chickens.
The tradition of burning wooden Buddhas has not yet vanished; The family chronicle of the "Owl-Bird" was heard firsthand.
Lighting the flower-candle of the awakened mind,
the land of Dengzhou shifts between the breath of life and the killing qi of Jianmen Pass;
the cloud-reaching galleries see the Jade Maiden with her pregnancy exactly half-finished— this profound and wondrous intent is difficult to distinguish as deep or shallow.
The heron stands in the snow, yet its color is not the same; The mountain of form and the jewel are not worth a single coin.
When both water and moon are forgotten, one ascends to heaven; Since the bottom is firmly established, one must surely cast down the dust and mire.
Within these different species, do not begrudge your diligent effort.
Before the hare-marked moon was yet divided, Xuán knew the six gates; others did not understand his intent.
After the ox-heads met face to face, How pitiable! The myriad flowers fall in profusion.
He secretly casts the golden shuttle to weave upon the loom of the ancient cavern; The *zhu* shuttle rings softly.
Fine strands of jade thread are arranged to open the cotton of Mount Cao; Clustered into patterns, they existed before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda.
Having gathered the Bodhisattva’s light of the hair-tip into a single palm, The night-bright curtain requires no borrowing;
Capturing the Master of Enlightenment, his brush-array sweeps away a thousand armies.

To casually utter a single phrase is the subtle grasp of the very center. Even if one were to use golden scissors to cut through the most dense and seamless places, one still does not fall into the realm of achievement.
— Chan Master Zhenxie Le.
The Master’s name was Qingliao. He was a native of Zuo-mian and his secular surname was Yong. Having first encountered Danxia and received his instructions, he subsequently visited Changlu Zhao.

Upon seeing him, Zhao recognized his potential and appointed him as his attendant. After more than a year, he was assigned to share the teaching seat. Not long thereafter, Zhao retired due to illness and entrusted the succession of the abbacy to the Master.
Students gathered around him like returning home. When it was time for the incense offering, Zhao presented the robe to the Master, instructing him to bring it forth.
When he saw that it was becoming like a sunset glow, he ordered those around him to pull off his robes.
The Master had prepared a *buddhagarbha* (patchwork robe) in his sleeve, which he then put on and showed to the assembly. Shaking his staff, he said, "Look, look! The entire trichiliocosm is shaking.
"Master Yunmen has attained this," [he continued]. "But it is not so under Xuefeng. He struck the ground with his staff and said, "The trichiliocosm..."
"Where does the world go? Do you understand? There shall be no second torrential rain; how could the rice seedlings fail to turn green?
Entering the hall, he ascended the summit of the peak and crossed the single-plank bridge. To walk straight on like this is still the place where people's feet are high or low.
If you see through it thoroughly, without leaving your room your body pervades the ten directions; even before entering the gate, you are already always there.

"In the inner chamber. If this is not yet so, it would be well to move some firewood while the weather is cool. Ascending the hall: To exhaust the subtle is to lose the root; to embody the wondrous is to forfeit the source.
A single phrase cuts off the current; the profound depths are exhausted. Therefore, where the golden needle is hidden, its sharp edge is not revealed;
when the jade thread passes through, it secretly displays extraordinary luster. Although this is so, it is still a mutual illumination of the two. Moreover—
"The Way is beyond skill or clumsiness; how can it be entrusted? After a long silence, he said: "Where the cloud-vines are exquisite, the green shadows close together;
on the crags and trees, high and low, the emerald locks are deep. He then ascended the hall and said: "The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. Thereupon, he performed a dance.
"Do you see? Do you see? Seeing it thus, one finds that 'the village wine is delicious beyond the bridge. He then performs a dance and says, "Do you see? Do you see?
Not seeing it thus, one finds that 'the wild flowers are fragrant on the opposite bank. He ascends the hall and says: "Moss seals the ancient path; it does not fall into empty stillness."
Frost and mist lock the cold forest; how could one fail to manifest the essential wind? The hook and needle are steady and subtle—whom can we call a fisherman nesting in a tree?
To accept things in this way is naturally ordinary and joyful. Is there anyone who possesses the eye that penetrates the barrier?

Even if you hear of it early and return at once, how can that compare to never having left the gate from the beginning? Ascending the hall, he said: "To turn function and occupy the position is to head toward the future."
A person. Like jade buried in the Jing Mountains, it is precious; shifting positions to fulfill its function, this is one who has returned. A flake of snow on a red furnace is spring.
When both function and position are transformed, the whole body is free from obstruction. Letting go of the hand, there is no longer any dependence. The stone woman ascends the loom at night;

the secret chamber has no one to sweep it. Entering the hall: For a long time I have kept this essential point in silence, not wishing to speak of it hastily. The Old Śākyamuni waited to explain it in full detail.
To flaunt it! Alas, even before emerging from the mother’s womb, one has already been seen through by others.
But tell me, what exactly was seen through? One cannot deceive Xuefeng.
The eulogy says:
A true native of Zuomian, he personally beheld the elder Danxia;
his breast-pond was crystal clear, his capacity vast and deep—a ten-thousand-acre expanse without a trace.
The moon of the mind is solitary and full, its reflection a perfect circle;
though divided by a thousand rivers, it is discerned before one's eyes as the master.
Seizing the *pāṭukāli* robe, he exchanges it face-to-face and turns his body amidst the clamor; with a single kick, he topples Mount Bōwùfēng.
The peony blooms like the face of a Bodhisattva; In the jade railing, the spring of the ancient cave is hidden.
The green willows knit their brows as the wooden man’s eyebrows frown; The precious mirror reflects the dawn of the Cao family.
Having attained realization amidst the heavy rains, I take advantage of my leisure to set down my staff for a while.
Crossing the solitary wooden bridge, one carries a load of firewood to enjoy the cool breeze;
the cliffs are fine and the trees lush, where green clouds and ivy merge. The verse for cutting across the stream distinguishes skill from clumsiness;
the wine is exquisite beyond the bridge, and the fragrance of flowers wafts from the opposite bank. Beholding the Dharmakāya, there is no small amount of carelessness.
Vastly凝 (congealed) yet not falling, the mud-bull roars at the moon;
The ancient path is left to be sealed by moss. Letting go of the hand, one loses reliance; the stone woman ascends the loom. In the secret chamber, no one sweeps;
the star-children and fragrant bait are excellent. They lure the crimson-tailed carp from the dragon abyss; with a flick of the tail, it swallows the hook.
A tiny bit of medicine is efficacious: it restrains the *bìbí* snake of the Southern Mountains as it slinks deep into the grass.
When function is transformed into position, and position is transformed into function, everything is overturned from the very bottom.
Even before the yellow-faced old Gautama had emerged from his mother’s womb, he was already seen through by this master.

Chan Master Hongzhi Jue, whose posthumous name was Zhengjue, was a successor of Danxia. He was the son of the Li family from Xizhou. His mother dreamed that a monk from the Zhengtai Monastery untied a ring and fastened it upon her right arm;
she subsequently conceived. Upon his birth, a ring appeared on his right arm. [He] ascended the hall [and said]: "The mind cannot objectify; the mouth cannot..."
Consider this: Even if you were to retreat and take up the burden, you must strictly avoid striking the forbidden taboo.

At the ancient ferry crossing, where the wind and moon are cold and clear, the night boat turns upon a ground of lapis lazuli. Entering the hall, he said: "The yellow gate curtains hang down—who transmits the family message?
The purple silk curtain closes—darkly scattering true pearls. At such a time, there is that which hearing and sight do not reach; there is that which words and explanations cannot express."
And so it is. How can one convey this message? "The dream returns as the night fades into twilight; with a smile, he points to the family tradition—a spring in full bloom.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the person who goes forth? He replied, "White clouds fall into the ravines; green peaks lean high against the void.
The monk asked, "What is the person who returns? He replied, "With a head full of white hair, he leaves the mountain valleys."
At midnight, he passed through the clouds into the marketplace and asked, "What is the person who neither comes nor goes?

[The Master] replied, "A stone woman calls back the dream of the third fruit; a wooden man sits cutting off the mechanism of the six gates. He then said, "To clarify the essence within a phrase is easy."
Within the school, the point of discernment is difficult to grasp. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? The frost-bound rooster has not yet announced the dawn in the home grove;
hidden, the traveler encounters the Snowy Mountains. His parting words were: "Dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—sixty-seven years.
The white birds vanish into the mist; the autumn waters join the sky."
The eulogy says:
Vajradhvaja, Compassion’s seed,
The ancient Buddha of Xizhou, Whose radiance remains unreleased.
The old monk of Wutai—when has he ever entered my dreams?
With the countenance of purple mushrooms and golden bones, a *qilin* among those of heaven;
With the magnanimity of Huangbo and a heart like brocade, a phoenix among monks.
Not falling into the ranks of the noble, what use are kings across the three periods of time?
If one engages in pure chanting, even a single poem need not seek to emulate the Tang or Song.
On the slippery floor of the lapis lazuli palace, a light stroke of the oar still carries the subtle mystery.
The yellow gate curtains hang closed, and news cannot pass; yet there still remain twenty li of pines toward which one once paid homage.
The surging waves of the pines overturn the moon in a clear sky; the stringless lute occasionally emits its pure tones.
The shadow of a hundred-foot tower dips into the clear pool; the work of the Unmaker fully manifests wondrous function.
The wind’s chisel skillfully carves a jade of linked cities; it is so transparent and clear that no trace remains.
A torch is lightly lit to illuminate the rhinoceros-hide on the islet; though it is a void stillness, it never stirs.
The azure peaks stand high in emptiness as white clouds cast themselves into the ravines; this must be the coming of a karmic mechanism that blinds the eyes of this monk.
The white crane vanishes into the mist as autumn waters join the heavens; providing a death-plea, he laughs until he splits the nostrils of others and tears asunder Mount Tai and Mount Hua.
He allows himself to be led out from the source of the Yellow River, swallowing the Buddhas of the three ages;
though it be a dead snake, it must be handled with life.
Chan Master Tiantong Jué was a successor of Zhenxie;
his name was Zongjué, and he was a native of Hezhou. In an address to the assembly, he said: "Taking steps before the kalpas, one casts the body across the world beyond.
This wondrous accord cannot be reached through the intellect; this true realization cannot be transmitted by words. It must result in a state of utter stillness."
The gathering mists fade as white clouds break against the cold crags; the numinous light pierces the darkness as the bright moon follows the night boat.

At such a time, how do you tread this path? Perversion and correctness never depart from their original station; whether horizontal or vertical, how could they involve the causes and conditions of speech? A monk asked, "What is the Way?

He replied, "At the crossroads, do not crane your neck in expectation. — Xuedou Qian *Note: "Xuedou" (Snow Valley) refers to Xuedou Chongxian (890–973), a prominent Chan master of the Song dynasty. "Jian" (Mirror) is his posthumous title.*

Upon entering Haishan, Mingfeng later remarked, "Those who attain self-realization without a teacher prior to the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja are [right], but those who attain self-realization without a teacher after King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja are immediately demons and heterodox practitioners.
Upon leaving the mountain, he heard a voice in the air saying, "Zheng Xingshan, a flesh-body Bodhisattva, has come to Changlu to see you and seek your seal of certification. The Master consented.
The Eulogy says:
The Military Aide is brilliant and elegant; The Governor-General is pure and fresh.
A single reed pavilion for the Ninefold Rite of the Auspicious Phoenix; A New Feng Grotto for the Five-Colored Omenous Qilin.
The Great Way is empty and solid; at the crossroads of the ten directions, it is a vain labor to crane the neck in expectation.
The profound mystery dissolves and melts away; beyond the world of King Weyin, it is precisely here that one may cast the body across.
True realization cannot be transmitted by words; though words fill the world, there is no fault in the mouth.
How can wondrous resonance be reached by the intellect? When the intellect is exhausted, all phenomena are severed from their roots and sensory dust;
the numinous light shines inwardly like a boat on a dark night carrying the shimmering moon, as the miasma vanishes into empty stillness, and the cold crags are stripped of drifting clouds.
Transverse and vertical, how could they involve the causes and conditions of speech? Scooping water to splash at the mandarin ducks makes it difficult to hide their traces;
biased and correct have never left their original positions. A withered stump binds a leprous horse in vain, its spirit and heart exhausted to death;
the seams of the brocade are lightly opened, as flowers spray fragrance and butterflies sleep in the clear dawn.
The shuttle and threads do not move; willows hold the mist as orioles weave the fragrant spring.

Having eyes but no sinews, he mistakenly certified Zheng Xingshan as an incarnate Bodhisattva, causing the sound of grievance to reach a thousand feet of flying snow and shaking the entire forest of monasteries.
Master Zide Hui succeeded Hongzhi as his dharma heir.
His name was Huahui, and he was the son of the Zhang family of Kuaiji. He ascended the hall and said: "The bird's nest knows the wind; the animal's burrow knows the rain."
The sweet is sweet, and the bitter is bitter; there is no need for calculation or deliberation.
Five times five is twenty-five from the start; all manner of arrangements arrive at the ordinary. This is the saying of those who have thoroughly studied in the monastic groves.

Do you all understand it yet? The rustic elder knows nothing of the virtue of Yao and Shun; they beat the drums *dong-dong* to sacrifice to the River God. Entering the hall, he said: "The skin and flesh..."

Freed from all boundaries and directions, one clearly realizes that body and mind are but a single thing, wherein not a single object exists. Wondrously entering the profound and tranquil realm of the Way, the jade-like person uprightly drives the white ox-cart.
In this field of wondrous luminosity, those who reach it are rare; where ordinary consciousness cannot arrive, only through realization can it be known.
The child of white clouds shines with spiritual clarity by itself; the staff of the green mountains stands firm and ever-present. The pivot of the mechanism is situated behind the crown of the head.
Light! Wisdom accords with the eye prior to kalpas. Thus it is said: "The road of Xinfeng is steep and still; the cave of Xinfeng is profound and lush.
Those who ascend do so without wavering; those who roam do so without haste. Though there are pavilions and halls, few people reach them;
though forests and springs exist, they do not grow ordinary trees. O practitioners of Zen, the supreme point above all is noble and majestic.
Difficult to clarify. Upon the lapis lazuli palace, one does not claim supremacy; before the emerald curtain, one must still keep company.

At such a time, when the needle and thread penetrate through, and the True Dharma has not fallen, how should one provide for it? With a head full of white hair, he leaves the Yangu Valley; at midnight, he pierces the clouds to enter the marketplace.
The Master has a "Diagram of the Six Oxen," the first of which says: "When first hearing the instruction of a spiritual friend..."
Upon hearing these instructions, he immediately gave rise to faith. Once faith has sprouted, it becomes the eternal foundation of the Way. Thus, there is a single white spot atop the ox's head;

a single thought of faith is the root, and a thousand lifetimes of entering the Path depend upon it. I pity myself for being deluded regarding the nature of awakening, allowing me to be defiled by dust and grime wherever I go.
Wild grasses turn green from time to time; wild flowers bloom anew day by day. Thinking of home, there is no way to reach it; I only feel my tears soaking my kerchief.
(2) Once faith has been awakened, one polishes the mind moment after moment until, suddenly, illumination is revealed. A joy arises in the heart.

This was the very first entry into the gate, which is why the hair at the crown is completely white. The "ox" that comes to inquire knows what is wrong—why is he so late? How many years has he wandered away from home?
For many kalpas, one has pursued delusion; now, moment by moment, one returns to non-thought, and thought after thought, one severs all that is thought.

From this point, the entry [into the Way] begins, and one realizes the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) in successive stages. Third: once illumination has been attained, one gradually undergoes refinement through perfuming, until wisdom becomes luminous and tranquil.
It has not yet reached a state of pure unity; though half its body is already white, it has grazed upon the pastures for many autumns and springs.

It is about to become a cow of the open field, leaving the wild weeds behind to roam near the Snowy Mountains. Although right mindfulness has returned to oneness, perverse thoughts still flow in a muddled stream.
Once the traces of anxiety are shed and exhausted, the six sense bases can no longer contain them. Fourth: there are no further deluded thoughts; there is only the single true mind, pure and serene.
Profoundly still, the entire body is luminous and clear; the six sense bases cannot encompass it. The *udumbara* flower blooms within the fire;
it is perfectly manifest, without attachment or dependence. Bright and pure, it is utterly free from even a speck of dust. Ropes and halters will be of no use; where then are the man and the ox?

Far beyond the distant void of kalpas, neither Buddhas nor patriarchs can fathom it. Fifth: when both mind and phenomena are forgotten, and both man and ox are extinguished, one forever transcends the realm of forms.

The sole emptiness of emptiness is called the Great Gate of Liberation. It is the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. When the news of man and ox has utterly ceased, the ancient path is severed of those who understand.
Mists roll away and a thousand crags are still; moss grows and the three paths grow deep. The mind is empty and possesses nothing;
when emotion is exhausted, it does not belong to the present. Where is the public who holds the hook? At Panxi, green shadows lock the stream. Sixth: where the life-root is severed.

Having passed away and returned to life, one receives a body according to one's kind; appearing on every stage as a performance, it is only the person of old that changes, not the place of one’s former conduct.

Wondrously exhausting all limits, then reaching through both obstruction and penetration, one returns once more among the six realms. In every speck of dust there is the Buddha-work; in every place is the family style.
Like white jade distinct from the mud, like refined gold encountered within the fire, one wanders freely upon the path of no interval. Following...
The likeness is like drifting pines and tumbleweeds.
The commentary says:
A spark of stone and a flash of lightning; amidst thunder and lightning, there is sudden silence.
Pure gold within the sands of the Yuezhi Creek; *Campaka* flowers amidst the thorns of Mount Zhulu.
Seeing Zhenxie adorning an old woman with flowers—how could she know shame?
Hearing Hongzhi chewing his food to feed an infant—how would one dare claim it as self-attained?
Treading upon and overturning the paths of light and darkness, The eyes and head are covered with thorns scattered across the ground;
Severing the roots of subtle conceptualization, Beneath the heels grow thorny brambles reaching toward the heavens.
In the full perfection of noble dignity, One mounts the fragrant carriage—how could it crush the sacred moss?
All along the way, it is as usual; Sacrificing to the River God, one knows not the power of Shun.
The mist clears and a solitary egret stands on the cold sands; At the head of the wild stream, the snow is still blurred.
The frost melts from the withered trees and the old dragon roars; Outside the bamboo door, there is no news of spring.
The Way dwells in a realm of profound stillness; The light behind the crown of the head precedes the kalpas.
Even the eyes are but golden dust while emotional consciousness has not yet merged; The green mountains are the father, the white clouds are the child— Together they form household rebels.
When both the "correct" and the "partial" are reached, How can the flowers of the Ten Continents avoid withering?
The gathering and releasing are not yet complete; what is so extraordinary about the Six Oxen Diagram?

Under the Gate of the Long Star (Chang-geng), one sweeps away a boisterous life. One believes that the divine colt possesses the merit of the "sweat-blooded" steed, and the golden rooster holds the virtue of heralding the dawn.
From Dongshan to this point, there are eleven generations comprising fourteen individuals.
*Praise of the Five Houses of the Orthodox Lineage*, Scroll Three;
*Praise of the Five Houses of the Orthodox Lineage*, Scroll Four.
The Yunmen School:
Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen succeeded Xuefeng.
His name was Wenyuan; he was a native of Xiuzhou and his secular surname was Zhang. He received his monastic training at Kongwang Temple and studied under the Fourth [Patriarch].
He divided the Vinaya and abandoned his views at Muzhou. As soon as Muzhou saw him, he shut the door and pressed against the master’s feet, saying, "A wheel from the Qin dynasty!
The master attained great enlightenment. Muzhou pointed him toward Xuefeng. When the master arrived at Xuefeng’s estate, he saw a monk and asked, "Are you going up the mountain?
The monk said, "Yes. The master said, "Please deliver this message to the Abbot: do not say..."

This was the speech of another person. The monk said, “Yes. The Master said, “When you, Senior, arrive at the monastery and see the Abbot ascending the hall while the assembly has gathered, go straight out, clasp your wrists together, stand on the ground, and say:
‘Why does this old fellow not cast off the iron cangue upon his neck?
Following the Master’s instruction, the monk spoke thus. When Feng saw the monk speak in this manner, he descended from his seat, grabbed him by the chest, and said, “Speak quickly!”
"Quickly! The monk remained silent. Feng pushed him aside and said, "That was not your words. The monk said, "It was my words. Feng said, "Attendant, bring the rope and staff!
The monk said, "It was not my words. It was an elder from Zhejiang on the manor who instructed me to come and speak this.
Feng said, "Everyone, go to the manor to welcome the Five Hundred Good Knowledge-holders (Upādhyāyas) here!"
The next day, the Master went up the mountain. As soon as Feng saw him, he said, "For what reason have you come to such a state?

The Master rubbed his eyes with his hand and hurried out. Feng marveled at this. For twenty years, Lingshu had not appointed a head seat (shouzuo). One day, when the Master arrived, Lingshu immediately commanded him to take the post;
the Master accepted the office without declining. Whenever Prince Liu entered the temple, Lingshu would not receive him; the Prince wished to investigate his transgression. Lingshu—
He was already aware of this and subsequently entered nirvana. When the King arrived, the assembly informed him. The King asked, "What words did he leave behind?

The assembly replied, "When the Master departed, he sealed a small casket and told us to wait for the King’s arrival before opening it. The King opened it and saw a small note that read: "The Eye and Treasury of Humanity and Heaven; the Head Seat of the Hall.
The King immediately commanded the Master to succeed him on the seat. This was due to the karmic causes of a previous life involving King Liu.
A perfume seller entered a temple and spat into the Sangha hall. The Hall Monitor happened to scold him, saying, "It is as if you had spat on my face.
They argued without ceasing. The Master (Zhaozhou) intervened and left. The Master possessed the "One-Word Barrier" of the Mirror of Retrospection and the Red Banner of the Bone-Dry Principle.
As he approached his passing, he left a testament stating: "For seventeen years, I have been weathering the winds and frost..."
Separated by thousands of li from north to south.
The eulogy says:
The reeds and rushes produce extraordinary timber; Its vast spirit swallows the Milky Way.
Departing from Kongwang Temple, he leaves no trace of the tangled vines of the Four-Part Vinaya;
He crosses the gate of Muzhou with his legs broken, awakening to the carriage-wheel of the Qin era.
The fruit, having weathered the frost, ripens; beneath the bright window, he knows how to arrange the sacred tree.
Gold becomes as soft as pliant thread when wound around a finger; yet, entering further into the great furnace of Xueqiao, it is smelted and refined.
Seeing Liu Wang, one recalls the monk who spat on his face while the spit was still wet, prompting Xuan Sha to laugh.
The fisherman’s boat is now entirely scorched and red-hot.
Releasing three blows of the staff at Dongshan—this is the thoroughgoing, compassionate heart of an old woman.
Erecting Yunmen’s “Single-Character Barrier” blinds the eyes of the masters.
The red banner on the water has not yet been lowered; how many times have horizontal bones been pulled from the darkness?
Although for seventeen years he endured wind and frost upon the roads of adversity, he established extraordinary merit over several hundred generations at the edge of a city of miasmic vapors.

He was a monk who was like a phoenix and a man who was like a dragon; who could have performed the *Jiucheng* music to stir the deep abyss, causing him to come forth in grace and soar upward for his ancestors?
In the late autumn of the courtyard, Chan Master Xianglin Yuan succeeded Yunmen;
his name was Chengyuan, a native of Hanzhou, surnamed Shangguan. When the Master [Yunmen] served as his attendant, he presented him with a paper robe.
He recorded these words and phrases. Later, he returned to Shu, where at the Crystal Palace (Shuijing Gong) he served tea and soup to those who came and went.
A monk asked, "Why does the exquisite flavor of *amṛta* turn into poison? He replied, "The paper in Daojiang is selling for a high price.

A monk asked, "What is the single bowl of lamp-light within the room? He replied, "Three people testify that a tortoise is a turtle. A monk asked, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? He replied, [as before].
[The Master] said, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains. A monk asked, "What is the single stream of spring at Xianglin? He replied, "Thoughts are uninterrupted.

[The monk] asked, "As for those who drink from it, how is that? He replied, "According to the region, the measure is different. The Master said to the assembly, "It took me forty years to finally achieve a state of total integration.
When he was about to pass away, he took his leave of the Prefect, Song Gongdang, saying, "I, this old monk, am going on a pilgrimage."
The Vice Prefect said, "This monk is mad; at eighty years old, where would he go on pilgrimage? Song said, "A great spiritual friend (mahā-kalyāṇamitra) is free to come and go as he pleases.
Yuan Luogong, seeking the Yunmen school, entered Sichuan and visited Master Renmianshan.
The eulogy says:
With five peaks soaring steeply, And three eyes born from his brow,
He stands amidst the elephant and dragon herds of Shao Stone, Having snatched away the rhinoceros.
Amidst the mountain caves of Min and E, the phoenix soars;
yet in the *Zhīyī Lù*, one borrows the phrases of others.
Mistaking fish eyes for bright pearls, one boils sand jars to prepare tea for guests, turning the finest clarified butter into poison.
In the crystal palace, cold fragrance drifts from the incense seals; leaning against a round *pú* mat, one partakes in the moonlight and wind.
Before the mountain face, emerald peaks stand like a screen; with a slender cane, one visits the green monkeys and wild cranes, proving the turtle to be a tortoise.
Within the chamber, the lamp’s radiance has faded.
The winter fire burns the mountains; the matter beneath one's robes is feared difficult to grasp.
For forty years it has been forged into a single piece—bright and clear, yet dark and obscure.
At eighty years old, he travels on foot through all quarters—lofty and towering, yet lively and agile.
Investigating and discerning the essential meaning of "Ei" (The Aha!), One follows the path of Master Yuanluo until the skin of one's feet is worn through.
Relying on the style of the Lai Gate, One partakes of the hardships of the Zizhi Gate.
As for the stream of incense from Xialin, it has been interrupted for a long time; If you wish to follow its course, you must adjust the measure yourself upon the scale.
Zhuo. Chan Master Chushan Shouchu succeeded Yunmen.
His secular name was Shouchu, and he was the son of the Fu family of Fengxiang. When he first visited Yunmen, Yunmen said, "Where have you recently come from?"
“Where are you from? He replied, “Chadu. “Where did you spend the summer retreat? He replied, “At Baoci in Hunan. “When did you leave there?

He replied, “On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. The Master said, “I grant you three blows of the staff. The next day, the Master went up to inquire after him and said, “Yesterday I received the Master’s three blows of the staff;
I do not know where my fault lay. The Master said, “You rice-bag! From Jiangxi...”

"Having gone to Hunan, I shall simply act in this manner," he said. The Master attained great enlightenment and subsequently declared: "In the future, I will establish a hermitage in a place where there is no human habitation.

I will not store a single grain of rice nor plant a single stalk of vegetable. I will receive those coming and going from the ten directions and help them all pull out their nails and extract their wedges;
I will strip away their greasy hats and cast off their foul-smelling robes, so as to leave them in a state of pure liberation."
"To become a monk of non-action—would that not be joyful! The Gatekeeper said, "Your body is no larger than a coconut, yet you open such a wide mouth.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Words do not unfold the matter; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish;
those who linger in phrases are deluded. Can you still attain it? Within the domain of you monks, upon reaching this point, you must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma."
[The Master] said, "Indeed. Yet, for Dongshan to speak in such a manner, there is a certain fault. Tell me, where does the fault lie?

A monk asked, "What is it like when Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra come to pay their respects? [Dongshan] said, "Drive them into the cowpen. The monk said, "Entering hell, you would be like an arrow shot from a bow.
[Dongshan] said, "It depends entirely on your own strength. A monk asked, "When the Master ascends the lion’s throne..."

"Please, Master, chant a *daoling* (song of the Way). He said: "When the weather is clear and dry, one opens a waterway; when there is no business, one establishes an office. [The monk] said: "If that is so, then I thank the Master for his instruction. He said:
"The feet of an old woman selling shoes are clumsy and uneven. [The monk] asked: "Setting aside the workings of the mind and consciousness, I ask the Master for a single phrase.

He said: "A Daoist priest dressed in yellow sits inside a jar. [The monk] asked: "The great assembly has gathered like clouds; I ask the Master to summarize [the essence] for them. He said: "The Daoist priest dressed in yellow sits inside a jar."
The Essential Pivot: A brief presentation of the general outline states: "A bubble floating on the water displays five colors; a shrimp under the sea calls out to the bright moon. Question:
"What is it like when the lotus has not yet emerged from the water? Answer: "The mountain of Chu stands upside down. Question: "What is it like after it has emerged? Answer:
"The Han River flows straight to the east. Question: "What is the Buddha? Answer: "Three pounds of flax. [He] questioned a monk: "What..."

[The Master asked: "Where have you come from? [The monk] said, "Ruzhou. [The Master asked: "How far is it from here? [The monk] said, "Seven hundred li. [The Master asked: "How many pairs of straw sandals have you worn out?

[The monk] said, "Three pairs. [The Master asked: "Where did you get the money to buy them? [The monk] said, "I used it to buy my bamboo hat. [The Master said: "Go to the hall for the assembly. The monk responded with an "Amen" (Āṃ).
The eulogy says:
A sage of an extraordinary age, a true vessel of the Dharma,
possessing compassion that transcends retribution yet remains within the realm of ordinary sentiment— it was only upon seeing Yunmen that he suddenly attained awakening.
The phoenix gives birth in ten thousand ravines; the tiger’s and leopard’s vital energy has already devoured an ox.
A flash of lightning topples a city; the dragon-horse colt’s hooves should display the talent of a swift steed.
Behold the entire body as being like a coconut—how many long spans could it possibly have?
Making grand boasts like a spinning wheel—how could you feel even the slightest shame before your former teacher?
When asked what fault you have committed, you deserve several strokes of the rattan.
You receive travelers in places where there is no human habitation, yet you do not store a single grain of rice.
Wine paints the faces of young gentlemen; Yellow-haired and blue-eyed, they stand head-downward over cesspools.
Flowers are stuck in the heads of beautiful women; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are driven off into the cowsheds.
The old woman selling shoes has feet that stumble and trip; Singing songs of the Way, the barbarian speaks his local dialect.
A Daoist monk sits atop a mound while wearing a jar; A Persian of miscellaneous consciousness enters a bustling market.
Great ocean bubbles and the croaking of a frog at the moon; Mistakenly claiming the "Tie" and "Shao" as the core principles of the Stone—Mount Chu stands overturned, the Han River flows east.
In vain, one smears and covers the lotus flower rising from the water.
Question: "How far is the road from here? Answer: "I have worn through several pairs of straw sandals. Question:
"How much hemp did the Buddha gather? Answer: "Three catties, all of it smelling foul.
When words fail to express the matter and speech fails to meet the occasion, though there is no lack of principles to be explained, this falls short of the tradition of Shaoshi (Bodhidharma).
White clouds ten thousand miles away.
Chan Master Mizu of Zhimen was a successor of Xianglin;
his name was Guanzhuo, and he was a native of Suizhou. In a formal address to the assembly, he said: "I remember when I was still in my mother’s womb."
There is a saying from the past that I shall present to the great assembly today.
You must not engage in intellectual deliberation; is there anyone here who can deliberate upon it? A monk asked: "What can be placed within the adamantine eye?
He replied: "A handful of sand. The monk asked: "Why is it so? He replied: "It is not your realm. Another asked: "When the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water..."
"How is it? he asked. "A lotus flower," [the monk] replied. "After it has emerged from the water, how is it? he asked. "A lotus leaf," [the monk] replied. Ascending the hall, the Master said:
"All of you carry your staffs slung across your shoulders, leaving one grove only to enter another grove. Tell me, how many kinds of groves are there?"
There are some sandalwood groves surrounded by sandalwood; some thornbush groves surrounded by thornbushes;
some thornbush groves surrounded by sandalwood; and some sandalwood groves surrounded by thornbushes.
As for these four kinds of monastic communities, in which one of them do you all establish yourselves and sustain your lives?
If you have no place to establish yourselves and sustain your lives, you will have wasted your straw sandals in vain; the day will come when King Yama demands payment for those sandals from you.
[Ascending the hall: Old Lady Li of the eastern house came to the western house to beg for fire; she stood outside the gate for a short while.
He scolds me for my lingering; in a fit of rage, he runs back home. He sits inside his empty house of the heart;
pitiful, that little child suffers hunger all day long. His eyes have no pupils; his skull is broken and left empty and locked away.
A monk asked, "What is the essence of Prajñā? He replied, "An oyster containing the bright moon. The monk asked, "What is the function of Prajñā? He replied, "A rabbit carrying a fetus."
Question: "What is the Buddha? He said: "Treading through straw sandals, walking barefoot. Question: "What is the matter beyond the Buddha? He said:
"Holding the sun and moon upon the tip of the staff. Question: "On the road to Caoxi, are there still worldly conversations? He said: "..."
The Sixth Patriarch was Layman Lu. A questioner asked, "What is it like when an ancient mirror has not yet been polished? He replied, "It is merely a piece of copper.
The questioner asked, "What is it like after it has been polished? He replied, "Just set it aside. When Xuedou saw the Master, he asked, "When not a single thought arises..."
"What fault is there? The Master called Dou Jin to come forward. As soon as Dou approached, the Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk.
Dou attempted to open his mouth, and the Master struck him again. Dou attained great enlightenment.
The Eulogy says:
The root of his tongue surges like a vast wave;

His breast is empty of things, as if the Blue Sea had personally given birth to a rhinoceros horn that gazes at the moon. From the Fragrant Grove, he releases a falcon soaring through the vast heavens.
A single word within the mother’s womb— Who would dare to deliberate upon this cluster of sharp blades?
A diamond eye is but a handful of sand; How can one scrub away these layers of cataracts?
The lotus leaf and the lotus flower emerge from the water, one before the other; This is not the mechanism for cutting across the stream.
Sandalwood and thorns encircle the grove; For a brief moment, he stands outside the gate of the Land of No-Birth.

Knowing that Old Lady Li-si has come to beg for the child of Bing-ding, Before the first thought arises, he seeks to reveal the Master’s [true nature]— Let him suffer the painful stroke of the tortoise-hair whisk!
The rabbit conceives while the clam holds the bright moon; the essence and function of Prajñā are buried.

On the road to Caoxi, there is a worldly saying: "The Layman Lu was so alert that he created a muddied pool.

Chan Master Xuedou Mingjue was a successor of Zhimen;

his name was Chongxian. He was a native of Suzhou and belonged to the Li clan. Initially he resided at Cuifeng, and subsequently at Xuedou, where his Dharma path flourished greatly, leading to him being hailed as the restorer of the Yunmen lineage.
Previously, he had served as the guest prefect at Dayang, where he engaged in discourse with visitors.
Regarding the story of the Cypress Tree: At that time, Han Dabo was leaning nearby and laughing to himself. After the guest had departed, the Master said to him, "Why were you laughing?
Han replied, "I laughed because the Guest Master has a tongue that can settle matters past and present, but lacks eyes that can settle matters past and present.
The Master asked, "Is there a reason for this? Han answered with a verse: "A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; A blue hawk sees it and instantly seizes it."
Later, the hunting dogs lost their supernatural efficacy; they searched in vain for the old site where the withered stumps once stood. The Master marveled at this and formed a friendship with him.
Once, when Vice-Director Li visited Chan Master Fuyan Ya, the Master was serving as the Librarian (Zangzhu).
While he was engaged in conversation with Li, a Daoist and a scholar suddenly arrived. Li asked, "Among the three teachings, which is the most honored? The Master rose and stood to one side.

Li said, "You have a mouth; why do you not speak? The Master said, "It is difficult to speak before a master such as you. Li said, "Enough! Enough! and rose. The Master said, "Just now, I was too hasty.
The Master then offered a verse on the public case of Dàlóng Jiāngùfǎshēn, saying: "I did not know [the answer] before."

Answer: Again, he does not understand. The moon is cold and the wind is high; in the ancient crags, the cypress trees are frigid. It is laughable that when meeting a man who has attained the Way on the road, one does not respond with either speech or silence. Holding a white jade whip in hand, he shatters the dragon pearls all at once. Had he not shattered them, flaws and blemishes would have increased. The state has its laws and regulations: there are three thousand articles of crime. This is a verse on the public case of National Teacher Huizhong’s “Seamless Stupa. As for the Seamless Stupa: The seamless stupa— How can it be entered? If you try to enter through the gate, You will surely be pierced by the thorns. To see it is difficult; a clear pool does not permit a blue dragon to coil within. Layer upon layer it falls, its shadow a perfect circle;
for ten thousand ages, it remains for all people to behold. (Self-praise: Three fingers up and down, seven horses back and forth.
Since the Flower was presented, he never smiled. Why? Stone calls it jade, yet the vessel must be distinguished; water hovers in the void, yet the moon is not below. Who knows who is standing by?
The Observer sends this to the Chan Master Chong Gao: Spring rain is like rich fat; spring clouds are like cranes. Now here, now there;
suddenly ceasing, suddenly arising. The withered roots lie scattered; the wind blows too slowly. Fragments of dark rock lie exposed; the vast sky is also perilous.
One flower and five petals—unlike anything else. Moving alone in solitary brilliance, one knows it for oneself. One knows it for oneself. Passing through the Wei...

Wandering through Liang was in vain; I have only brought my own obscurity upon myself. In painting the scenes of those years, I cherish the love for Dongting Lake, where seventy-two peaks rise green from the heart of the waves.
Now, reclining in high repose, I reflect on past events, which has added Lu Gong’s figure leaning against his stone screen.
The eulogy says:
The pearl that illuminated a chariot from the Marquis of Sui, The jade disc worth a succession of cities from the State of Zhao—
Having seized the splendor of Mount Min and Mount E, It manifests as the refined essence of his brows and countenance.
He distinguishes the flows of the Jing and Wei rivers; within the source of his mind, he unceasingly strips away and reveals the myriad phenomena.
He excels in the talent of Su Hanzlin, who captured the beauty of brocade and embroidery;
he is enriched by the pen of Lu Siku, who composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals* to praise and censure the Five Schools.
The bowl-basin of the Suifu has its handle securely set;

he laughs at the midnight transmission of Huangmei as not yet being the ultimate truth, seeing instead the cold spring dung-stick emitting light. He trusts that the single word from Shaoshi is a true offering;
the white jade whip strikes the black pearl without adding a speck of flaw—its radiance is brilliant and cool as ash.
The seamless stupa requires a clear pool where the azure dragon does not lie;

its shadow is round and black as lacquer, a gazeless eye fixed neither on past nor present. It was captured alive on the road by Han Taibo’s fierce hawk, which clearly distinguished between Confucianism and Buddhism;
it caused Director Li’s tiger to break into a sweat all over his body.
Before the Many-Sons Stupa, he never once plucked a flower or smiled; what use is it to dangle the "three fingers" or the "seven horses" on one's lips?
In the snow of Shaolin, there was originally no severing of arms or settling of the mind; the "five leaves" and "one flower" are but a weary pointing of fingers.
"Dwell well at Cuifeng! Dwell well at Xuedou!"—a dog licking a hot oil cauldron.
Some speak of the Zen of the Patriarchs, others of the Zen of Words;
The snail-script on the fresh mud wall sprays flying snow, a cascade over a thousand feet in height.
From his breast flows forth his love for Dongting, its seventy-two peaks together with the Stone Screen; He gathers them all back into his collection of scrolls.
High-flying spirit and transcendent melody, from antiquity to the present; only one person may be permitted to match them, like the Northern Dipper.
Mount Tai appears ever higher as one looks up at it; one cannot reach its summit.
Thus was Chan Master Dongshan Cong.
This master was the successor of Wenshu Zhen; his name was Xiaocong, and he was the son of the Du family of Shaoyang Prefecture.
Initially, upon seeing Wenshu address the assembly, saying, "A straight hook catches the black dragon; a curved hook catches shrimp and earthworms. Is there any dragon here?

After a long silence, he added, "Toil without merit. At these words, the master attained realization. While serving as the head lamp-keeper at Yunju, he heard a monk speak of the Great Sage of Sizhou.
Recently, he appeared in Yangzhou. Someone asked, "He is the Great Sage of Sizhou; why has he instead appeared in Yangzhou?
The Master said, "A gentleman loves wealth, but he acquires it through the proper way. Later, a monk recounted this to Master Xiang of Lotus Peak.
The Master was greatly astonished and said, "The descendants of Yunmen still exist! In the middle of the night, he gazed toward Yunju.

He paid his respects. Ascending the hall, he raised [the koan]: Hanshan said, "Red dust arises from the bottom of the well; white waves rise upon the high peaks. The rock-woman gives birth to a rock-child;
tortoise-hair grows an inch at every joint. If you wish to study Bodhi, simply observe this appearance. He remained silent for a long while.
He said, "Do you still know where it lands? If you do not know where it lands, look! Look! Bodhidharma has entered the Sangha Hall.
(He stood for a long time. A monk asked, "Before Bodhidharma transmitted the Mind-Ground Seal, and before Śākyamuni untied the jewel in his topknot—"
At this time, if one asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey: "Is there still a meaning to the Westward Journey, or not? He said:

"In the sixth month, the rain pours down, broadening the hearts of the myriad people. He said: "If that is so, then the clouds disperse and every house has its moon; spring comes and flowers bloom everywhere. He asked:
"From the soles of the feet down to the Golden Wheel Ocean, how many miles is it? The monk was speechless. Thereupon [the Master] said: "The Patriarch came from the West."
He specifically sang this matter. Since then, the *upādhyāya* has failed to recommend it. Therefore, those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure;
to mistake the shadow for the head—is this not a great error? Now that the Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing this matter, why must he further speak at length before the assembly?
Take care. [Ascending the hall: The morning cock announces the dawn; after the congee is served, the sky grows bright.
"The lantern is still dozing; the pillar, however, is wide awake. He spoke again: "Wide awake is truly wide awake; clearly distinct is truly clearly distinct.
Tomorrow and the day after, do not mistake the servant for the master. Take care! Addressing the assembly, he said:
"While the sky is clear, roof the house; while there is leisure, reap the grain. Once the tribute has been paid to the King, one can beat their belly and sing aloud. A monk asked: "Virtue..."
As soon as [a student] enters the gate, Shanzhou strikes him with his staff; this is still nothing more than tracing out patterns and drawing models. As soon as Linji enters the gate, he shouts;
this cannot avoid being like pressing one's eyes until flowers appear before them. Apart from these two paths, I do not know how Dongshan would have acted for the sake of others.

The Master said: "The sky has been clear for a long time without rain; lately, clouds have begun to rise. [The student] asked: "If someone were to ask about the fundamental principle of Dongshan on another day, what would you teach?"

"How would you express this? he asked. [The monk] replied, "The vegetables in the garden have withered away; I am carrying water to sprinkle on the spinach. A monk asked, "What is the phrase that transcends sound and form?
He replied, "Jambudvīpa in the south; Uttarakuru in the north. The monk said, "In that case, I, your disciple, recognize your kindness without fail.
He replied, "How deep are the four great oceans? One day, as the Master was unwell, he ascended the hall to take his leave.

The assembly recited a verse on the Dharmakāya, saying: "In practicing Chan and studying the Way, do not be lost in confusion. Having thoroughly questioned through to the Dharmakāya, the Northern Dipper is hidden away.
Now I am old, decrepit, and extremely frail; I lack the strength to engage in discussion with others. Only my hoe knows my Way;
when planting pines, it once again ascends the Diamond Mountain. Having finished speaking, he passed away in stillness.
The eulogy says:
Cutting off the cage and snare, leaving no trace—
erecting the dark barrier before the Xinfeng Cave.
He manifested the mechanism of transformation within the city of Jinyang, having slipped off the hook of Mañjuśrī;
entering the lair of the fierce dragon, who would dare guarantee him?
He answered the pivot-word of Sizhou with reckless indifference; as a descendant of Yunmen, you have no leisure to strike him down.
Polishing the ancient mirror amidst the dust; before the Yellow Crane Tower lies Parrot Isle.
Seeing a tall man entering the water; beneath the feet of the blind donkey lies the Diamond Limit (*vajrabhūmi*).
To study Bodhi, look at the stone woman giving birth to a child.
Bian Nu-lang needed a lantern;
he dozed off while roofing his house and paid his taxes in full. Singing songs and drumming his belly, he enjoys the peace and prosperity at will;
do not deliberate over Zen meditation or the study of the Way. Shoulder the hoe and plant pine trees; this is merely intended for recreation.
Turning over to hide behind the Big Dipper is not yet a sound strategy;
pouring water on a pomegranate plant is to misunderstand the fundamental principle.
To stray from the phrase "beyond sound and form" while vainly claiming "North Uttarakuru" or "South Jambudvīpa"—even if one were to deceive others thus, it would be in vain.
Monk: It is difficult to deceive oneself.
Chan Master Yunju Shun, whose name was Xiaoshun, was a successor of Dongshan. He was a native of Ruizhou and surnamed Hu. Initially, he went to study under Dongshan. One day, Wu...

Chang went out to beg for alms. His first stop was to visit Layman Liu, a man of lofty conduct who was revered by his contemporaries; whatever he intended to grant or withhold, no one failed to comply with him.
At that time, the Master was young and, unaware of the Layman’s extensive training, treated him with some degree of casualness.

The Layman said, "I have a question for you, old man. If our minds accord, I shall open my door; if they do not, I ask that you return to the mountain. He then asked: "The ancient mirror before it has been polished—"
"How is it at that time? he asked. [The Master] said, "Black as lacquer. "After being polished, how is it? he asked. [The Master] said, "It illuminates heaven and earth.

The scholar gave a long bow and said, "Please return to the mountain for now," then brushed his sleeves and entered his residence. The Master returned feeling dejected. Later, when Shanshan asked about the matter, the Master recounted what had occurred.
Shanshan said, "If you had asked me, I would have told you. The Master then posed the previous question again. Shanshan said, "From here to Hanyang, it is not..."
Yuan was departing. After the Master had gone, Shanshan said, "Before the Yellow Crane Tower lies the Parrot Isle. At these words, the Master attained realization.
Later, while the Master resided at Xiqian on Mount Lu, the District Magistrate Huai, who was governing Nanchang, stripped him of his monastic robes out of private resentment.

Da Jue Lian, having previously entered the Master’s quarters, heard that he had returned to lay life; he sent someone to fetch him back to Jingyin Temple and lodged him in the main hall, while Da Jue himself occupied a peripheral room.

In his quarters, Emperor Renzong summoned Zhiqiao several times to enter the inner palace, yet Zhiqiao never spoke of serving as a teacher. One day, Prince Jia received an imperial decree to go to Jingyin Monastery to provide a meal for the monks;
there he saw Zhiqiao attending to his master with great reverence. Upon his return, he reported this to the Emperor, who then summoned Zhiqiao for an audience in the private hall.

Upon seeing him, he sighed and remarked, "The resonance of his Way is extraordinary and magnificent; he is truly a man of realization for the mountain forests. He wrote upon a fan: "I grant Xiao Shun permission to remain as a monk;
by special imperial decree, he shall once again reside at Xie-xian Temple. Furthermore, he is granted purple robes and a silver bowl. The Master retired from Xie-xian.
At that time, two porters carried him in a sedan chair to Luo-han Temple. The two porters said, "Since you are not the abbot of our temple..."
