The old man was unable to travel far; he abandoned his sedan chair and returned. When the Master took up residence once more, he sent someone ahead to comfort the two men, saying, "What you did at that time was correct.
Simply set your minds at ease; there is no need for suspicion or fear. When the Master entered the monastery, he ascended the hall and said:
"Without cause, I was slandered and unjustly met with misfortune. For more than half a year, I lived as a layman. Today I return once again to Sanxia Temple."
"How much joy, how much anger? [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "I cite Jia Shan, who said: 'Recognize the Son of Heaven at the gate of the bustling marketplace;
realize the old monk atop the hundred blades of grass. Yunju, however, was not like this: 'The wife shakes the loom, *za za*;
the child plays with his mouth, *wa wa*. The Master often ridiculed Tianyi for preaching "entanglement Chan. One day, when Huiquan passed away, the Master...
In the Dharma Hall, [the Master] said, "I am glad that the thicket of entanglements has been toppled. At that time, Xiu Yuan-tong was serving as the *karmadāna* (Vina) within the assembly.
Whenever he saw [the Master] scolding or reviling others, he would say to his colleagues, "I must settle accounts with this old fellow once and for all."

When it was nearly nightfall, [Huai] again began to revile him. Xiu stepped out from the assembly with a stern voice and said, "Have you not seen what is taught in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*?
The Master abruptly said, "I have stood before the great assembly for a long time; I pray you all take care. He then returned to his quarters.

Xiu remarked, "This old fellow has eyes all over his body; he has truly rebuked Master Huai. Later, while giving a formal lecture, [Xiu] said, "In various quarters, there are those who dangle the head of a snake or stroke the tail of a tiger."
Leaping across the great ocean; concealing one’s body amidst the edges of swords. Here at Yunju, one washes one’s feet in hot water on a freezing day;
at night, one takes off one’s socks and sleeps; at dawn, one quickly ties on one’s leggings. When the wind blows the fence down, one calls for laborers to split bamboo and bind it back up.
Entering the hall [to preach], he said: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all dust motes. The shrimp and earthworms each have their own burrows."
Hole. Crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons also have nests. At such a time as this, for what kind of person does one preach the Dharma?
After a long silence, he said: "The square gathers with its kind; things divide according to their groups. Ascending the hall, he said: "Yunju does not understand Zen;
he washes his feet and goes up to bed to sleep. The winter melon is straight and blunt; the gourd is curved and winding. One day, the Master cited the words of Salt Official (Yanguan).
The story of Mazu calling for his attendant to bring the rhinoceros-horn fan: [Mazu] took it up and said, "At the height of the three months of summer, one truly needs a fan.
Yet because the attendant did not understand the matter, [the fan was broken]. Although this is so, Yanguan was far too verbose.
Why not simply let everyone cut off their attachments? Had the attendant, at that time, heard Yanguan say, "Since the fan is broken, return my rhinoceros," [what would have happened?]
"Come," he said, and immediately pointed toward the path, saying, "It has already been cast into the heap of wooden clogs.
He praised this, saying:
"Coming from amidst hardship and distress, the numinous clarity remains unobscured."
Tall bamboos in the deep courtyard reach toward the Milky Way; Ancient pines on the cold cliffs defy snow and frost.
His body returns to the temple of the Three Gorges, Adding to the Five Elders’ mountain range;
His feet stride across the Yingwu Isle, Shattering the ancient mirror into a hundred fragments.
The wife shakes the loom with a *za-za* sound; in the midst of the bustling market, one recognizes the Son of Heaven, yet he is not yet truly real.
The child plays with his mouth, making it crooked; upon the hundred grasses, the old monk is presented, yet none understand that his entire body is eyes.
Tianyi Huixiang joyfully upturned the thicket of entanglements.
A mound rises from level ground; Laughing at the Official of Huai for wrongly being charged with the crime of wearing civilian clothes.
Washing one's feet, removing socks, and sleeping; From the start, there was no extraordinary way of life.
Calling out to someone to split bamboo and bind a fence; This too is the ordinary household economy.
The nests of magpies and sparrows, the burrows of frogs and toads—within these, a solid and dense body appears amidst the dust.
A gourd is clumsy and blockish; a melon is crooked and bent. The Zen of the Patriarchs transcends all words:
playing with the head of a snake, poking the tail of a tiger. Listen to how, throughout the various quarters, they reveal their shadows and conceal their bodies within the edge of a sword.
Breaking the fan to strike the rhinoceros—Yanguan’s dung heap forms into lumps and clods, yet his dharma resonance is extraordinary and magnificent.
He earned the reputation of a realized master of the mountains and forests; like the return of pearls from Hepu, he drove away the sea monsters, remaining entirely free of flaw or blemish.
Chan Master Dajue Lian was a successor of Letan;
his name was Huailian. He was the son of the Chen family of Zhangzhou. His mother dreamed of a monk before he was born, and for this reason he was given the childhood name Sizhou.
The Master went to the Dharma seat of Letan, where he attained realization and received certification. He served him for over ten years before departing.
While traveling through Mount Lu, he served as the *zhǎngjì* (chief record-keeper) under Yuantong Ne. Emperor Renzong summoned Ne, who was weary; the Master was requested to act on his behalf.
An imperial decree was issued for him to reside at Jingyin Temple. He was summoned to the Huacheng Hall for an audience, where the Emperor inquired about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma.

His responses pleased the Emperor, who bestowed upon him the title Dajue. Later, the Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to ask: "As soon as you set down your staff, people will stand ready to oppose you. The Master replied with a verse: "Having a joint..."
"Not a dry bamboo stalk. Three stars encircle the lunar palace; one person dwells beneath the sun. He is not like the common crowd. Upon reading this, the Emperor was greatly pleased.

He summoned the Master again for an audience in the private hall and bestowed upon him a silk fan inscribed with the "Eulogy on Yuanji" and the poems and verses exchanged between the Emperor and the Master.
The Emperor wrote this and bestowed it upon him. It consisted of seventeen chapters in total. During the Zhìhé era, he requested to retire to the mountains in his old age, offering this eulogy:

"For six years in the imperial capital, I chanted the Patriarch’s mechanism; Twice in the golden halls, I received the Heavenly Majesty. Now departing to hide among the green mountains, what joy could be greater?"

He returned with only a box full of Imperial verses. The Emperor’s response verse was not permitted; the Emperor issued a proclamation saying, "The mountain is the very substance of suchness (*tathatā*).
Where would you go? He was thus ordered to reside once more in the capital and to promote the Buddha-dharma. The Master again submitted a verse of thanks, saying:
"The Imperial Messenger proclaimed my release from the palace precincts, Commanding me once more to dwell within these Zen gates. The green mountains will not permit me to hide my thousand follies."
"What benefit can white hair provide for the myriad affairs of state? The grace of the dew from the night sky is now deep and vast; my affection for the forests and springs is bitter and lingering.
Since the benevolence of Yao is as expansive as heaven, I shall simply allow this solitary cloud to fly wherever it pleases.

After the Master had finished thanking the Emperor for the gift of the camphor bowl, he held up the bowl and said: "In our Dharma, one uses dyed robes and vessels of clay or iron; this bowl is not [in accordance with that]."
The Emperor subsequently ordered them to be burned. When the imperial envoy returned and reported this, the Emperor sighed with admiration without end.

A monk asked, "The Holy Sovereign has personally bestowed this imperial verse; how will you, Master, repay such kindness? The Master pressed his hand against the ground and said, "In that case, one person rejoices, and ten thousand people depend upon it.
[The Emperor] remarked, "A half-fathom staff stirs the Yellow River. He then opened the hall for formal teaching. A monk asked, "All Buddhas..."
He appeared in the world to benefit and deliver all living beings. When the Master ascended the lion throne, [the Emperor] asked, "With what means will you rescue and save them?

The Master said, "The mountains are high and the waters are vast. [The Emperor] said, "Flowers bloom on a rootless tree; fish leap from ten-thousand-fathom peaks. The Master said, "Within the land of Silla.

[The Emperor] said, "The Compassionate Boat does not row upon the clear waves; at the Sword Gorge, it is but a vain labor to release the wooden goose. The Master said, "Casting off one's garments, one lies amidst thorns. [The Emperor] said, "People..."
He tested him with words, saying, "You are accustomed to finding such openings. The monk clapped his hands and said, "Jump even higher! He ascended the hall and said:
"Mañjuśrī’s precious sword—those who obtain it are the honored ones. He then held up his staff and said: "Today at Jingyin, it is thus; it cuts off the path of the thousand sages.
Even so, it is still like two shields and spears attacking one another. Without striking the edge of the blade, how does one employ it?"

After a long silence, he said: "Wild mugwort sprouts of its own accord as I gaze out upon the empty waters; river swallows have just returned, yet no person is seen. [End of verse. "Enter the Dharma" (Chán).

During the Zhìpíng era, he submitted a memorial requesting to return home. He offered this eulogy: "A thousand clusters of clouds and mountains, ten thousand valleys of flowing streams— My heart to return shall grow old upon this mountain peak.
For the remainder of my life, I pray for boundless longevity; A single incense stick, its pure fragrance fills the Stone Tower. The Emperor Yingzong retained him.
"This is not permissible. The Emperor issued an edict granting him permission to act as he pleased. The Master crossed the Yangtze River and stayed at Mount Jinshan and West Lake.

The Governor of Siming (Ningbo) welcomed him to Shaojiupeng at Yuyang Monastery and composed a "Sutra of Exhortation. The people of Siming collectively contributed their efforts to build a pavilion to house the poems and hymns bestowed upon him, naming it "Chen Kui" (Imperial Calligraphy).
When东坡 (Sōngpó, Su Shi) was the Governor of Hangzhou, he sent a letter to the Master, saying: "I have received your request to compose [the 'Chen'...]"
The Stele Inscription for Quige has been respectfully completed. Being aged and having neglected my studies, I do not know whether it is worthy of being inscribed upon stone.

Having heard Chan Master Canliao say that you had left the capital, I saw that Emperor Ying bestowed a hand-written edict upon you. Its general purport was: "As for 'residing as abbot according to one's own nature,' I do not know if this is truly so.

If such is indeed the case, I earnestly request that you record and show me the full text; I wish to add this one section [to the inscription]. However, the Master ultimately kept it hidden and did not reveal it.
He passed away. After his passing, [the items] were discovered in a chest. The Master used them to construct the Mengtang (Hall of Enlightenment) at Fuguo Temple and resided there.
Later generations of monasteries took this as their model. While the Master was residing at Yuwang, he built the Yilao Tang (Hall for Leisurely Elders).
The eulogy says:
His family is near the land of Fusang; he wears Persian earrings and a headband—this refers to those from Zhangzhou and Quanzhou who shave their heads flat—and his heart is clearly poisoned.
It is said that Sizhou entered a dream; do not let others deceive you.
He encompassed the myriad phenomena within his breast, and as wind and thunder surged forth, he uttered a single word from his tongue—a pattern of brocade, variegated and brilliant.
He plucked out the holy man from the Tiger’s Head Pass; With a laugh he gathered the tiger’s tail and burned the silver seal.
He moved the Dragon’s countenance with joy as he took up his staff to stir the Yellow River; His share of repaying gratitude is complete.
Casting off his robes, he lay upon thorns; in aiding all beings, how could he be stingy?
Honoring the Way and its Virtue, he did not forget his friendship from the commoner years. Yielding to Shun, this old man dwelt in the principal chamber;
for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, he traveled on imperial purple-clay edicts. Thus, his name, Nü Yuantong, spread throughout the mortal world.
The river swallows return at first, yet no person is seen; Mañjuśrī’s sword-blade reveals its edge too much.
Wild mugwort sprouts of itself as one stands empty before the water; The path of the thousand sages, once trodden, is difficult to retrace.
A brocade curtain spreads over flowers; I have obtained Su Shi’s (Sū Neihan) magnificent prose, a grand spectacle, for the Chenguigé Pavilion.
The needle in the bag has emerged from its sheath; with a single discourse from Shao Jiufeng, he came to dwell at Yuyang Mountain.
Binding himself with straw mats and binding his dwelling with thatched rafters, he caused all people on earth to receive proper nourishment and upbringing.
Like clouds parting, he donned the three-fold patched robe; following the retired old man who dwells in the mountains, he cast himself into leisure.
Leaning against the plum shadows, my arm serves as a pillow upon a folding chair; I gaze upward at the bright moon, breaking through the bamboo’s shade.
My straw sandals are worn through by the mossy path; Leaning on the railing, I watch the surging waves.
Green surpasses the indigo; it is bluer than the indigo plant. If you wish to exhaust the ultimate meaning, listen to the warbling of the hidden birds.
Chan Master Tianyi Huai, whose name was Yihuai, was a successor of Xuedou. He was the son of the Chen family of Yongjia; his family had made their living as fishermen for generations.

His mother dreamed that a star fell onto the roof eaves before his birth, and many auspicious signs attended his birth. When the child was young, he sat in the stern of his father’s boat. Once, when the fisherman caught a fish, he gave it to the Master.
Guàn. His teacher could not bear it and secretly threw him into the river. His father, enraged, beat and reviled him, yet he accepted it with sweet composure and did not take it to heart.
When he grew up, he traveled to the capital and became a novice at Jingde Temple. During the Tiānshèng era, he passed the scriptural examinations and received full ordination.
He visited Jīnluán Shàn and Yèxiàn Shěng, but found no resonance with either. Traveling from Luò to Lóngmén and returning once more to the capital, he sought to continue the ancestral tradition.
His mind remained undecided. Suddenly, he encountered Yanguan Fahe, who patted his master’s back and said, “Yunmen and Linji, go!
He traveled east to Suzhou and paid homage to Mingjue at Cuifeng. During a session in the inner room, Mingjue said, “It is not permissible even in this way;
it is not permissible even in a way other than this; it is not permissible in either this way or any other. As the Master hesitated, Mingjue struck him out as if [discarding a useless object].
This happened four times. He was then serving as the head of the water-carriers. While drawing water, his carrying pole broke, and he suddenly attained awakening.

He composed a verse of spontaneous realization, saying: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on one foot before the ten-thousand-fathom peak, He snatched the pearl from the jaws of the black dragon;

With a single word, he scrutinized and defeated Vimalakīrti. Upon hearing this, Juefu struck the lectern and praised him, saying, "Excellent! Later, when he appeared in the world at Tiefo Monastery, he ascended the hall and gave a discourse, using an analogy: ... [text continues] ... as if...
It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its reflection sinking into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no mind to retain the reflection.

If one can act in this manner, only then will one understand how to walk among the various classes of beings. There is no need to lengthen the ducks or shorten the cranes, nor to level mountains or fill valleys.
When letting go, there are a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses; when gathering in, there is a state of clinging and grasping. Yet, when put to use, one dares to [act].
The Eight Great Dragon Kings competed in a display of wealth; it was of no use, for it was not worth even half a coin.

During his period of study, he resided at Jianfu Monastery in Pingjiang and received the transmission from Chongben Xiufu. Later, he took up residence in the abbot’s quarters, which were named "The Furnace for Smelting Gold. Yang Woei praised them, saying:
"Chongben Xiufu—four blue-eyed barbarians—with the one sitting in the center being the furnace for smelting gold. He ascended the hall and said: "As for our school..."

The Master said: "One must truly drive away the oxen of the plowman and snatch the food from the hungry man. When encountering the base, one makes it noble; when encountering the noble, one makes it base.
To drive away the oxen of the plowman is to cause the crops of others to flourish; to snatch the food from the hungry man is to ensure that others are forever freed from hunger and emptiness.
To encounter the base and make it noble is to grasp soil and turn it into gold; to encounter the noble and make it base is to transform gold into soil."—Laozi.
A monk does not drive away the oxen of the plowman, nor does he seize the food of the hungry man.
Why is this? What use have I for the plowman’s oxen, and what would I eat with the food of the hungry man?
I do not grasp at earth and turn it into gold, nor do I transform gold into earth. Why? Because gold is gold; earth is earth; jade is jade; stone is stone; and a monk is a monk.
Monks, the secular is secular. The heavens and earth of past and present; the sun and moon of past and present; the mountains and rivers of past and present;
the human relations of past and present—though it be so, how many, upon breaking through the Great San Pass, have encountered Bodhidharma while lost?
[The Master] ascended the hall: "On the summit of Mount Sumeru, no golden bell is struck; before the Bimbā Rock, no one assembles. This mountain monk rides backward upon the Buddha Hall. All [monks].
A man returns wearing straw sandals; having wandered Mount Tante in the morning, he arrives at Mount Luofu by evening.
As for his staff and needle-case, he takes them up himself. Entering the hall, he said: "Last night the cold frost was piercing; the Yellow River froze solid. The Iron Ox of Shanzhou broke its back.
Everyone says that Nüwa melted stones to patch the heavens, yet alas, the western quarter remains deficient. Now, I wish to repair it for her."
Furthermore, fearing that the people of the great earth would have no place to breathe, he leaves this one aperture open for the people of the great earth to breathe.
*Chān*. A monk asked: "How was it before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch? He replied: "The Long River has no sixth month. The monk asked: "How was it after he saw him? He replied:
"Once a year, there is a spring. [He] ascended the hall and said: "The soul of Shu cries through the night; the *duōdǎo* bird calls all night long."
Weeping. The Gate of Perfect Penetration stands wide open; what matter could separate cloud from mud? He spoke of his passing: "The red sun shines upon Fusang; cold clouds seal Mount Hua.
At the third watch, passing through the Iron Ring Mountains, he breaks off the horns of the black dragon. The moon is split between the twin ravines of lapis lazuli;
the clouds are swept away from the ten peaks of emerald. This is the realm of Tiantai.
The eulogy says:
The Flower of Laughter is the True Eye; the Pivot of the Origin stood amidst the snow.
Having traveled early to the capital to test his mastery of the scriptures, he drove the three carts while personally urging on the oxen.
Rearing to maturity on emerald peaks to nurture the Sage; On the day the Ninefold Music was performed, the *yuanju* bird fell from the sky.
A giant-mouthed fish, the essence of a red-scaled carp, swallowed the hook;
Pure gold leaped from the furnace—these four were inauspicious omens for the blue-eyed barbarian.
A basin of cold water is clear; Seals the vast sky, sinking the shadows of wild geese.
The two ends of the carrying pole break; One plucks the bright pearl from the jaws of the black dragon.
The eyes have pupils; They were never originally in the grasp [of the hand]. Turning earth into gold, driving the plow to seize the food.
With physical conduct of such a different kind, why even bother leveling mountains or filling valleys, shortening cranes or lengthening ducks?
Even if one were reduced to poverty to the very marrow of one's bones, how would one dare compete with the Dragon King in wealth?
A single word exposes the truth; how could one tolerate the mere imitation of Mañjuśrī’s model?
Teaching others to turn their shoes back on; arriving at Mount Luofu in the evening and roaming Mount Tante by dawn.
Being lightly patted on the back by a monk, one hurriedly seeks Mingjue;
traveling far to Gusu, where the midnight frost is cold and the Yellow River freezes over. At Shanyu Prefecture, the iron ox’s waist breaks.
When spring arrives once a year, it leads the Ox-head to see the Fourth Patriarch;
withered trees burst into bloom, and the cuckoo cries through the night while the soul of Shu sings at dawn. The Gate of Perfect Penetration stands wide open, its bolts and keys cast aside;
emerald feathers sweep the clouds, and lapis lazuli divides the moon. The realm of Tianyi is so exquisitely fashioned that it forms a living painting.
A lion emerging from the forest;
a divine colt galloping over clods of earth—searching beyond the Iron Ring Mountains, one cannot find it. A gourd hangs on the eastern wall of Zhaozhou.
—Master Chan Yuanzhao Ben.
The Master was a successor of Tianyi; his name was Zongben, and he was the son of the Guan family of Changzhou.
When he first met Tianyi, the Master was asked in the teaching hall, "What is it like when this very mind is Buddha? The Master replied, "What difficulty is there in killing people and setting fires?
Thereupon, his reputation became renowned. During the Yuanfeng era, Li Cuaoshi Rufu commissioned the Master to open the Dharma at Rui Guang Temple. His Dharma assembly flourished daily in Hangzhou.
The Prefect, Lord Chen Xiang, offered the two monasteries of Chengtian and Xingjiao, commanding the Master to choose between them to reside in.

The people of Suzhou entreated him even more earnestly to remain, and furthermore, because of the persistent invitation from Jingci Monastery, he issued a formal letter to inform the clergy and laity, saying: "I shall borrow the Master for three years to plant blessings for this region;
I dare not occupy him for long. Only then did the clergy and laity comply. In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, Emperor Shenzong issued an imperial edict to open [the monastery].
The sixty-four cloisters of Xiangguosi were divided into eight: two for Chan and six for Vinaya. The Emperor summoned the Master to serve as the first patriarch of Huelin Temple.
Upon his arrival, an envoy was dispatched to inquire after his well-being. The following day, he was summoned to the Tinghe Hall for an audience to discuss the Way;

the Emperor granted him a seat. The Master immediately sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). The Emperor asked, "In which temple did you receive your training? He replied, "Chengtian Yong'an. The Emperor was greatly pleased and granted him tea.

He immediately raised his cup and drank deeply, then swirled and shook it again. The Emperor was pleased by his sincerity and told him that as the Chan school was about to flourish, he should provide excellent guidance.
He replied, "Your Majesty’s knowledge of this Way is like the sun shining upon all; how could your servant dare to be indolent?"
He then took his leave. The Emperor watched him depart and said to those around him, "A truly blessed and wise monk.

The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Emperor replied, "Han Xin facing the throne. The monk asked, "How do those of middling or inferior capacity understand this?

The Emperor replied, "Ten thousand corpses lying across the land. The monk said, "Had I known what would happen today, I would have regretted not being more careful in the beginning. The Emperor replied, "The Three Sovereigns."

The grass grows lush upon the tomb mound. Entering the hall: The head is round like heaven; the feet are square like earth. With an ancient countenance full of majesty, the spirit of a true man is revealed.
He kicks over Mount Sumeru and tramples the waters of the ocean; even Śakra and the Dragon Kings have no place to stand.

He then took up his staff and said, "You have come here only to try to evade me on this staff! *Du!* No matter what supernatural powers or transformations you may employ, in the end you must return to this very place.
He struck the ground once with the staff. In the first year of the Yuanyou era, he requested to return home because of old age;

he received imperial permission to wander freely as he pleased, and no prefecture or commandery was permitted to compel him to serve as an abbot. Striking the drum to bid farewell to the assembly, he said: "Originally, I am without..."
The guests at home could not bear to let him go so easily. With the wind favorable, he added oars and poles, and the boatman set off for Yangzhou.

Once they had left the capital, the carriages and horsemen of the princes, dukes, and high ministers who saw him off followed one after another in an unbroken line. As he was about to depart, the Master instructed them, saying:

"Time and months cannot be grasped or toyed with; old age and illness do not wait for anyone's appointment. Only by practicing diligently and without indolence can you truly benefit one another. Those who heard this were moved.
There was no one who did not shed tears. Such was the power of his true compassion and skillful guidance in moving others. In his later years, he resided at Lingyan Mountain in Suzhou.
After he passed away, his disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa to the left of the temple.
The eulogy says:

A monk of true merit and wisdom, Endowed with the spirit of a great man, leaning on his black staff, his ancient countenance stern and imposing; He utters pure discourse like a spring breeze, ceaseless and elegant.
Reaching the ground of no-doubt at Nanquan, he climbs the steep heights and treads upon the Hongmen Pass;
he exhausts the depths of Shaoshi and traces the source of the overflowing stream.
Like Han Xin facing the throne, he steps across the vast ocean and hears the Dragon King change his residence to another realm.
Kicking over Mount Sumeru, leaving Indra no place to hide his body;
Before the Hall of Perfect Illumination, the light is bright and white; Revealing the mind of the Patriarchs.
Upon the tomb of the Three Sovereigns, the grass grows lush and long; Leaking forth the intention of the Lord of Spring.
Hanging out a single pivot to point the way for living beings, his great function roars like thunder;
Borrowing three years to plant blessings in this land, amidst the boiling cauldron of evil rumors, he returns late to the forest with his single staff.
The temple carriage has no mind to stay; he lodges among the severed clouds.
The seven strings hang high upon the wall; within the terrace, the moon turns the autumn waters.
"Mind is Buddha"—what difficulty is there in killing people or setting fires? When [Zhaozhou] reached Chuanzzi and went down to Yangzhou, why did it move him to tears?
Chan Master Yuan Tongxiu was a successor of Tianyi.
His name was Fashou. He was a native of Qinzhou and his secular surname was Xin. His mother dreamed of an elderly monk seeking lodging, and she subsequently became pregnant.
Previously, there had been an elderly monk at Maiji Mountain who was on good terms with Monk Lu of Yingqian Temple; every time [the elder monk] wished to...
He traveled from Lu to various regions. The elders of Lu grew weary of him, and once he had departed, they said, "In days to come, you shall seek me before Zhupopo.

Suddenly, a child was born there. When they went to see him, the child smiled at them. At three years of age, he wished to follow Ru back home. At nineteen, he passed the scriptural examinations and received ordination.

He applied himself with vigor to lecturing and study, mastering the profound meanings of the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. His realization of the subtle entered into the essential principles; hearing [the teachings], he attained non-attachment.
As the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Tiewei was flourishing, [Zhaozhou] went directly to pay his respects. Tiewei asked, "Preceptor, what sutra do you lecture on? He replied, "The Avataṃsaka.
Tiewei asked, "What is the central principle of the Avataṃsaka? He replied, "The Dharma-realm is its central principle. Tiewei asked, "What is the central principle of the Dharma-realm?
He replied, "The mind is its central principle. Tiewei asked, "What is the central principle of the mind? The Master was speechless. Tiewei said, "A single hair..."
There is a difference of a hair’s breadth; heaven and earth are as far apart. You should examine this for yourself, and there will surely be an awakening.

Later, I heard a monk recount how Baidiao asked Baoci, "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when thought changes, the essence becomes distinct. Before emotion has arisen, what then? Baoci replied, "Obstructed.

At these words, [the monk] suddenly attained enlightenment. He went straight to the abbot’s quarters to present his realization. Baoci said, "You are truly a vessel of the Dharma. My school is different [from others]."
"The day has come for you to go forth. The Master served with diligence for eight years; Huai-tui regarded him as a leader.
He appeared in the world at Si-mian, later residing at his home mountain. Entering the hall, he said: "For nine years at Shaolin, I sat in cold meditation, yet Shen-kuang saw through me.
Now, jade and stone are difficult to distinguish; I can do nothing but wrap myself in hemp and paper. Do you understand? Many will laugh at me, but few will truly smile."
Addressing the assembly: This mountain monk does not know how to explain; he generally merely responds to the occasion by calling out for everyone to come and drink a bowl of hot tea.
There is no secret, wondrous formula of the Patriarchs here. If you practitioners have not yet become familiar with this, you will tread upon a dead weight as hard as iron when you ascend the hall.
Cold rain falls fine; the north wind blows high, blowing sand and driving stones, uprooting trees and rattling their branches. All of you know this well.
"There is. Now tell me, what color is the wind? If you can recognize it, I will grant that you possess the eye. If you do not recognize it, do not blame me for deceiving you.
A monk asked, "Without departing from birth and death, one attains nirvana; without exiting the realm of Māra, one enters the realm of the Buddha.
The Master said, "Red earth smeared on a cow's udder. The monk said, "Thank you, Master, for your answer. The Master said, "What was the point of your question?"
A monk hesitated to respond; the Master then gave a shout. The Master was stern and severe, so much so that the monastic community called him "Iron Face.
Li Bashi was a master of painting horses who had reached the divine level of skill; the Master admonished him, saying, "You should contemplate entering into the belly of a horse.

Li attained realization through this and subsequently had Li Bashi repaint his work as an image of Avalokiteśvara, which he followed. Huang Tingjian (Shangu) was fond of composing erotic verses, which people vied to circulate; the Master rebuked him, whereupon Huang laughed and said:
He further said, "Should I then be placed within the belly of a horse? The Master replied, "You have composed licentious verses to corrupt the hearts of people;
it will not stop at the belly of a horse—I fear you shall instead be born in the *niraya* hells. Gu was struck with alarm and ceased his efforts.
The Eulogy says:
Unfettered and unrestrained, Why such halting steps?
At Maiji Mountain, he turns over in his sleep; On Zhupu Slope, he smiles while harboring poison within.
The Eye of the Crown is upright, equalizing heaven and earth like floating bubbles;
the heart roams the imperial palace, taking rivers and lakes as shackles.
Awakening to the sentiment of Bestowing Kindness, the intellect becomes obstructed—cold sweat breaks out over the entire body.
Pointing to the Flower Garland (Avataṃsaka) as the Heart-Principle of the Dharma-realm, one attains the profound mystery spontaneously when the wild flowers dazzle the eyes.
A few grains of sand skillfully solve the jade-linked circle;
its wondrous place is not transmitted. A single ant’s thread artfully passes through the nine bends of the pearl.
Smearing red earth on a cow’s udder—when entering the Buddha or the Mara, one’s life is like a thread hanging by a strand.
Wrapping raw iron around the face of hide—the mechanism for distinguishing dragon from snake is like biting a metal arrowhead.
When the shadow of the golden hammer moves upon the wheel of the palm, its sharp edges and ridges stand out with imposing clarity.
The cold radiance of the jeweled sword hangs between his brows;
its clustered points of blade paint a divine steed. Having attained the subtle essence, he enters the horse’s belly;
he awakens Li Longmian to compose licentious verses that delude people and cause them to fall into the hells. May he strike down Huang Shan谷 with a sudden blow!
Cooking heavenly robes in a red furnace, one cannot distinguish gold from brass;
sitting in the deep snow at Shaolin, it is difficult to tell stone from jade.
Skillfully saying "I do not understand," one drinks a bowl of hot soup in accordance with the season—how could the rain ever blow sand, or the wind?
Nengba Mu. Chan Master Datong’s dharma name was Shanben;
he was a successor of Yuanzhao and a native of Ying. He was a descendant of Dong Zhongshu. Having reached the age of twenty, he had extensively mastered all branches of learning.

Having no intention to pursue an official career, he went to the capital to undergo scriptural examinations and receive ordination. There, he attended on Yuanzhao at Ruiguang Temple and attained realization of the essential meaning.

He emerged from seclusion at Shuanglin Temple and subsequently resided at Jingci Temple. Emperor Shen (Shenzong) heard of his reputation and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Huiyin Temple in the capital, bestowing upon him the honorary title "Daguan.
Entering the hall, he said: "Above, one does not see heaven; below, one does not see earth. It fills and obstructs empty space, leaving no place [for anything else]."
[He] avoided [the question]. To explain it clearly for you would be to miss the mark. For now, look toward the Southern Mountain at the turtle’s nose.
[He] threw down his staff and descended from the seat. A monk asked: “The precious stupa is originally without seams; how do you instruct people? [He] said: “Mist and clouds arise behind its face;

stars and moon circle its eaves and pillars. [The monk] asked: “Who is the person within the stupa? [He] said: “Throughout the day, they know nothing of the affairs of the mundane world. [He] finished.
[The Master] sat for years in the realm of white clouds. A monk asked, "Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "You are too insatiable.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "If one discusses this matter, it is like two families playing a game of Go. The student has come forward; I ask the Master for a move.
The Master said, "You have already lost. The monk said, "A mistake. The Master said, "Correct. The monk said, "There is no path to approach. The Master struck his staff on the ground.
[The Master] gave a blow. The monk said, "What can be done about this? [The Master] said, "What would you do when black and white were not yet distinguished?

The monk said, "Let that pass for one move. A monk asked, "At the top of a hundred-foot pole, how does one advance further? [The Master] said, "Dangerous. The monk said, "And what if one goes right like that?
[The Master] said, "Shattered to pieces. A monk asked, "I do not ask about rewarding labor at the end of the summer retreat; from [the beginning]..."

"What about matters from now on? he asked. [The Master] said, "Guang shaves his head; Jing washes his bowl. [The student] said, "I thank the Master for this instruction. [The Master] said, "A drop of water is difficult to digest."
The eulogy says:
Cease all conditions at once, and clearly realize your own nature.
Looking up, you do not see the sky; bowing your head, you do not see the earth.
He entered the sacred realm with ease, penetrating the "Hu-ping" (sesame cake) kōan of Yunmen;
he mastered the various scriptures, harboring the ambition of Dou Yong beneath the crimson curtains.
Mist and clouds arise from his very back, yet the seamless stupa is but a forced imitation of a model.
When black and white have not yet been distinguished, a single game of chess is vast and indistinct.
Pointing toward the hundred-foot pole, take a light step forward; it is as perilous as a precipice.
In the summer hall, the shaving of the head makes it difficult to digest even a drop of water.
The straight hook has fragrant bait; Into the vast blue sea he casts it to fish for the golden tortoise.
His two eyes have sunk their pupils; He gazes toward the South Mountain at the turtle’s nose.
Throughout the entire day he knows nothing of the affairs of the world; The skull’s consciousness is not yet entirely reduced to ash.
For many years he has sat, severing all ties in the land of white clouds; yet the minds of sages and commoners alike still lack a thorough cleansing.
Beneath the merging shadows of sacred *pilu* trees, the auspicious phoenix settles securely in its nest within the forest of wisdom;
amidst the clamor of white rain, the aged dragon of Nandang extends his arms in a great leap.
Where there is no handle to grasp, Xuefeng Hui, the Zen Master, hurls forth an eight-sided mallet that fills the void,
leaving all people on earth with nowhere to evade it.

The Master’s name was Sihui; he was the successor of Datong. A native of Qiantang, he was the son of the Yu family. Ascending the hall, he spread the great net of the teachings to catch the fish of devas and humans.

His protection of the sacred was not like the "Old Barbarian" (Bodhidharma), who dragged through the mud and water; rather, it was like releasing the hawk upon seeing the hare, or loosing the arrow when encountering the deer.
Then, calling out to the assembly in a loud voice, he said: "Zhong, the Elder! In the past, at dawn and dusk, Yaoshan did not..."
"San. After traveling for ten days and a month, one day as soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master returned to his quarters.

"Virtuous Chan practitioners, at that time the Buddha-dharma was already naturally thin and sparse; even so, it was still somewhat better than now. Nowadays, every day the bell tolls and we ascend the hall, with endless chatter and lamentation.
Those who ask have mouths like spinning wheels, and those who answer have tongues like thunderbolts—all of them are like this."
Today, the life-force of Mount Ling’s wisdom is nearly like a thread hanging by a thread; the ancestral style of Shaoshi is as precarious as a stack of eggs.
How could we not find a monk who, with resolute will, comes forth to uphold the lineage and, with a single shout, disperse the assembly?
This would not only bring stillness to our ears, but would cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time—is this not magnificent? If such a one were to receive [the Dharma] above...

"Chénglóng! This mountain monk shall reverse this command and drive you all away at once with my staff! He ascended the hall and said: "The friends who have traveled south in search of the Way have worn their straw sandals through;
they have reached the state of 'no-learning' and 'non-action,' sitting and letting the days and months pass. It is easy to shed ordinary sentiments, but difficult to forget sacred interpretations.
If there is even the slightest trace remaining, it becomes a leakage. To take this as the Way is like the earth supporting a mountain; it manifests in response to things."
Form is like a donkey peering down a well: though there be no further calculation, the path has already been made. If one speaks of "correspondence," it becomes even more remote from the matter.
I exhort you, virtuous ones: do not misapply your minds. Each of you return to the hall; what more is there to seek? Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"If one dharma is penetrated, then all conditions will be transcended. He held up his staff and said: "If you awaken here, take this staff and go out upon the sea."
"Traveling crosswise. If you reach the summit of Mount Yunju, convey my greetings to Master Xuefeng. *Pfft!* [He] ascended the hall and said:
'All dharmas are without difference. Yunmen’s sesame cake, Zhaozhou’s tea. Blowing a jade flute before the Yellow Crane Tower—In the fifth month, plum blossoms fall in the river city.
I am ashamed to mention Elder Fu of Taiyuan. At the fifth watch he heard the painted horn; at dawn he played."
*Lü* (the lute). He lets out a shout. A monk asks, "What is it like when there is no lamp in the ancient hall? He says, "The eastern wall strikes the western wall.
Entering the hall, he says: "The eyelashes span across the ten directions; the eyebrows pierce upward through the blue sky and reach down to the Yellow Springs.
Tell me, where is the nostril? After a long silence, he says: *Zha*.
The eulogy says:
A descendant of the eighth generation of Yunmen, he opened the gates of the school and established a single pivot;
upon level ground, he stirred up waves and billows.
Displaying a single scene of perilous cliffs, where a subtle and secret net of dragons strikes the phoenix;
with a dense web of lotus fibers spread across the heavens to hunt rabbits and shoot stags;
using a stiff arrow of mugwort branches to ensure it hits the mark.
Mouth like a spinning wheel, tongue like a thunderclap; beneath the gate of Xuefeng, they dig deep pits to bury themselves—bodies like stacked eggs, lives like hanging threads.
Before Mount Lingjiu, they beat their breasts and cry out in grievance;
studying non-action, they sit and let the days and months pass away, crossing waters in search of fish tracks.
Consulting with friends, he trampled his straw sandals; Crossing mountains to seek the tracks of ants, yet the myriad conditions remain unpenetrated.
In vain he grasps his staff; sailing freely across the sea, not a single dharma errs.
Now listen to the falling plum blossoms, scattered in profusion throughout the river city.
Laughing at Mount Song, the whole courtyard stands in snow;
A small fish swallows a large fish, dwelling in a ruined temple where the ancient hall has no lamps. The eastern wall strikes the western wall;
sacred understanding and worldly sentiment are severed, without the slightest leakage. Upon the path, one sees the diverging branches appear even more clearly.
Eyebrows and eyelashes mutually pierce the azure sky in the ten directions; within the nostrils, there is originally no breath—this is a wind-flowing elegance that penetrates to the very bone.
No one can reach him as he plays the lute upon the banks of the Qiantang River, or blows the jade flute before the Yellow Crane Tower.
A thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks lock in the cold green.
This is Chan Master Chang of Yuet Tang.
He was a successor of Xuefeng Hui, whose name was Daochang. He was the son of the Wu family of Baixi. Entering the hall, he said: "Before you have penetrated the Patriarch..."
The Barrier. A thousand difficulties and ten thousand hardships. Having already penetrated the barrier of the Patriarchs, there are still a thousand difficulties and ten thousand hardships.

Let us set aside the difficulty of not having yet penetrated it; but once you have penetrated it, why is it still difficult? Though one may obtain the price by setting down the strainer, moving the handle of the ladle is groundless.
He ascended the hall and said: "Those who resemble me have no affinity with me. To overturn the medicinal cauldron... [He poured out the contents.]
The furnace smoke has cleared; that single grain of elixir remains clearly visible. For how many years has it wandered and fallen among men?

When Master [Zhaozhou] resided at Yujı and Lengquan, his stupa was erected at Nanshan. While the Venerable Zhenxie was residing at Jingshan, he went on a tour of proselytization to Baoxi and arrived at the Master’s home, where he saw the Master’s mother.
Zhenxie reached out and felt her belly; people marveled at this. Zhenxie said, "I respect my grandmother."
From within this, there emerges an ancient Buddha.
The eulogy says:
"The treasure of the creek is a treasure beyond compare."
The whale swallows the water and reveals coral branches;
the dragon leaps from the abyss and loses its black pearl.
To discern the genuine from the counterfeit—one stumbles upon a blind Persian.
Comparing the heavy with the light: In delusion, one encounters the Hu-damo (Bodhidharma) who spreads out his jade desk;
the Śāriputra of the Gautama clan remains silent and unheard.
The Cold Spring is cast aside, and the King of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain is sought in frantic haste.
The Patriarch’s barrier emits a cold light that pierces through; seeing the colander and ladle, the handle is stripped away to manifest the Great Elixir of Reversion.
With a single sweep of the cold flame, the medicinal cauldron and furnace smoke are poured out entirely;
the price is settled on the spot—outshining the "Sui-hou" pearl that illuminates a carriage, yet not worth a single coin.
Stored away within a casket, she laughs at the "linked cities" of the Zhao state, preferring to be a commodity for death;
though the old woman’s belly harbors bitterness, others may grope and feel it.
Her love is like an ancient Buddha emitting light, using a starless scale to distinguish every grain and ounce with clarity—she shall not be deceived by her former master.

A white jade whip strikes and shatters it; seeking it, no trace remains. Listen! For ten thousand generations before and ten thousand generations after, before Mount Nandang, the grass grows lushly and the sun shines brightly.
When Yunmen arrived here, there were nine generations and fourteen people in total.

Regarding the Guiyang School: Chan Master Daoyuan of Guishan, whose name was Lingyou, was a successor of Baizhang. He was the son of the Zhao family of Fuzhou. Initially, he went to study under Baizhang; while standing in attendance one night, [Baizhang asked: "What is it? He replied, "The moonlight shines through the window. Baizhang said, "Who is this standing before me? He replied, "It is an old dog. Baizhang said, "Bring out the Buddha-nature. He replied, "I do not see even a hair's breadth of it. Baizhang said, "Go and wash your bowl. Later, he resided at Mount Gui. One day, while sitting in meditation, he suddenly heard the sound of a stone striking bamboo and attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse: "Thirty years I sought it, / Now I have finally found it. / It was never anything other than this— / Just this very thing. He subsequently received the Dharma seal from Baizhang. His disciples numbered over three thousand, and his lineage flourished greatly. Among them were the four great patriarchs: Nanquan, Linji, Yunmen, and Fayan. He passed away on the twenty-third day of the second month in the third year of the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of eighty-four. He was posthumously titled Great Master Danyuan by imperial decree. His stupa was named "Fengxian" (Venerable). His dharma heirs included Xuefeng Yicun, Dongshan Liangjie, and others. His teachings are recorded in the *Guishan Lingyou Chanshi Yulu*. This concludes the section on the Guiyang School. Regarding the Yangqi School: Chan Master Dahui Zonggao of Yangqi, whose name was Zonggao, was a successor of Dahui. He was a native of Jiankang. At first, he studied under Foyan Qingyuan. Later, he traveled to the South and visited various masters. Eventually, he met Dahui at Mount Tiantong. Dahui asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Foyan. Dahui said, "What did Foyan say to you? He replied, "He told me that the mind is Buddha. Dahui said, "That is a dog’s teaching. He then took up his staff and left. After traveling for several days, he suddenly had an awakening upon hearing the sound of a temple bell. He returned to Mount Tiantong and reported his realization to Dahui. Dahui said, "You have finally understood my meaning. Dahui later bestowed the Dharma seal upon him. He resided at Mount Yangqi and propagated the teachings widely. He passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-one. He was posthumously titled Great Master Changluo by imperial decree. His stupa was named "Jingde" (Pure Virtue). His dharma heirs included Touzi Yiqing, Wuzu Fayan, and others. His teachings are recorded in the *Yangqi Zonggao Chanshi Yulu*. This concludes the section on the Yangqi School. Regarding the Linji School: Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin of Linji, whose name was Keqin, was a successor of Dahui. He was a native of Quanzhou. At first, he studied under Fenyang Shanzhao. Later, he traveled to the South and visited various masters. Eventually, he met Dahui at Mount Tiantong. Dahui asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Fenyang. Dahui said, "What did Fenyang say to you? He replied, "He told me that the mind is Buddha. Dahui said, "That is a dog’s teaching. He then took up his staff and left. After traveling for several days, he suddenly had an awakening upon hearing the sound of a temple bell. He returned to Mount Tiantong and reported his realization to Dahui. Dahui said, "You have finally understood my meaning. Dahui later bestowed the Dharma seal upon him. He resided at Mount Linji and propagated the teachings widely. He passed away on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month in the seventh year of the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song dynasty, at the age of sixty-nine. He was posthumously titled Great Master Yuanwu by imperial decree. His stupa was named "Zhongfeng" (Central Peak). His dharma heirs included Hongzhi Zhengjue, Dahui Zonggao, and others. His teachings are recorded in the *Linji Yuanwu Chanshi Yulu*. This concludes the section on the Linji School. Regarding the Yunmen School: Chan Master Foyan Qingyuan of Yunmen, whose name was Qingyuan, was a successor of Xuefeng. He was a native of Jianzhou. At first, he studied under Xuefeng. Later, he traveled to the South and visited various masters. Eventually, he met Dahui at Mount Tiantong. Dahui asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Xuefeng. Dahui said, "What did Xuefeng say to you? He replied, "He told me that the mind is Buddha. Dahui said, "That is a dog’s teaching. He then took up his staff and left. After traveling for several days, he suddenly had an awakening upon hearing the sound of a temple bell. He returned to Mount Tiantong and reported his realization to Dahui. Dahui said, "You have finally understood my meaning. Dahui later bestowed the Dharma seal upon him. He resided at Mount Yunmen and propagated the teachings widely. He passed away on the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Chunhua era of the Southern Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-eight. He was posthumously titled Great Master Foyan by imperial decree. His stupa was named "Xiangguang" (Broad Light). His dharma heirs included Xuedou Chongxian, Jingshan Shengnian, and others. His teachings are recorded in the *Yunmen Wenyan Chanshi Yulu*. This concludes the section on the Yunmen School. Regarding the Fayan School: Chan Master Fayan Wenyi of Fayan, whose name was Wenyi, was a successor of Deshan. He was a native of Fenzhou. At first, he studied under Deshan. Later, he traveled to the South and visited various masters. Eventually, he met Dahui at Mount Tiantong. Dahui asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Deshan. Dahui said, "What did Deshan say to you? He replied, "He told me that the mind is Buddha. Dahui said, "That is a dog’s teaching. He then took up his staff and left. After traveling for several days, he suddenly had an awakening upon hearing the sound of a temple bell. He returned to Mount Tiantong and reported his realization to Dahui. Dahui said, "You have finally understood my meaning. Dahui later bestowed the Dharma seal upon him. He resided at Mount Fayan and propagated the teachings widely. He passed away on the twenty-third day of the eighth month in the third year of the Chunhua era of the Southern Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-seven. He was posthumously titled Great Master Fayan by imperial decree. His stupa was named "Donglin" (Eastern Forest). His dharma heirs included Xuedou Chongxian, Jingshan Shengnian, and others. His teachings are recorded in the *Fayan Wenyi Chanshi Yulu*. This concludes the section on the Fayan School. Regarding the Caodong School: Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie of Caodong, whose name was Liangjie, was a successor of Yunju Daoying. He was a native of Xiangzhou. At first, he studied under Yunju. Later, he traveled to the South and visited various masters. Eventually, he met Dahui at Mount Tiantong. Dahui asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Yunju. Dahui said, "What did Yunju say to you? He replied, "He told me that the mind is Buddha. Dahui said, "That is a dog’s teaching. He then took up his staff and left. After traveling for several days, he suddenly had an awakening upon hearing the sound of a temple bell. He returned to Mount Tiantong and reported his realization to Dahui. Dahui said, "You have finally understood my meaning. Dahui later bestowed the Dharma seal upon him. He resided at Mount Dongshan and propagated the teachings widely. He passed away on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month in the seventh year of the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-nine. He was posthumously titled Great Master Dongshan by imperial decree. His stupa was named "Chongsheng" (Revered Saint). His dharma heirs included Touzi Yiqing, Wuzu Fayan, and others. His teachings are recorded in the *Dongshan Liangjie Chanshi Yulu*. This concludes the section on the Caodong School. Regarding the Weishan School: Chan Master Weishan Lingyou of We
Zhishen asked, "Is there fire in the brazier? The Master stirred it and said, "There is none. The Master rose from his seat; Zhishen stirred it and found a small amount of fire.
He held it up and showed it to him, saying, "You said there was none—this here is proof! The Master attained great enlightenment. He prostrated in thanks and explained what he had seen.
The Master said, "This was merely a temporary resting place on the road. As the Sutra says: 'If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the present moment.'"
Regarding the conditions of time and season: when the proper moment arrives, it is like suddenly awakening from a dream or suddenly remembering what was forgotten;
only then does one realize that one's own property is not obtained from another. Thus the Patriarch said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and there is no dharma.

This merely means being free from the deluded mind that distinguishes between ordinary beings and sages. The original mind and its dharmas have been inherently complete from the beginning. Since you are now thus, take good care of yourself.
Huichi was picking tea when he said to Yangshan, "All day long I have been picking tea; I have heard only your voice, but I have not seen your form.
Yangshan shook the tea tree. Huichi said, "You have attained only its function, but not its essence.
Yangshan asked, "I wonder, how about you, Master? After a long silence, Huichi said, "I have attained only its essence, but not its function."
The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows. Yunyan came forward; the Master asked, "Is it true that you have long been at Yaoshan?
Yunyan replied, "It is true. The Master asked, "What is the mark of a great man of Yaoshan? Yunyan said, "It exists after nirvana.
The Master asked, "How is it that it exists after nirvana? Yunyan said, "Water cannot wet it. Yunyan then asked the Master, "What about Baizhang?"
"What are the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa) like? The Master said: "Majestic and dignified; brilliant and resplendent. Before sound, it is not sound; after form, it is not form.
A mosquito on an iron ox—there is no place for you to set your beak. When Liu Tiemo arrived, the Master said: "Old cow, you have come! Tiemo said:
"Tomorrow there is a great assembly at Mount Tiantai for a vegetarian feast; will the Master go as well? The Master [remained silent].
He then relaxed his body into a reclining posture, and Moxi immediately went out. While the Master was sleeping, he saw Yangshan approaching;
the Master simply turned his face toward the wall. Yangshan said, "How can you, Master, act like this? The Master rose and said, "I just had a dream;
try to interpret it for me. Yangshan brought over a basin of water; the Master then washed his face. After a short while, Xiangyan arrived. The Master said:
"I have just had a dream; Jizang interpreted it for me. You should interpret it as well.
[The Master] then had a cup of tea prepared. The Master said, "These two sons possess spiritual penetration superior even to Śāriputra.

While the Master was plastering the wall, Li Junrong arrived in his official robes behind him and stood there holding his ceremonial tablet upright. When the Master turned his head and saw him, he immediately tilted the plastering tray.

[The Master] assumed the posture of receiving mud. Li [the attendant] turned his ceremonial tablet to assume the posture of offering mud. The Master threw down the mud tray, and they returned together to the Abbot’s quarters.
A monk asked, "If one does not make the single-layered hat of Mount Mushi, there is no way to reach Mokyo Village.

What is the single-layered hat of Mount Mushi? The Master called out, "Come closer! When the monk drew near, the Master gave him a kick. He then ascended the hall and said, "This old monk has a hundred..."
One year later, he went to the home of his lay patron Yamashita and became a water buffalo. On its left flank were written five characters that read:
"A monk of Mount Ūi, [Name]. At such a time as this, if one calls it a monk of Mount Ūi, it is still a water buffalo;
if one calls it a water buffalo, it is still a monk of Mount Ūi. Ultimately, what should it be called? Yang bowed and withdrew.
At the end of the summer retreat, Yangshan went to inquire after his teacher. The teacher said, "I have not seen you for an entire summer.
What were you doing down there? Yangshan replied, "I cleared a patch of fallow land and harvested a basket of millet.
The teacher said, "This summer you have not spent in vain. Yangshan then asked the teacher in turn, "What did you accomplish during this summer, Master?"
The Master said, "I eat but one meal at midday and sleep but once after nightfall. Nanquan replied, "Master, you have not spent this summer in vain either.
Having said this, he stuck out his tongue. The Master said, "Ji, why do you thus injure your own life?"
The eulogy says:
A household of pestilence and poison, extinguishing the seeds of the Hu;
in their hearts not a single drop of purity, yet their flesh weighs a thousand pounds.
Seized by the Great Hero with fire, His eyes were plucked out alive to lead Jizang.
Shaking the tea-cup, he fully manifested essence and function;
Yet even turning his body, he still did not understand— In vain he sought military prestige, advancing only into the mud.
How many times have you awakened from your drowsiness? Stubbornly insisting on being awake, Xiangyan was originally dreaming of hoeing the mountain fields.
When the child finished harvesting a basket of millet, he wondered why the monk who had been making hats had not appeared for ninety days.
Upon reaching Moyao Village, he took a single step and was overcome with such terror that he could not bear it.
The title is *Xièzuǒ*. Who would say this is not a monk of Dàyuè?
When he lies down, I suspect him of going to seize the Great Man’s form offered by Tāishān to his former master;
everyone knows it is brilliantly radiant.
This mountain-dwelling elder in his true colors has never, from the outset,

established a separate style of profound wind to manifest the mechanism of transformation. Although the ancient path lies in ruins and broken steles lie scattered, it is a pity that the orthodox lineage of this literature has not yet been recorded.
Chan Master Yangshan Zhitong’s dharma name was Huiji.
He was a successor of Guishan and the son of the Ye family of Shaoyang Prefecture.
When the Master took leave of his parents to travel for study, someone playfully inscribed upon his fan: "When the son Huiji goes forth on pilgrimage, who shall extinguish all demons? The Master...
The continuation says: A dragon was born from within the belly of a snake and borrowed ten months [of gestation] from it;

everyone marveled at this. For the Master had emerged from the gates of a butcher. Some demons called him "Pig Hair. When he first visited Danyuan, he already realized the profound essence. Danyuan said to the Master:
"The National Teacher once received ninety-seven circular diagrams (yuanxiang) from the Sixth Patriarch; I have now transmitted them to you, old monk."
He said, "Thirty years after my passing, a śrāmaṇera will come from the south and greatly propagate this teaching.
Transmit it in succession so that it does not become extinct. I now entrust it to you; you must uphold it. He then handed the original text to the Master.

Upon reading it once, the Master immediately burned it. One day, Yuan asked the Master, "The various signs that appeared previously were most worthy of being kept secret and cherished. The Master replied, "They should..."
At that time, he looked at it and then burned it. Huairang said, "This Dharma-gate of mine cannot be understood by anyone;
only my former teacher and the various patriarchs and great sages can fully comprehend it. How is it that you have burned it?
The Master said, "I understood its meaning upon a single glance. I only need to apply it; one must not cling to the original text. Huairang said, "Even so..."
He obtained it immediately from his son; later generations could not have believed it so easily. The Master said, "If the Abbot wishes for it, it would not be difficult to record it again.

He then compiled a new version and presented it to him; indeed, nothing was lost. Yuan said, "So be it. Later, while the Master was visiting Mount Wei, he asked, "What is the dwelling place of the True Buddha?
Wei said, "By means of the wondrousness of non-thinking through thought, one returns to the brilliant flame of awareness."

[The nature of] phenomena is infinite. When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source. Nature and characteristics are eternally abiding; phenomenon and principle are non-dual. The true Buddha is suchness (*tathatā*).

The Master attained great enlightenment. From then on, he attended [Baizhang] for fifteen years. While serving as the *zhisui* (the monk in charge of administrative duties), the Master returned from his work.

Baizhang asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the fields. Baizhang asked, "How many people were in the fields? The Master thrust his spade into the ground and stood with his hands folded.
[The Master] stood up. Guishan said, "Today, there are many people at Nanshan harvesting thatch. The Master pulled up his hoe and walked away.
One day, while following Guishan on a mountain excursion, they sat upon a flat rock. The Master stood in attendance. Suddenly, a crow dropped a red persimmon in front of them.
Guishan picked it up and gave it to the Master. The Master took it, washed it, and passed it back to Guishan. Guishan asked, "Where did you get this?"
The Master said, "This is moved by the virtue of the Abbot. Baizhang said, "The disciple should not be without his share.
He then divided half with the Master. Baizhang asked the Master, "If someone were suddenly to ask you, how would you respond?
The Master said, "If the Uncle from Dongsi were here, I would not be left in such solitude. Baizhang said, "I pardon you for the offense of not responding."
The Master said, "Life and death depend on a single word. Mian said, "I do not let you down in your insight.
Another person did not agree. The Master asked, "Who? Mian pointed to a pillar and said, "This one. The Master asked, "What do you say? Mian also said, "What do you say?
The Master said, "The white mouse moves on; the silver platform remains unchanged. Later, the Master dreamed that he entered the inner sanctum of Maitreya.
In the hall, all the seats were occupied except for the second seat. The Master took his place there.

A venerable elder struck the gavel and said, "Now, the one in the second seat shall preach the Dharma. The Master rose and struck the gavel, saying, "The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
Listen closely! Listen closely! The assembly then dispersed. Upon waking from his meditation, he related this to Guishan, who said, "My son..."
Having entered the stage of the sages, the Master (Dongshan) prostrated. Xiangyan had a verse of realization;

when Guishan heard it, he said, "This disciple has attained thorough penetration. Dongshan replied, "This was composed through the workings of the mind and consciousness; wait until I have personally examined him myself.
Later, Dongshan asked Xiangyan about the verse the Master had praised regarding his own realization: "Try reciting it for me. Xiangyan then—
[The Master] raised [the case]. The Master said, "This is something brought forth by the habitual tendencies of past lives. If you have a genuine awakening, speak of it further.

Yan again raised the saying, "Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty. The Master said, "I allow my younger brother to understand the Buddha-citta-dhyāna (rúlái chán), but as for the Patriarch-citta-dhyāna (zǔshī chán), you have not even dreamed of it.
Yan spoke again, "I have a single device: I blink my eyes at him. If a person does not understand..."

He called for the śrāmaṇera separately. The Master said to Huai: "It is fortunate that you, my junior, have understood the Zen of the Patriarchs. Later, Nan-ta Yong went to visit Linji. Afterward, he returned to serve his own master. The master asked, "What have you come for? Yong replied, "To pay my respects to the Master. The master asked, "Have you seen the Master? Yong replied, "I have. The master asked, "How is the Master like? Yong replied, "Like a donkey. The master said, "How is it that you are like a donkey? Yong replied, "Because I carry a load. The master said, "How is it that the donkey carries a load? Yong replied, "The donkey does not know how to speak; I do not know how to carry a load. The master said, "How is it that you do not know how to carry a load? Yong replied, "If I knew how to carry a load, I would not be carrying this load. The master said, "How is it that the donkey does not know how to speak? Yong replied, "If the donkey knew how to speak, it would not be a donkey. The master said, "How is it that you are not a donkey? Yong replied, "If I were a donkey, I would not be here before the Master. The master said, "How is it that you are not here before me? Yong replied, "If I were here before the Master, I would not be seeing the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not see the Master? Yong replied, "If I saw the Master, I would not be seeing the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not see the Master? Yong replied, "The Master is like space; how can one see space? The master said, "How is it that space is like the Master? Yong replied, "Space has no form; the Master has no form. The master said, "How is it that you have no form? Yong replied, "If I had a form, I would not be able to respond to the Master. The master said, "How is it that you cannot respond to the Master? Yong replied, "If I could respond to the Master, I would not be responding to the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not respond to the Master? Yong replied, "If I responded to the Master, I would not be responding to the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not respond to the Master? Yong replied, "If I responded to the Master, I would be a donkey. The master said, "How is it that you are a donkey? Yong replied, "If I were a donkey, I would not be able to answer the Master. The master said, "How is it that you cannot answer the Master? Yong replied, "If I could answer the Master, I would not be answering the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not answer the Master? Yong replied, "If I answered the Master, I would be answering the Master. The master said, "How is it that you answer the Master? Yong replied, "If I answered the Master, I would not be answering the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not answer the Master? The master said, "How is it that you cannot answer the Master? Yong replied, "If I could answer the Master, I would not be answering the Master. The master said, "How is it that you do not answer the Master? Yong replied, "If I answered the Master, I would be answering the Master. The master said, "How is it that you answer the Master?
