"Venerable Sir, I see that the Upādhyāya does not resemble the Buddha either. The Master said, "If he does not resemble the Buddha, what does he resemble?
Yong said, "If there were anything to which he resembled, how would he differ from a donkey? The Master was greatly surprised and said, "Both the ordinary and the sage are forgotten;

when affective attachments are exhausted, the true essence is revealed. For twenty years I have tested people with this, yet none have reached a definitive realization. You may take charge of this. The Master [said] every time...
Pointing his finger at the man, he said, "This child is a flesh-body Buddha.
The eulogy says:
A pearl from the dragon palace; a cub of the venomous dragon.
In the tenth month, he was born from the belly of a serpent; A single pearl fell, coiled by a dragon, as it turned and rolled forward.
With palms joined before him, he grasped the sharp edge of the single transmission that points upward;
Exhausting all thought, he returned to the source, Pressing out the inexhaustible flames of spiritual brilliance.
The second seat at Tuṣita preaches the Dharma; The sound of the mallet strikes, and souls flee in terror.
In the South Mountains, many gather thatch grass; They pull up their spades—when have they ever dreamed of the Way and its Virtue?
A crow carries a persimmon; sitting upon a flat rock, they share it.
Life and death reside in a word; the white rat shifts, yet the Silver Terrace remains unchanged.
He burned away all the circular diagrams, leaving Tanzhou in bitter frustration.
When the Master encountered this little Śākyamuni, he was smeared by the barbarian monk right before his face.
He called out to the śrāmaṇera, saying, "Seal the incense and understand the Zen of the Patriarchs.
How does this compare to a donkey leading [the way]? Nan-ta drew forth his "Blowing-Off-Hair" sword, a sight that only brings him loathing.
Yet, in this matter, we allow only the father and son of that house to know it. Nevertheless, throughout the ages, this sublime legacy remains—though even the Buddha’s hand cannot reach it.
It is likewise difficult to conceal.

Chan Master Yong of the Southern Pagoda, whose name was Guangyong, was a successor of Yangshan. He was a native of Fengcheng and the son of the Zhang family. On the evening his mother nursed him, a divine light shone forth.
The horses in the stables were all startled; consequently, he named it Guangyong (Surging Light). From his youth, he was brilliant and quick-witted.

He relied upon Mount Yangshan for his tonsure and ordination, where he realized the Great Matter. A monk asked, "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; does Mañjuśrī have a teacher? The Master said:
When a monk encountered him on occasion, he asked, "What is Mañjuśrī? The Master held up his whisk. The monk said, "Is it not just this?
The Master lowered the whisk. The monk asked, "What is the single phrase of wondrous function? The Master said, "Water reaches the ditch; the channel is formed.
The monk asked, "Where does the True Buddha dwell? The Master said, "Without form beneath a word; nor is it elsewhere."
While at Chushi Qinghua, during a formal inquiry session, [Changsha] asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Ezhou. [Changsha] asked, "What is the name of the Governor of Ezhou?
He replied, "I dare not offend him while under his jurisdiction. [Changsha] said, "In this place, one does not even fear that. He replied, "A great man—why must we test one another?
The Master laughed heartily and subsequently granted him certification. This was recorded as the "Great Chan Buddha" beneath Jiyun Peak in the *Fozu Tongji*.
Fully recorded.
The encomium says:
Light ascends from the milk-chamber; The sword is hidden in Fengcheng.
Lightning overturns the sky and the abyss, the dragon rouses from its hibernation; The colt falls to the ground and the stallion herd is startled.
Visiting Linji, life and death were like a dream from yesterday;
Meeting Yangshan, both ordinary and holy are forgotten.
Suddenly, he was greatly startled; the strange man before him pointed and said, "The Buddha of Flesh and Bone!
With a broad smile, he knew that the transformation had ended and dared not presume to touch the name of the Lord.
Only the True and Constant remained revealed, like the moon appearing when the clouds have gathered.
Fully manifesting essence and function, it is like water reaching the channel;
The shadow of Nanta’s pagoda—Mañjuśrī mistakenly raises his whisk;
Beneath Jiyun Peak—Mahākāśyapa erroneously calls out, "Elder Brother!"
Once again, I examine the mirror of Dongping: for twenty years, dust has filled my face.
Laughing, I test the eyes of men; though the eyes are blind and devoid of pupils, there is no form beneath words.
Thus, it is certainly not found elsewhere. Yet, as for the dwelling place of the True Buddha, all skillful means are exhausted.
It is ultimately difficult to clarify.
Chan Master Bajiao Qing, whose dharma name was Huiqing, was a native of Silla who succeeded Nanta. The Master said to the assembly: "When I was eighteen, I arrived at..."
Yangshan saw Nantang ascend the hall and said, "If you people here are true men, as soon as you emerge from your mother’s womb, you should be able to let out a lion’s roar;
do you understand? At these words, Yangshan found rest in body and mind and remained there for five years.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "If you have a staff, I will give you a staff; if you have no staff..."
“Staff-bearer! I shall take away your staff,” he said. A monk asked, “What is the school of Deva? The Master said, “The red banner is on the left.
A monk asked, “What is the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West? The Master said, “Alone and desolate, crossing the river in the dark.
A monk asked, “When a thief comes, one must strike; when a guest comes, one must welcome them. But what if both guest and thief arrive at once? The Master said:
[The Master] said: "Inside the house there is a pair of worn-out straw sandals. [The monk] asked: "As for those worn-out straw sandals, are they still fit for use? The Master said:
"If you take them with you, it will be ominous in front and inauspicious behind. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said:
"It is like a person walking along who suddenly encounters a precipice ten thousand feet deep ahead, while a wild fire presses from behind, and thorny brambles on both sides. If he moves forward..."
Falling into pits or down into ditches; if you retreat backward, wild fires will burn your body; if you turn to the side, you will again be obstructed by thorny thickets.
At such a time, how can you avoid this? If you can avoid it, you must possess a way to emerge from this situation.
"If you cannot avoid it, you are a corpse fallen from its body. A monk asked, "I do not ask about two heads or three heads; I beg the Master to point directly to my original face.
The Master sat silently and upright. The monk asked, "What is the 'blow-off-hair sword'? He replied, "Step forward three paces.
The monk asked, "And as for one who uses it? He replied, "Step back three paces. The monk asked, "When one hides the body within the Big Dipper..."
"What? he asked. [The monk] said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one. He asked, "Do you understand? [The monk] said, "I do not understand. He said, "One, two, three, four, five. Thus he questioned him.
"How was it before the ancient Buddhas had appeared? He replied, "The root of a thousand-year-old eggplant.
"How was it after they had appeared? He replied, "The eyes of Vajrapāṇi. After Chengtian Que had attained enlightenment while under the master’s guidance, a monk asked him:
"When the myriad sins are like frost and dew, and the sun of wisdom is able to dispel them—what then? Que replied: "Deep night rain on the courtyard terrace; the pavilions..."
Jingshi Zhong said, "For what reason does one receive the retribution oneself when causes and conditions meet?
Que said, "The pen manages to write; the tongue understands how to speak."
The eulogy says:
Before his feet had even stepped onto the gunwale, he traveled throughout the various patriarchs of the Great Tang;
he established the school of Deva, snatched back the red banner from the non-Buddhists, and returned.
Answering the meaning of the Westward Journey: Bodhidharma crossed the river and departed;
his staff granted and withheld throughout his life. Never once did he strike out the Jade Qilin;
born from the mother’s womb for ten months, When has it ever roared as a golden lion?
Misfortune ahead and no good fortune behind; Torn straw sandals, difficult to find when one wishes to wear them.
The fire recedes while you advance into a deep pit; In a forest of thorns, where is there a path to escape?
A person from Silla finds it hard to discern the language; At the Imperial Capital, it is truly "ding-ding."
Stably concealed within the Northern Dipper, One, two, three, four, five—two mouths and one tongueless.
Behold the stone lock opened at the brook’s edge, both ends swaying;
Poisonous filth enters deep into the heart, Causing the Heavenly Supporter to vomit it forth from the courtyard dais amidst the midnight rain.
Silently sitting upright—the face of original nature is not found on two heads.
How does the one who employs it act? Is the "blowing-feather" sword restricted by three paces?
Green surpasses the indigo; blue surpasses the indigo. Truly, the descendants of Muzhou and Yangshan soar like phoenixes and dance like cranes.
Chan Master Bazhao Che (also known as Jiche) was a native of Guangxi. He succeeded Bazhao Qing. Initially, he visited Fengxue, who asked him, "What is the True Dharma Eye?
He replied, "A clay pellet. Fengxue marveled at this. Later, he studied under Bazhao, who was giving a formal lecture and said:
"Two mouths, neither with a tongue—this is my fundamental principle. [The monk] attained great enlightenment. A monk asked, "What is the place of ultimate depth?
He replied, "The stone man opens the stone door; the stone locks shake at both ends. He asked, "What is the scene by the stream?
He replied, "There are mountains and there is water. He asked, "When all is silent and without reliance, what then? He replied, "That is not yet within the portion of a true monk."
[The Master] said: "What is the matter regarding the portion of the monks? [He] replied: "When one wishes to walk, one walks; when one wishes to sit, one sits. He asked:

"If there is a person who neither abandons birth-and-death nor realizes nirvana, will you still take him up and carry him? [The Master] said: "I do not take him up and carry him. [The questioner] said: "Why not?"
"Why do you not carry it? He replied, "At the riverside, I roughly recognized what is good and what is bad. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, when the Brahma King requested the Tathāgata to turn the Wheel of the Dharma, the Tathāgata did not stop there;
he humbled his own school’s style and taught according to the capacities of beings. Thus, the names of the Three Vehicles have been circulated throughout heaven and earth until the present day."

To glorify and propagate [the Dharma] so that it does not fall is a matter of the ancestral gate; yet, compared to the vast difference between heaven and earth, those of the highest capacity transcend this suddenly without distinction.
What is the single phrase of total integration? Is there anyone who can speak it? If you can, [then you have it].

One who possesses the eye of study may find that, even if they do not attain the Way, heaven is vast and earth is narrow. To the assembly: When there is no film in the eye, there are no flowers in the sky;
as the water rises, the boat floats higher; with much mud, the Buddha grows larger. Do not bring questions here; I have no answers. Do you understand?
The answer lies within the question; the response resides within the inquiry. As the verse says: "The essential meaning of the plantain tree does not hang upon lips or teeth;
the wooden child sings in harmony, and the stone woman leans her ear."
The commentary says:
A human face with a serpent’s tail; A sharp blade hidden within honey.
Whether walking or sitting, one seeks only to boast and exaggerate; Even those who discern good from evil cannot believe such a person.
A lump of clay serves as the Eye of the True Dharma; how could one know that Old Fengxue wraps thorns and eggplant roots in cotton?
He responds to the prompt of the Ancient Buddha; he does not study the "interfusion" verses of the former Bajiao, such as "silk wrapping a stone," where the ground is narrow yet the sky is vast.
Facing the stream, the scenery is such that the mountains are deep and the waters are azure.
When meeting a monk who asks about nirvana and birth-and-death, If you wish to lead him, wait for a donkey’s year.
To disparage Gautama’s teachings of sudden and gradual, partial and complete, Is to bend the ancestral wind; there will never be an end to it.
The meaning of the Westward Transmission— The sweat of the skin-tight robe has soaked through a thousand layers.
Matters of the Zen School: Three feet of mud beneath one's heels;
the wooden boy sings and the stone man listens. Who would deign to utter the essential principle?
When there is no film before the eyes, there are no flowers in the sky. Do not trouble yourself to bring forth idle words.
Everyone says that at Mount Míu, after five generations, the lineage reached the Master [Dōgen] and then fell silent, with no further transmission.
Little do they realize that the gate and walls of ten-thousand-fathom height are like silver mountains and iron cliffs for those who attempt to climb them.
The lineage of the Guiyang and Yangqi schools reached its fifth generation at this point.
As for the Qingliang Fayan school, there was the Chan Master Fayan.
The Master’s name was Wenyi. He was the son of the Lu family from Yuhang. Having shaved his head, he went to Vinaya Master Jue of Kaiyuan Temple to receive full ordination.

When Jue flourished in his propagation of the Dharma at Siming, the Master went there to study the *vinaya*. He was skilled in literary composition, and Jue marveled at him, declaring him to be the "Yan Hui and Zixia" of our school.
Once the profound mechanism [of his awakening] was triggered, he cast aside all miscellaneous affairs and, shaking his mendicant staff, traveled southward until he reached...

In Fuzhou, he first met Changqing, but attained no realization. Together with Jìn and Xiū, he planned to travel beyond the lakes. Once they had set out, they encountered rain and rested briefly at Dizang Temple west of the city.
Entering the hall, he saw Dizang sitting by a charcoal brazier. He asked the Master, "Where are you going on this journey?
Dizang replied, "I am traveling as a pilgrim. He asked, "What is the matter of traveling as a pilgrim? Dizang said, "I do not know. He remarked, "Not knowing is most intimate."
The three men were sitting by a fire. They began to recite the *Zhaolun* (Treatise by Sengzhao), arriving at the passage concerning how "heaven and earth share the same root as I.
Zang then asked, "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as oneself, or are they different? Xiu replied, "They are the same. Zang held up two fingers and stared at them intently.
The two of them rose and departed as the rain cleared. As they were leaving, Xuefeng saw them off and asked, "Upādhyāya, you usually say that the three realms are mind-only.
Now, point to this stone in the courtyard and tell me: does it reside within the mind, or does it reside outside the mind? The Master said, "It resides within the mind.
Xuefeng said, "What kind of reason would a traveling monk have for placing a block of stone upon his head? The Master [remained silent].
At a loss for a reply, he finally released Bao, and they both sought definitive resolution. After nearly a month, Bao presented his insights and expounded upon the principles.
Baizhang said, "The Buddha-dharma is not like this. Bao replied, "I have reached a point here where my words are exhausted and my reasoning has run out. Baizhang said:
When it comes to the Buddha-dharma, all views are already established. The Master attained great enlightenment and emerged into the world at Chongshou Temple in Linchuan.
One day, while offering incense before the ancestral shrine, he was asked by the monk Zifang: "Master, you have long been close to Changqing, yet you have instead inherited Dizang. Why is that?
The Master replied, "Because [Zifang] does not understand Changqing’s teaching that 'within the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Zifang then raised his whisk to demonstrate.

The Master said, "Do you negate the myriad phenomena, or do you not negate the myriad phenomena? Fang replied, "I do not negate the myriad phenomena. The Master said, "Then your body is revealed alone. Fang replied, "I negate the myriad phenomena.

The Master said, "Within the myriad phenomena, your body is revealed. At this, Fang awakened to the essential meaning. Later, as two monks were entering for an audience, the Master pointed to the curtain.
The two monks both went to roll it up. The Master said, "One has gained, and one has lost. He then addressed the assembly, saying: [The text continues with the Master's further instructions.]

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all is brilliantly clear, without so much as a single thread of hair. If there were a single thread of hair, it would simply be that single thread of hair.
When Baoyuan of Jinling first visited Qingfeng, he asked, "What is the student’s own self?

Qingfeng replied, "The child of the fire element (Bingding) comes seeking fire. Not attaining realization, he went to see you, Master. You asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Qingfeng."
The Master asked, "What words did Qingfeng say? [The monk] then related the previous story.
The Master said, "How do you understand this, Senior Monk? He replied, "Bing and Ding belong to fire; yet to seek fire further is like seeking oneself by means of oneself.
The Master said, "Even if you understand it thus, how can that suffice? He asked, "I have understood it only in this way; I do not know how the Master understands it. The Master said:
"You ask me; I shall tell you. He then repeated the previous question. The Master said, "A child of the Bing-Ding trigram comes seeking fire.

At this, the monk was enlightened. A monk asked, "What is the student's single scroll of scripture? The Master said, "The title is clear. While the Master was discussing the Way with King Li, they were looking at peonies.
The King commanded him to compose a verse on the spot, and he immediately said: "Clad in coarse wool, facing a fragrant thicket," "The spring breeze blows through the blossoms."
"Since time immemorial, our paths have been different. My hair has turned white from this day forward; the flowers were red last year. Their brilliance follows the morning dew;
their fragrance pursues the evening breeze. Why wait for them to wither and fall before one realizes they are empty? Upon hearing this, the King attained awakening. The Master then spoke a verse:
"The warbling of the hidden birds is like the sound of flutes; The willows sway, their golden threads long. The clouds return and the mountain valleys are still; The wind carries [the scent]..."

The fragrance of apricot blossoms fills the air; throughout the long day, I sit in serene detachment. With a clarified mind, ten thousand anxieties are forgotten. I wish to speak, yet words fail me. It is best to deliberate beneath the trees.
To speak of the "Gate of Illumination through the Hundred Dharmas" is to address the fundamental framework of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The Eulogy says:
In youth he manifested profound faculties; Traveling everywhere in search, he cast aside the roots of the Hīnayāna and left his teacher.
When an evil adversary encounters Master Chen, a single stone is placed within his square inch of mind; yet even when shattering it upon the immediate occasion, he still lingers in subtle refinement.
Within the ten thousand phenomena, his whole body is revealed; though he exerts all his strength to support it, it remains muddled and crude.
Pointing at two monks who roll up the curtain and depart, gain and loss remain unclear;
examining the lad as he comes seeking fire, right and wrong are difficult to settle.
Like the words of a solitary bird in the bamboo grove, the spirit of the mountain forest is a distinct standard of character.
Clad in coarse wool, facing fragrant clusters; A poem on peonies, who has stolen its model?
It is but a single drop from the Cao River source; Insects gnawing wood, accidentally forming patterns.
For those who seek learning, it is a single scroll of scripture; Flies boring through paper, utterly devoid of direction.
Mind-only, consciousness-only; at the road of Stonehead City, a thousand differences are arrayed.
No dharmas, no person; atop Tongxuan Peak, clouds span across layered ridges.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all is bright and clear, without so much as a single thread. Arriving here, the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas.
One should simply collect and preserve [the teachings].
National Teacher Shao of Tiantai, whose dharma name was Deshao, was a successor of Fayan. He was the son of the Chen family of Longquan in Chuzhou. In his youth, he relied upon Longgui Temple.
Dudu received the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He went to visit Longya and asked, "Why can one not approach the Most Honored One who is so majestic?
Longya said, "It is like fire meeting fire. The Master said, "What if water were to suddenly come upon it?
Longya said, "You do not understand my words. He asked again, "Heaven does not cover it; earth does not support it. What is the principle of this? Longya said, "It is fitting."
The Master did not understand the meaning and requested further instruction. Layā said, "Dharma Teacher, you will understand it yourself in the future.

Later, while bathing at Tongxuan Peak, the Master suddenly attained realization. He then burned incense, faced toward Longya, and prostrated, saying, "If he had told me this back then, I certainly would have scolded him.
Upon meeting Shushan, he asked, "Who is the one who [surrounds] a hundred times and a thousand layers?"

Jingjie said, "I twist straw ropes on the left to bind the sons of ghosts. Jingshan said, "It does not fall within the categories of past or present; please explain this for me. Jingjie said, "I will not speak. Jingshan asked, "Why do you not speak?
Jingjie said, "Within this, existence and non-existence cannot be distinguished. Jingshan said, "Master, you have now spoken well. Jingshan was struck with awe by this.
In this manner, he studied under fifty-four teachers of the Dharma. Later, he visited Fayan; upon seeing him, Fayan held him in high esteem.

As for this, Master [Zhaozhou] grew weary of formal inquiries and merely followed the assembly. One day, when Master Xueyan was ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is a single drop of water from the Cao source?
Xueyan replied, "It is a single drop of water from the Cao source. Thereupon, the Master attained great enlightenment beneath the seat.
He then rolled his eyes upward in a stare of disdain. The Eye said, "In the future, you shall become a teacher to the king, causing the Way of the Patriarchs to shine with great brilliance;
I am not your equal. From that time on, he resolved all divergent doctrines from various quarters and the profound keys of antiquity and the present, leaving behind no trace of hesitation.

In the first year of the Qiandao era, King Zhongyi succeeded to the throne and dispatched an envoy to welcome him, whereupon he performed the rites of a disciple toward his master. He addressed the assembly, saying:
The skillful means of the ancient sages are like the sands of the Ganges. The Patriarch said, "It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is your mind that moves.
This is the unsurpassed heart-seal and the most subtle Dharma-gate. We who call ourselves disciples under the Patriarch’s gate—how should we understand the Patriarch’s meaning?
If you say the wind and banner do not move, yet your own mind is deludedly moving; if you say [the wind] is not being stirred...
Regarding the "banner," this refers generally to the location where the wind and banner meet. If you ask, "What is it at the place where the wind and banner move?

and if you say that one clarifies the mind by relying on an object, yet need not recognize the object itself; or if you say that form is emptiness; or if you say that it is not the wind or the banner that moves—these must be understood with subtle penetration.
Such understandings have no connection whatsoever with the intent of the Patriarch. Since such interpretations are not permitted, O Venerable Elders...

One should certainly know this. If one attains awakening here, what dharma-gate would not be clarified? Though there are hundreds of thousands of expedient means of the Buddhas, they will all be thoroughly understood at once.
If it is not like this, even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will merely exhaust oneself in vain;
such a thing is impossible. While residing on Tongxuan Peak, he composed a verse which says: "At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is not of this human world. Outside the mind, there is no dharma."
With green mountains filling his eyes, he heard them and said: "This single verse alone can revive my school. He addressed the assembly: "The ancients said:
'If there is one dharma lacking, it is not the Dharmakāya; if there is one dharma in excess, it is not the Dharmakāya;
if there is even a single dharma present, it is not the Dharmakāya; if there is not even a single dharma present, it is not the Dharmakāya. This is the true essence of Prajñā."
Furthermore, it is said: "All questions and answers are like the meeting of needle points; there is not the slightest discrepancy.
No matter is unpenetrated, and no principle is incomplete. This is truly because all speech and all samādhis—whether horizontal or vertical, deep or shallow—are [thus]."
"Manifestation and concealment, coming and going—these are the gateways to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas. It is simply a matter of verifying them right now, at this very moment.

Be careful. He further said: "When speech issues forth, it is not sound; when form appears before one, it is not a thing. Only then does one realize that all under heaven is at peace, and that the Great King enjoys long life."
[The Master] had been standing for a long time. A monk asked, "An ancient worthy said: 'To ascend to heaven one does not borrow a ladder; throughout the world there is no path to walk.
What is 'ascending to heaven without borrowing a ladder'? The Master said, "Not leaving behind even a hair's breadth of ground.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'throughout the world there is no path to walk'? The Master said, "What did I just say to you? [Another] asked, "The Precious Seal of the Dharma-Eye was personally transmitted by the Master. Has it not?"
"Examine this single assembly today: to whom is it entrusted? The Master said: "The drum thuds; struck at one end, it rings at both. He asked: "An ancient said:
'Striking the void, it rings *ko-ko*. Stone men and wooden men respond in unison. In the sixth month, snow falls in profusion.
This is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment (*Mahāpariniṣpanna-vijñapti*). What is the striking of the void?"
The Master said, "A child from Mount Kunlun wears iron trousers; with every stroke of a staff, he takes a step.

He continued, "If that is so, then the stone man and the wooden man both respond in unison. The Master asked, "Do you hear them? [Another] asked, "When Kāśyapa held Śākyamuni’s robe of sixteen feet..."
"Waiting for Maitreya’s descent at Mount Jizu, one takes a robe of sixteen feet and drapes it over a body of a thousand feet;

the fit is exactly right. Now, if Śākyamuni’s body is sixteen feet tall and Maitreya’s body is a thousand feet tall, does this mean that Śākyamuni’s body is understood to be short, or that the robe is understood to be long?
The Master said, "You have understood it correctly. Ming then shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said:
"You little son! If I, this mountain monk, were unable to answer your question, there would surely be karmic consequences.
If you were not [as you claim], I would have seen it through. The next day, Ming returned and vomited blood. Master Fuguang urged him, saying, "Go quickly and repent!
When Ming arrived at the abbot’s quarters, he wept bitterly and said, "I pray that the Master will show compassion and grant me permission to repent. [Fuguang] replied, "It is like a person..."
He fell to the ground. Rising from the ground, [the Master] said, "I never taught you how to rise or fall.

Ming then said, "If you grant that I may repent and serve you for the rest of my life," the Master spoke these words on his behalf: "The Way of Buddha after Buddha is equal; yet there is high and low.
Śākyamuni and Maitreya are like a seal pressing into clay. There is one who transmits the Tiantai teachings and principles named Ji; he is Luoxi. He spoke thus repeatedly.
The Master said, "The teachings of the Wise One have existed for many ages; I fear they have been largely lost over time. Now, the kingdom of Silla possesses them in their entirety.
Were it not for the compassionate power of the Venerable Monk, who else could have brought them here?
Upon hearing this from the King, the Master dispatched envoys across the sea to transcribe the texts, returning with them complete. To this day, they flourish throughout the world.
The eulogy says:
When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, one walks alone through heaven and earth;
ascending to heaven without borrowing a ladder, there is no path anywhere on the ground.
The spark from striking flint shatters the Stonehead Citadel;
Gripping the Dragon Spring sword, one laughs as the dragon returns to the temple.
Heaven covers and earth sustains all, yet Longya painfully offers moldy rice to the idle gods.
A hundred circuits and a thousand layers, draped over the sparse mountains like twisted thorn-ropes;
binding the ghost-child, it moves between concealment and manifestation, clarifying the true reality of all Buddhas.

Yet, for the most part, it is coarse and incomplete, lacking the fullness of speech regarding existence and non-existence; in explaining the true principle of Prajñā, it cannot help but be crude and rough.
This is a single drop from the source of Cao; awakening to the mysterious mechanism, one takes a pea for a pearl.
Pointing to the profound mystery, mountains fill the eye; arising within our school, one turns a sweet melon into a bitter gourd.
A guest beneath the Gate of the Patriarchs, he discerns the wind and the banner, trailing water and mud.
The Great King of Long Life casts aside external sounds and forms, scattering sand and dust;
he has attained the Dharma-eye and the personally transmitted precious seal.
The drum of tanned hide resounds from both ends as the wooden man strikes it against the void; the child of Kunlun wears iron trousers.
He lamented that the teachings of Nanyue and Tiantai were fading away, so he traveled to Silla to copy out the scriptures and bring them back for discussion.
He examined the relative lengths of the robes worn by Śākyamuni and Maitreya, and exhorted the monks who promoted these teachings to cease their hemorrhaging of blood.

He resolved various divergent doctrines from all quarters; his profound keys to the past and present were decisive and left no lingering traces. Thus, he was not mistaken in being the sole authority for the nation.
The Master’s fame resounded throughout the world.

Chan Master Yongming Qiao, whose name was Yanshou, was a successor of National Teacher Shao. He was the son of the Wang family of Yuhang; from his youth, he knew how to revere the Buddha-vehicle. Once—

He wore a ceremonial cap and abstained from pungent vegetables, meat, and wine, eating but one meal per day. He recited the seven lines of the *Lotus Sūtra* with such devotion that he moved a flock of sheep to kneel and listen.
At the age of twenty-eight, he served as the military commander of Huating, at which time Chan Master Cuoyan moved his residence to Longce Monastery.

He extensively propagated the profound transformation [of the Dharma]. The Master subsequently sought ordination and petitioned the court; King Wenmu granted his wish, and he took Chan as his teacher.

He performed manual labor to provide for the community, wearing nothing but a single cotton robe. Later, he went to Mount Tianzhu on Mount Tiantai, where he practiced meditative concentration for ninety days.

A bird resembling a *chīyàn* (a small sparrow) nested within the folds of his robes. When he went to pay his respects to the National Teacher, he was immediately recognized and held in high esteem upon their first meeting.
He secretly transmitted the profound essence to him and further said to the Master, "You have a karmic affinity with the Commander-in-Chief;
one day you shall perform great Buddhist work. It is a pity that I shall not live to see it. Initially residing at Xuedou, he ascended the hall and said:

"At this place, Xuedou, there is a torrential waterfall a thousand fathoms deep, where not even a speck of dust can rest. There are wondrous cliffs ten thousand cubits high, where there is no place to set foot. You people of all—where will you turn?"
He was in a state of progress. A monk asked, "How does one tread upon the single path of Xuedou? He replied, "Step by step, cold flowers form; word by word, the bottom is ice. He also spoke a verse:
"The lone monkey’s cry drops the moon from the central cliff; The wild guest’s chant ends as the midnight lamp fades.
Who attains the meaning of this scene at this moment? A meditation monk sitting deep within the white clouds. In the first year of the Jianlong era, Zhongyi...
The King invited him to enter Lingyin Monastery, where he served as the first abbot. The following year, he was invited to reside at Yongming, serving as the second abbot.

A monk asked, "What is the essential meaning of Yongming? He replied, "Add more incense. The monk said, "Thank you for the instruction. He [the Master] said, "I am glad there is no connection [between us]. There is a verse that says:
If you wish to know the meaning of Yongming, Look at the lake before the gate. When the sun shines upon it, its radiance is bright.
"Birth. When the wind comes, waves arise. A monk asked, "I have been at Yongming for a long time;
why do I not understand the house style of Yongming? The Master said, "Understand it where you do not understand. The monk asked, "How can one understand where one does not understand?

The Master said, "An elephant calf born from an ox's womb; red dust rising from the azure sea. The Master composed the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Source-Mirror) in one hundred fascicles, which was disseminated beyond the seas. High...
The King of Koryŏ, having reviewed the Master’s teachings, dispatched an envoy bearing a letter to express his status as a disciple.

He further sent thirty-six monks to inquire about the Way, all of whom received the seal of transmission. They subsequently returned to their home country, each transforming the region they inhabited.
On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of Gaebō, he manifested parinirvāṇa at Jingci Monastery. His stūpa was enshrined at Daci Mountain.
The eulogy says:
Once he has emerged from his concealment, his wind-signal is utterly distinct;
having abandoned his post as a town commander at Huating, he now wears a precious sword at his waist.
Relying on the old monk Longce, his body clad in hempen robes, he recited the Lotus Sūtra with seven lines flowing simultaneously.
Moved by this, a flock of sheep knelt to listen at the edge of his seat;
after practicing Great Samādhi for three months, he finally returned, finding a swallow’s nest nestled within the folds of his robe.
Tiantai attained the essential meaning from a single phrase; In every thought-moment, illusory conditions are empty.
At Milk Peak, he pointed out the one path to the profound mystery;
With every step, cold flowers form upon a thousand-fathom waterfall that never ceases, not even for a speck of dust. Probing the water with a staff, the mark left is deep.
Extraordinary cliffs ten thousand fathoms high, utterly beyond climbing; gazing at the precipice, the path of the mind is cut off.
A calf born from a cow’s womb, an elephant’s offspring—these are shown with extreme clarity.
Red dust rises from the azure sea; the family tradition is fully revealed once more.
Reclining on a bed of sorrel, he calls back his pure dreams; The wild guest finishes his verse by the midnight lamp.
Leaning against a rush-cushion, he sits amidst the severed white clouds; A solitary monkey’s cry drops the moon from the central crag.
He has authored over one hundred volumes of the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), Turning iron into gold.
Sealing thirty-six monks of Goryeo—proving the tortoise to be a turtle, their secret practice and subtle function are difficult even for the Buddha-eye to discern.
A true banner of diligence, before the Peak of the Sun of Wisdom, it shall endure for a hundred generations;
its radiance shines forth brilliantly.

Regarding the Dharma-eye that reaches back through the three periods of time: although the Master certified thirty-six monks from Goryeo, their names and karmic encounters are not recorded in the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp). Therefore, I shall not elaborate further on them here.
The end of the *Zhengzong zan* (Praise of the True Lineage).
Written with incense burning and prostrating with bowed head, by the junior disciple Ju Jing at Lufeng.
